#3039. Shoe Station (SHOE) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management is reversing store rebannering after a sharp traffic-driven sales slump.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:12PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Shoe Station (SHOE -18.39%) reported revisions to its retail operations following a quarter where comparable store sales declined 5.1%. Management reported that the company will reverse previous rebannering efforts by returning 27 locations to the Rogan's banner and approximately 75% of other rebannered stores to the Shoe Carnival name. The company stated that it will also invest $4 million to revert 74 stores to their original angled floor layouts to address customer feedback regarding shoppability. Despite these challenges, management reported that early fourth quarter traffic and sales have improved as seasonal weather drove demand for boots.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Shoe Station Group's Third Quarter Fiscal 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today's conference call is being recorded and is also being broadcast via webcast. Any unauthorized reproduction or rebroadcast of any portion of this call is expressly prohibited. Management's remarks today contain forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause the company's actual results to be materially different from those projected in such statements. Forward-looking statements should also be considered in conjunction with the discussion of risk factors included in the company's SEC filings and today's earnings press release. Investors are cautioned not to place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which speak only as of today's date.

The company undertakes no obligation to update or revise the forward-looking statements discussed on today's conference call or contained in today's earnings press release to reflect future events or developments, except as required by law. Management's remarks today will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliations of those measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in today's earnings press release. I will now turn the conference over to Mr. Cliff Sifford, Interim President and Chief Executive Officer of Shoe Station Group for opening remarks. Mr. Sifford, you may begin.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. With me on the call are Kerry Jackson, our Chief Financial Officer; Tanya E. Gordon, our Chief Merchandising Officer; and Marc Chilton, our Chief Operating Officer. Tanya and Marc are both available to take your questions during the Q&A portion of the call. Our third quarter results were below the expectations we shared with you in September. This morning, I will cover what happened in the quarter, what our customers are telling us and the work we have completed and still have ahead of us across our three groups of stores, Shoe Carnival, Shoe Station and our Rogan's stores, which have been rebannered to Shoe Station at Rogan's.

That includes two strategic decisions we have made about our rebannered stores, which I will describe in detail. Kerry will then take you through the financials and our updated outlook. Comparable store sales declined 5.1% in the quarter, and the quarter had two distinct parts. In fiscal August, during back-to-school, comparable store sales declined 2.7%, a meaningful improvement from the second quarter. When we spoke in September, we expected the third quarter to be approximately flat depending on when the weather turned. Unfortunately, once the need for back-to-school shoes dissipated, a combination of macroeconomic issues, including higher gas prices and warmer-than-expected weather across all regions combined to once again reduce the traffic in our stores.

In addition to that, our own advertising was lighter in September and October than a year ago because we weighted our second half spending toward the holiday season. As a result, our comparable store sales declined approximately 7% each month. E-commerce growth moderated significantly from the second quarter. The softness was broad-based as we experienced this across all banners, and the footwear marketplace remained highly promotional throughout the quarter. In early November, as fuel prices begin to drop, we began to see an improvement in our store traffic and as traffic improved, sales also improved. More on that later. The pattern underlying our sales results is consistent with what we described last quarter.

Store conversion improved again by almost a full point for the company with improvement in all banners. Customers who came into our stores bought. What declined was traffic. Traffic was weakest in our rebannered stores, and that fact is the starting point for the decisions I will describe in a few minutes. Since August, our new Chief Marketing Officer, Tracy Dick and her team have been studying how customers view our two largest banners, Shoe Station and Shoe Carnival. That work combined formal customer research with direct feedback from our store managers who hear from customers every day. I'll come back to what we learned.

Let me turn to the product because the category results show where the assortment work is taking hold and where we still have work to do. Adult athletic, our largest business at roughly 38% of sales, declined low single digits for the quarter. Men's athletic increased low single digits with running up mid-single digits and basketball up high single digits. Women's athletic declined high single digits with running down mid-single digits and the fashion athletic styles down considerably more. Women's nonathletic declined high single digits. Within that, due to the very warm September and October, sandals increased mid-single digits and casuals were approximately flat, while women's sport casuals were down double digit and accounted for most of the decrease.

Men's nonathletic declined mid-single digits with casuals down double digits and work boots up low single digits. Children's shoes declined mid-single digits. Children's nonathletic was flat, which is progress in a business we intend to own, while children's athletic declined high single digits once back-to-school ended. Boots are the category I ask you to watch. For the full quarter, boots were down low single digits and the trend improved as the season opened. In October, women's boots were approximately flat on a comparable sales basis with average unit retails up high single digits and improved margins.

As a peek into the first few weeks of the fourth quarter, once the weather turned seasonal, women's boots have produced a comparable store increase in the teens. Men's boots increased low single digits in October, led by work boots, which increased high single digits. Customers are responding to newer, better product at higher prices with less promotion. That is what we expected from this assortment and is the most important metric we have going into the fourth quarter. When I returned in February, we set out to address the business store group by store group. It is useful to describe where we stand the same way. The first group is our Shoe Carnival stores.

These stores needed assortments localized to the customer who shops them. This includes the moderate price points that Shoe Carnival shopper expects from us. We also needed to reengage those customers with in-store promotions along with our iconic Spin 'n Win Wheel. These elements are part of what has made Shoe Carnival a fun place to shop, a family tradition and a great shopping experience. That work has been accomplished. What remains is letting the customer know and that is the purpose of our intensified advertising in the fourth quarter, which is designed to drive traffic and invite customers to experience the brand again.

The second group is our Shoe Station stores, which have always been Shoe Station, the 21 stores we acquired and the 12 new stores we have opened. The needs were similar, localized assortment and brand-specific promotions. While much has been accomplished here as well, we still have work to do to further differentiate the Shoe Station assortment and shopping experience from Shoe Carnival, and that work continues. The corrective action plan is in place, and our fourth quarter marketing is designed to drive traffic and invite customers to experience the brand again. The third group is our rebannered stores, and this is where we have reached a different conclusion. We listen to our customers and our store managers.

And as we said on our last call, we analyzed the customer demographics of each rebannered store. We conducted focus groups in many of our large markets. What we learned is clear. Our strategy to merchandise each store based on the customer who shops there is the correct one. The localization of our assortments continue. And in most cases, the right assortment for that customer looks like a Shoe Carnival assortment inside a Shoe Station store. Customers in our focus groups also told us they see the rebanner store as a Shoe Carnival store with a new name. The Shoe Station banner needs to be perceived as an elevated store with an elevated assortment.

And in many of these locations, the demographics and the cotenancy do not support that. Customers also told us that the new store layout is harder to shop. The Shoe Station format uses straight-line shelving, what we call flow. When customers walk in, they see a wall of shoes that limits their view of the product further back in the store. Our loyal customers could not easily find what they came for and new customers could not see the full breadth of the assortment. Based on that, we have made two decisions.

First, during the fourth quarter, we plan to return to shelving in 74 rebannered stores to their original angled aisle layout and reflow the product to make the shopping experience easier and more natural. We have already tested this in two stores. And in both, we have seen favorable customer comments along with improved conversion and sales. We expect this work to cost approximately $4 million and to be completed in the fourth quarter. Second, we plan to return rebannered stores to the original banner where the demographics and cotenancy align with that banner. We currently operate 131 rebannered stores. Of those, 27 are Shoe Station at Rogan's locations, and they will return to operating solely under the Rogan's name.

We are evaluating the remaining 104 stores now and will determine the exact number over the next few weeks. We currently estimate that 75% or more of them will return to the Shoe Carnival banner. Because of the time needed for permits and new signs, we expect these changes to take place in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Let me explain why we believe this is the right course. Many of these stores are in markets where decades of advertising and operating have built brand awareness and loyalty to both Shoe Carnival and Rogan's. In addition, we believe the Shoe Station name is the banner that offers us the best opportunity for long-term growth.

We believe the clear delineation of the two banners allow us to grow both Shoe Station and Shoe Carnival. Shoe Station is the better branded shoe in an accessory business, and Shoe Carnival is a moderate-priced footwear store for the entire family. Rogan's remains an important banner that services the blue-collar worker through its stores and trucks. Shoe Station growth is expected to come from new stores located in higher-income demographic areas of the cities we already serve under the Shoe Carnival banner and new cities where we have not yet opened a Shoe Carnival store. For that strategy to succeed, we cannot continue to operate Shoe Station stores in Shoe Carnival type centers or with Shoe Carnival product assortments.

We entered the holiday season with the strongest boot assortment we have offered in years, localized product in our stores, intensified advertising and comparisons that ease as the quarter progresses. We expect the promotional environment to continue, and our guidance does not assume that it improves. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kerry to review the financials and our updated outlook. Kerry?

W. Kerry Jackson: Thank you, Cliff, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter results were below the expectations underlying the guidance we provided in September on lower sales and lower gross profit margin, and they include a noncash goodwill impairment charge. This morning, I will review the balance sheet, the quarter, our year-to-date results and our updated fiscal 2026 guidance, which we have lowered. I will start with the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $116 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, an increase of $8.4 million compared to the end of the third quarter last year. We recently renewed our $100 million credit facility for an additional five years, and we have no borrowings under it.

During the quarter, we paid our 58th consecutive quarterly dividend and repurchased approximately $10 million of our common stock. Year-to-date, we have returned approximately $31 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Inventory ended the quarter at $421.1 million, down $14.2 million or 3.3% from last year, with inventory per store down 1.4%. We remain on plan for a reduction of approximately $50 million in inventory by fiscal year-end. Net sales in the third quarter were $280.0 million compared to $297.2 million last year, a decline of 5.8%. Comparable store sales declined 5.1%. By month, comparable store sales declined 2.7% in fiscal August and approximately 7% in each of fiscal September and October.

By banner, Shoe Carnival net sales were $180.3 million, representing 64% of total net sales and declined 4.7% with comparable store sales down 3.7%. Shoe Station net sales were $99.3 million or 36% of the total and declined 7.7% with comparable store sales down 7.6%. Comparable e-commerce sales increased 2.1% compared to the growth of 18.8% in the second quarter. Part of that slowdown reflects stronger prior year comparisons and e-commerce softened in September along with our stores. Gross profit margin in the third quarter was 31.9%, a decrease of 570 basis points from last year.

Merchandise margin decreased 480 basis points and buying, distribution and occupancy costs reduced gross profit margin by 90 basis points, primarily from deleverage on the lower sales base. The drivers of the merchandise margin decline are the same three we described last quarter. First, the third quarter of last year included a temporary benefit from raising retail prices ahead of tariff-related cost increases, which did not repeat. Second, we priced competitively in a promotional marketplace. And third, we continued to liquidate aged and excess inventory. The rate of decline moderated from the second quarter when merchandise margin decreased 630 basis points.

One additional item, we received approximately $660,000 of tariff refunds during the third quarter, which were recorded as a reduction in cost of sales. SG&A in the third quarter was $87.0 million, a decrease of $6.2 million from last year, driven by lower selling costs, including advertising and other rebanner-related expenses as well as lower performance-based compensation. As a percentage of net sales, SG&A was 31.1% compared to 31.3% last year. On advertising, our spending in the third quarter was below last year. Our second half advertising is weighted toward the holiday season, and we expect fourth quarter advertising to be above last year.

We recorded a noncash goodwill impairment charge of $18.0 million in the quarter, which represents all the goodwill on our balance sheet. The charge reflects our recent financial performance and updated expectations for the business. It is presented on a separate line of the income statement and is not included in SG&A. It is a noncash and does not affect our cash flow or liquidity. We also tested our Shoe Station and Rogan's trade names and concluded that neither was impaired. We recorded an income tax benefit of $2.1 million in the quarter, and the effective tax rate was 14.6% compared to 25.5% in the prior year quarter.

The GAAP net loss for the quarter was $12.3 million or $0.46 per diluted share compared to net income of $14.6 million or $0.53 per diluted share last year. Excluding the goodwill impairment charge, non-GAAP adjusted net income was $1.3 million and non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $0.05. Through the first 9 months, net sales were $835.0 million, down 5.2% with comparable store sales down 4.8%. The GAAP net loss year-to-date was $11.7 million or $0.43 per diluted share. Excluding the first quarter charges related to the CEO transition and our strategic review and the third quarter goodwill impairment charge, non-GAAP adjusted net income was $13.8 million. Adjusted EPS was $0.51 per share and non-GAAP adjusted SG&A declined $18.1 million year-to-date.

Before I turn to guidance, let me cover the financial treatment of the two actions Cliff described. We expect to incur approximately $4 million of expense in the fourth quarter to return certain rebanner stores to the original layout. Returning stores to the original banners is expected to cost between $2 million and $3 million, which we expect to incur an expense primarily in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The expected layout revert expense is included in our fiscal 2026 GAAP guidance and excluded from our adjusted guidance measures. The anticipated banner expense falls in fiscal 2027 and does not affect fiscal 2026 guidance.

We are lowering our fiscal 2026 guidance to reflect results through the third quarter and current family footwear industry trends. For the fourth quarter, we expect comparable store sales in the range of flat to up 2%. For the full year, we now expect net sales of $1.087 billion to $1.092 billion, representing a decline of approximately 4.3% to 3.8% versus fiscal 2025, a GAAP net loss per share of $0.84 to $0.76 and adjusted EPS of $0.20 to $0.28. Gross profit margin of approximately 31.4% to 31.6%, representing 500 to 520 basis points of compression versus fiscal 2025.

GAAP SG&A up approximately $5.9 million versus fiscal 2025 and a reduction of adjusted SG&A of approximately $11.6 million, inclusive of our fourth quarter advertising investment, and a GAAP tax benefit rate of approximately 11% and adjusted tax rate of approximately 38%. Our adjusted guidance measures exclude the $13.6 million of first quarter charges and the expected $4 million fourth quarter expense to revert our store layouts and adjusted EPS and adjusted tax rate also exclude the $18 million goodwill impairment charge. A reconciliation is included in today's press release. Let me describe the assumptions behind this guidance. We are not assuming the promotional environment improves, and we are not assuming margin recovery in the fourth quarter.

We are assuming a fourth quarter comparable store sales result of flat to up 2%, supported by drivers that are in place today. The boot assortment as a result since the season opened, localized assortments in our stores, intensified holiday advertising, the return of our rebanner stores to a layout customers find easier to shop in a prior year comparison that eased as the quarter progresses. With that, I will turn the call back to Cliff.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Thank you, Kerry. And before we open the line for questions, I want to thank our teams in our stores, our distribution center and our support centers. They have reset assortments, managed inventory with discipline and given us candid feedback on what our customers want. The decisions we announced today come directly from listening to them and to our customers. Our work is not finished. Our focus for the fourth quarter is execution, the right product in the right stores, a store that is easy to shop and a clear message to the customer. Operator, we are ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Mitch Kummetz with Seaport Research Partners.

Mitch Kummetz: I think I'm going to probably break your rule about the one question and one follow-up. Let me start with Shoe Station. So Cliff, I think you said 131 of the stores are rebannered. What's -- remind me, I don't know if you said it in your prepared remarks, what's the total Shoe Station number right now?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Total Shoe Station?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: 163 as of today.

Mitch Kummetz: So 131 of those are rebannered versus like 32 that were either original or were just new stores, right?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct.

Mitch Kummetz: Okay. And can you speak a little bit to the -- so Shoe Station comp in the quarter was minus 7.6%. Can you speak to the comp performance of the 131 rebannered stores versus the 32 other non-rebannered stores? I assume those performed better.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: I'll give you -- I can tell you directionally that those stores that were rebannered performed worse than the stores that we originally bought. And Mitch, there's reasoning behind that as we -- on the rebannered stores, again, remember we have to remember always that those rebannered stores were in Shoe Carnival Centers or Shoe Carnival cotenancy, Shoe Carnival customers. And when the decision was made to upgrade the product in those stores, we alienated that Shoe Carnival customer that was there for years. She came in, she looked, she couldn't afford. And basically, that was backed up.

That fact was backed up through our focus groups when the customers within our focus groups told us that we rebannered -- we put a new name on the outside of the store and raised the prices. So I believe -- and again, one of the other things I said in my prepared remarks is that we do believe that Shoe Station is the future for our company and that we can grow that banner in markets that we are currently in and in new markets -- but we can't do that if we continue to operate them as Shoe Station Shoe Carnival stores.

If we change the product to the customer that shops those stores today, they essentially become Shoe Carnival stores with a Shoe Station banner on the outside. We can't operate those stores that way and expect to get the growth that we're looking to get out of Shoe Station. It's a dramatic change. -- but it's a change. It has to be made.

Mitch Kummetz: Yes. And then on the return to the original shelving layout on the 74 stores, when exactly -- I know you said you're doing in the fourth quarter, but when exactly in the fourth quarter? I assume you're going to try to get that done before holiday selling really kicks in? And are you doing it in a way that like that's happening when the stores are closed, so there's no sales disruption in the process?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Yes. We'll send teams in after a store closes. We will not disrupt our sales as we move that. And basically, it's a big deal, and I don't want to downplay it because it is. But as the store closes, a team of many will come in and make the change overnight.

Mitch Kummetz: And again, is that going to happen pretty soon?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That's going to happen after this week. It will begin the first two weeks of December.

Mitch Kummetz: Okay. And then on boots, can you remind us what your boot penetration is in the fourth quarter and kind of what boot comp is assumed for your overall sort of 0% to 2% comp guide?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Boots represent roughly -- and I need Tanya to back me up on this, but I think it represents roughly 25% of our sales during the quarter. It obviously, a higher percentage of that in women's.

Tanya E. Gordon: That's correct. And Mitch, just to follow up on the -- can you hear me? On the comps that we're expecting, so we were down low singles for the quarter, and we really saw a big shift when the warmer weather hit. When it was cooler and they hit, we saw double-digit comp increases, then slid down when it got warmer. And then right when they -- the cool weather hit about a week ago, we saw double-digit increases in the teens again pop back up. So we are expecting double-digit increases through the fourth quarter.

And everything that we have based on style, penetration of short versus tall, for, all of that is lined up and teed up very well as we go through the fourth quarter, which would give me every confidence that as the weather remains cool, we will enjoy those increases through the fourth quarter.

Mitch Kummetz: And then last question for me. On the -- on the gross margin, I mean if I take the high end of your revised guide, 31.6%, that's about -- I mean, that's 500 basis points down from last year. I know there's sort of 3 buckets that are contributing to that. Kerry, how much of that do you think is possible to get back next year? Or maybe just can you talk about how much of that 500 basis point hit is from the inventory liquidation? Because I would imagine that's the one that's you could get back next year, not necessarily knowing what the promotional environment might look like next year.

W. Kerry Jackson: Well, we're not going to get specific about next year's margin. But you're correct, the inventory liquidation is that on the excess and aged inventory is basically done at this point in time. So we're back to more normalized clearance that we normally have in the fourth quarter. So we'll get that benefit next year. We'll also have difficult compares against '25's margin this year because of the raising the prices beyond what our customers would comfortably pay, and we saw the effect of it in our sales, and we've been reversing that this year. So those are 2 items that we won't see repeated in '27.

But in March, we'll be in a better position after we see how the customer responds to our advertising or promotions to better level set about what the margin expectations will be on a go-forward basis.

Mitch Kummetz: Can you at least say how much of the 500 basis point decline this year was due to the inventory liquidation, which is now basically done?

W. Kerry Jackson: That's not as easy as a number to finitely give to the Street. It was significant, but to try to actually pin that down is difficult, and we're not -- I prefer not to do that.

Operator: Your next question comes from Sam Poser with Williams Trading.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Can I just follow up on the -- I just want to walk through the stores very specifically, and then I got a couple of other things. There are 131 rebannered stores, of which 31 are Rogan's. Is that correct?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: 27 are Rogan's.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. And then those 27 are going to go back to Rogan's, correct?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct. And Sam, can I interject something there? And we'll get to the rest of your question. It's important that we take the station name and separate it from the stores that are going to be highly promotional for our future growth. So it wasn't 100% necessary for us to take the station name away from Rogan's. But if we want a pure brand that we can grow at higher price points and better product, it doesn't need to be associated with a promotional retailer.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: I completely agree. It's -- I mean, what you're doing is localizing everything and letting the customers know who you are. I'm just trying to get the numbers here. So then you have 104 rebannered stores, of which 77 of those are going to be rebannered as Shoe Carnival or rebannered as back to Shoe Carnival.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Yes, we didn't give an exact number, but your calculator is working really well.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: I didn't even use it for that one. And then does that leave us with 20-some-odd stores that are -- that really belong -- are supposed to be -- that they're in the right place to be Shoe Station? Or are those stores that could just say see you later down the road?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: No. Those -- there may be a couple of those stores that will see you later, okay? But for the most part, those stores are performing well under the Shoe Station banner.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. So then that leaves us with you're not going to -- you're going to remerchandise and reset up the 77 stores over the next few weeks, correct overnight.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That is correct.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: In those 77 stores. Now how? The traffic is still going to be a problem? How are you going to let the customers know in the short term that these 77 Shoe Station stores are Shoe Carnival stores, and they have better assortments to take advantage of this? Or is this -- is this just counting on the traffic and is why the comps in Q4 are still going to be -- I mean, I guess the for that stuff is going to be challenging and not get positive. I mean, because it still appears to be those stores will -- the traffic issues in those stores will remain, but you're anticipating the conversions to improve because of that.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We do expect conversions to improve, but the #1 thing is we're not just going to change the banner on the outside of the store and hope for the best. We are going to market it. And it's a we're back kind of a marketing campaign along with -- we won't be.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: But you're not changing signage until spring, correct?

Samuel (Sam) Poser: The signage. So in the meantime, I understand for spring. I get that for spring. I'm really talking about holiday because in holiday, you're going to have the Shoe Station name with the Shoe Carnival layout and the Shoe Carnival assortment in those stores. So how do you bring more customers to the store in holiday when there's the most traffic. I understand the plan for spring, but can't say we're back with Shoe Station stores.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That's right. And I apologize for that. But the -- for misunderstanding the question. Here's what we're going to do, Sam, is that we have intensified our advertising for the fourth quarter, television, every aspect that we -- every medium that we normally use, we've intensified the marketing to get customers into both our Shoe Station stores and Shoe Carnival stores. And I -- and when they come into a Shoe Station, what they see as a Shoe Station store, but with a Shoe Carnival layout and Spin 'n Win Wheel, they'll see -- they'll experience the fact that Carnival is coming back. And at that point, our people can communicate.

We'll have the mic going again, and our people will communicate to the customers the change in plans.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: And then I mean, on my math, which is always so good, the -- it looks like sort of on the lower end of your gross margin guidance, which would get the higher cost of sales. I mean, your fourth quarter purchases or like sort of receipts, though there's other stuff in it, are really -- are you planning the fourth quarter receipts down in the $20 million range year-over-year to get to the $50 million lower inventory?

Tanya E. Gordon: Hang on, Sam. I am getting that financial report.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: She wants to give you a good number.

Tanya E. Gordon: I want to give you an accurate number. And yes, you are correct. Receipts are down about $20 million. But a lot of that, Sam, just for clarification, last year was not true spring receipts that were received in fourth quarter. A lot of later receipts came in that hit the fourth quarter number. So we will have, based on where our inventory sits today, that is all new spring-driven receipts. So we will be much better positioned in percent of units and lack of aged inventory this year versus last year. So we will be much better positioned in fresh new inventory to start spring '27.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: And then lastly, when we think about that and we think about as you -- it's not really lastly, I have one more, but as you move into spring, I mean, like the -- I assume that the units of that -- the units -- the average selling prices are higher year-over-year just given the inflation within those receipts. So the units are down more than the dollars, like the $20 million...

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: That would be correct. That would be correct.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: Okay. And then, Kerry, if you -- because you're going to lap the $660,000 refunds in third quarter next year. Why not just back that out for clarity? And if we -- and would the tax rate, if we did back it out, still be in that 63% range if we backed -- if we just added back in the $660,000 in the cost of goods because you're not going to lap that next year.

W. Kerry Jackson: That's correct. There's enough noise in our margins right now. We chose not to back that out and show that as adjusted items, but really focused on the strategic changes we're making in our business like the rebanners, the reflows, items like that. But you can make the argument, but it wouldn't change the overall tax rate significantly because a lot of that excess rate is due to more of the permanent items that are being reflected in there and the lower income against them.

Samuel (Sam) Poser: So if all other things are equal, everything is equal as of right now, nothing changes from the world, except for your actions that you're taking. I mean, how should we think about gross margin recovery into '27? I mean, on the stuff you can control and say the macro is exactly the same. I mean...

W. Kerry Jackson: Well, it's a fair question. And obviously, our margins are depressed because of some of the activities we've had to occur this year. We've underestimated the challenge of what we looked at the beginning of the year, and we're making corrective actions such as the reflow, changing the banners back. We'd like to get through this holiday season where we have a significant increase in advertising. We have to localize assortments and see what the promotional cadence that's going to be necessary to drive traffic in our stores again. And that's the key right there, is we have to increase the traffic, which will drive the sales longer term.

We don't want to underestimate the challenge of that in the fourth quarter, and we'll be in a better position to give better information in March after we go through this holiday season and see the benefits of the actions we've taken.

Operator: Your next question comes from Jim Chartier with Monness, Crespi, and Hardt.

James (Jim) Chartier: I just wanted to kind of talk about the fourth quarter comp guidance, flat to up 2%. It's a pretty significant acceleration from where you were in third quarter. Just aside from what seems like a strong start to November, can you just kind of give us some more details as to what's driving your confidence that the business can inflect that way?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We announced -- Jim, we announced last quarter that we had increased our marketing spend significantly for the fourth quarter. That marketing spend really kicks in around the first part of December. And we've had a little in November, but it really kicks in around our boot assortment -- around our total assortment to the first week of December. And we have confidence that, that is going to reintroduce ourselves to the customers that have not shopped us over the past year because of the changes that were made with our stores. And we believe that the message that we're giving them will drive them into the store or convince them to give us another shot.

So that's the reason we think in December being the largest month of the quarter, the second largest month of the second half, I believe I'm right on that. And the -- we can drive the customers in the store. We have proven time and time again this year that we can convert them. So we're putting a lot of faith and trust in the promotion -- excuse me, in the marketing spend that we put in place for the fourth quarter.

James (Jim) Chartier: Can you quantify how much you've increased the spend for holiday? And then can you kind of compare that to your back-to-school? Was advertising up for back-to-school? And if so, how does that increase compared to what you're doing for holiday?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: It's about a 50% increase in spend, but it is still somewhat lower than what we spend at back-to-school. And the reason for that is back-to-school is really a six- to eight-week time period where you have to market during the entire time, and it's inserts. It's television. It's digital. It's all-encompassing where this is going to be digital and television. So -- but about a 50% more than a year ago.

James (Jim) Chartier: Okay. And then I thought the plan was to leverage the loyalty program during back-to-school and let some of those lapsed customers know that you had improved -- return the assortment closer to what they were expecting. Was that the case? And if so, how did those customers respond to the e-mails that you sent out?

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: We did do exactly that. And the response rate was great. Unfortunately, it didn't show up in the total company as the kind of increases that we were expecting, but we did get a good response rate and a good return, especially on those lapsed customers. They did come back at a pretty good rate, just not strong enough to get the business turned around. And so that -- what we've decided to do was continue that marketing campaign to those lapsed customers. Although being very careful because one of the reasons they're lapsed is because we were over marketed to them. So we've adjusted the cadence of how often we reach out to them.

And again, happy with the return rate on that program. It just wasn't enough yet to tell you that, that turned our business.

Operator: There are no more questions at this time. I'll now turn the call back to Cliff Sifford for closing remarks.

Clifton E. (Cliff) Sifford: Thank you for joining us today. I hope you all have a great holiday season. We look forward to speaking to you again in March.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3038. 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In today's job market, do applicants really have a choice of whether to comply with AI hiring tools?

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

New data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

“As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

The report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse said, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson said.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report said.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse said.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson said. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”

#3037. Roku Drains Iconic Fish Tank Screensaver to Reel Viewers Into Roku City

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Home Entertainment > Media Streamers

Fans of the Roku Aquatic Life screensaver will need to find a new way to just keep swimming.

Roku users may be getting that sinking feeling, as the platform is retiring its classic animated Aquatic Life screensaver.

The popular animation featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.)

That doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

“It seems like this is a way for Roku to convert a popular screensaver into a way to make money, or at least generate more engagement, via the Roku City version,” said CNET Senior Editor Ty Pendlebury, who covers home entertainment options including the Roku streaming boxes.

A Roku representative didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the company chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

The Aquatic Life screensaver loss is a drop in the ocean compared to other changes at the streamer this year. Roku was purchased by Fox for $22 billion in June, which puts the streaming platform under the same ownership as Fox’s Tubi and Fox One channels. That deal is expected to close in 2027.

#3034. The Flipper One is more than a Zero 2.0 – it’s a $399 Linux computer with a $13M Kickstarter

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Backers are going big on the $759 Ultimate Bundle, but Flipper warns that rising RAM prices could affect production.

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

If you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this new platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

The Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

Keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also says on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

#3033. How to Turn Off Apple Intelligence Feature by Feature in iOS 27

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Whether you want to drop a few AI features or as many as possible, here's where each control can be found in iOS 27.

iOS 26 lets you turn off Apple Intelligence with one toggle. iOS 27 doesn’t. Apple folded its AI settings into a new Siri menu centered on Siri AI and dropped the master switch along the way, so opting out now means working through several parts of Settings. Siri AI’s controls are in the Siri menu, Screen Time can block Writing Tools and image creation, notification summaries have their own switch and each app’s Siri & Search settings control what Siri learns from it. This guide walks through every step in order.

Individual features can still be disabled, but they’re scattered across several menus in Settings and Screen Time rather than being consolidated in one place. Here’s the current map of what can be turned off and where to find each control.

If your device is not running the newest software, turning off Apple Intelligence all at once only takes a few taps in Settings and doesn’t affect any core iPhone functionality. Here’s how to do it on iPhone, iPad and Mac.

You can still disable some of Apple’s AI features if your iPhone is running iOS 27. It just won’t be as easy as tapping the main toggle.

To disable Siri AI, go to Settings > Siri and toggle off the control. Beware, though, that this will disable your voice assistant entirely, as well as disable conversations in the new dedicated Siri app and block you from using Apple’s Visual Intelligence. Additionally, your HomePod speakers will not be able to recognize your voice or help with personal content if they’re on the same iCloud account as your iPhone.

Keep reading for how to disable some of the individual Apple AI features.

Since the first Apple Intelligence features rolled out in iOS 18.1, some people have opted out of the new technology. Tools such as Image Playground, Genmoji and message summaries can use up to 7GB of your device’s internal storage — a sizable chunk, especially if you tend to run against the upper limit of its free space.

Even if storage is not an issue, you just may not be interested in Apple’s set of AI features. A recent CNET survey finds that just 19% of US smartphone owners are choosing to upgrade their devices to take advantage of new AI features. And a recent ZDNET/Aberdeen survey reveals that the majority of US adults say they will not use most AI features, and just 8% would consider paying extra for them. Some AI features are more welcome than others, with 58% of respondents saying using AI for photo editing would be valuable.

Or, honestly, you may not want to deal with features that are creating inaccurate summaries or that can be replicated without Apple Intelligence.

(Earlier iOS 18 updates re-enabled Apple Intelligence automatically even if you had turned it off, but as of iOS 18.4, the setting is honored.)

Read more: Did a well-meaning friend send you a message about Apple Intelligence possibly reading your private information? Here’s what’s actually going on.

I’m not an AI crank — I appreciate features such as notification summaries and the Clean Up tool in the Photos app. And yet, Apple Intelligence is also a work in progress, an evolving set of features that Apple is heavily hyping while gradually developing. I wouldn’t hold it against you if you wanted to not be distracted or feel like you’re doing Apple’s testing for them (that’s what the developer and public betas should be for).

Remember that Apple Intelligence works only on the new iPhone 18 lineup, the iPhone Duo, iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, iPhone 17E, iPhone 16, iPhone 16E, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro or M-series Macs and iPads, plus the newest iPad mini.

If you’re concerned about the storage requirements of Apple Intelligence, you can find out how much the system is using by going to Settings > General > iPhone (or iPad) Storage > iOS (or iPadOS).

See how much space Apple Intelligence is using in Settings. This is what it looks like running iOS 26, but the settings flow is the same.

Note that even after turning off Apple Intelligence, the storage still shows up in the iOS Storage list. However, I was able to confirm that if the phone’s storage fills up and the system needs that now-inactive space, iOS reclaims what it needs.

Maybe you’re finding some Apple Intelligence features helpful while others are annoying (or just highly amusing). You can turn off specific features in the settings for apps to which they apply.

For example, to disable text summaries in Messages notifications, go to Settings > Apps > Messages and switch off the Summarize Messages option.

Some features are not as app-specific. Writing Tools, which use Apple Intelligence to proof or rewrite text, appear as an option when you select text, regardless of the app. To turn that off, you need to disable Apple Intelligence system-wide.

Also note that nearly every app includes an “Apple Intelligence & Siri” option in Settings, with a Learn from this App option (turned on by default). That applies just to whether Apple Intelligence and Siri can monitor how you use it to make suggestions; it doesn’t affect any particular Apple Intelligence features.

Another option for restricting what Apple Intelligence can do is buried in the Screen Time settings. Screen Time is designed to control which apps and features can run on another device, such as the iPhone used by a child in your household. But it’s also helpful for tracking how much time you’re spending on the device and, in this case, turning off some components of Apple Intelligence.

Turn off selected Apple Intelligence features in the Screen Time settings. This is what the settings look like with iOS 26. It may look different if you are using iOS 27. The settings flow is the same.

If you haven’t upgraded to iOS 27 yet, make a good backup first.

If you aren’t on iOS 27, you can turn off Apple Intelligence with one tap. (You can see what software your iPhone is running by going to Settings > General > About and seeing what iOS version you’re running.)

If you’re on iOS 26 or earlier, here’s how to disable Apple Intelligence. Open Settings (iPhone or iPad) or System Settings (Mac) and choose Apple Intelligence & Siri. Then turn off the Apple Intelligence option. Confirm your choice in the dialog that appears by tapping Turn Off Apple Intelligence.

Turn off Apple Intelligence entirely with one switch if you are running iOS 26 or an earlier software version.

Curiously, the Clean Up tool in Photos sticks around even when Apple Intelligence is turned off, perhaps because the first time you use it the app downloads resources for it and holds onto them.

#3032. Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are Everywhere

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

AI is rewriting the web in its own imperfect image, making software flaws easier to find and easier to exploit, while introducing plenty of its own imperfections.

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some issues. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

Something must be behind all of this, you might think — a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these issues, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counteradversary operations at cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

If it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

Artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

At the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should update. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

Another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

When I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. New AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning.

In September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers said.

Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” said Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

It still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”

And defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

That’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” said Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with important, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

And patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s issues on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents new problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing issue.

In the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

Big Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says.

That means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into new software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

“I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more important than ever.

“You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet says. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

#3031. Your Google AI mode searches can stay private now with ‘temporary threads’ – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With temporary threads, any searches you run in Google’s AI Mode won’t be associated with your account or saved to your chat history.

Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training

New to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

This option is currently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a new thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Also: Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills

Certain limitations are in effect with a temporary thread. Specifically, you can’t do any of the following:

Are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:

“Temporary threads will not be saved to your Google account and disappear after 24 hours,” Google said on a support page. “They won’t be used to train Google’s generative AI models, unless you submit feedback or it’s necessary for safety purposes. Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”

Google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot all offer a temporary chat mode that also promises to keep your chats private and unconnected to your account. Claude and Perplexity provide the same feature but call it incognito mode.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Bluetooth trackers have never been cheaper

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you've been thinking about picking up a Bluetooth tracker to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, or other valuables, now is probably the best time to get one. Apple launched its second-generation AirTag 2 earlier this year, but the tracker is already down to its lowest price yet for Black Friday. You can now grab a single Apple AirTag for just $18 at Amazon, down from its usual $29 price.

And if you're an Android user, there's a pretty good deal for you as well. The Moto Tag 2, which offers many of the same features as Apple's AirTag, is currently down to just $19 at Amazon.

Apple's latest AirTag features an improved Precision Finding range, a 50% louder speaker, and up to a year of battery life. It works seamlessly with Apple's Find My network and is now down to just $18 (38% off).

The second-generation AirTag offers up to 1.5 times the Precision Finding range of its predecessor. Apple has also upgraded the built-in speaker, making it 50% louder than the original AirTag, and features a new, more distinctive chime. this makes it a lot easier to locate your belongings when they're nearby.

One of the biggest reasons to get an AirTag over most other Apple Find My-compatible trackers, though, is Precision Finding. While other key finders and trackers also let you locate your belongings through the Find My app warn you if you leave something behind, the AirTag takes things a step further with its ultra-wideband (UWB) technology.

If you've misplaced your keys somewhere around the house, for example, you can simply open the Find My app on a compatible iPhone, and it'll show you exactly which direction to walk in and how far away your AirTag is — rather than just relying on a sound to locate it.

And if you're planning to put AirTags on multiple belongings, there's also a deal on the AirTag four-pack, which is currently down to $79 from its usual $99 price. That said, at $18 apiece, buying four individual AirTags actually works out slightly cheaper.

If you're on the Android side of things, the Moto Tag 2 is arguably one of the best alternatives to Apple's AirTag. Much like Apple's AirTag, the Moto Tag 2 features ultra-wideband technology, which means you can use precision finding on compatible Android phones to pinpoint the location of your items.

It also works with Google's Find Hub network, so you can locate your items even when they're outside your phone's Bluetooth range.

The Moto Tag 2 brings an AirTag-like tracking experience to Android with UWB Precision Finding, Google's Find Hub integration, over 600 days of battery life, and IP68 water resistance. It's currently down to just $19 from $30.

But there are a couple of things the Moto Tag 2 does even better than Apple's AirTag. For starters, Motorola claims over 600 days of battery life, which is considerably longer than the year of battery life Apple promises. You can also use the button on the Moto Tag 2 as a remote camera shutter, which is particularly handy for taking group photos or selfies.

You also get features like left-behind notifications and an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, so you don't have to worry too much about attaching it to your backpack or other belongings you carry outdoors.

On the whole, I think $20 is a pretty reasonable amount to spend on something that could save you a lot of trouble if you ever lose your keys or luggage. And if you've been holding off on buying an item tracker for your phone, now's a pretty good time to get one, regardless of whether you use an iPhone or an Android phone.
