#3010. Danaos (DAC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Backlog climbs as dry bulk rebounds and a special dividend lands for shareholders.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:23PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Danaos (DAC -2.91%) reported significant growth in both net income and revenue for the third quarter, supported by a strengthening container market and a sharp recovery in the dry bulk sector. Management capitalized on scarce open tonnage to expand the contracted revenue backlog to $5 billion, extending visibility through 2030. The company maintained a conservative balance sheet while significantly increasing shareholder distributions through a higher quarterly dividend and a large special dividend. Despite ongoing geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East and evolving global trade policies, the company continues to execute its massive newbuilding program and strategic investments in related shipping sectors.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Danaos Corporation conference call to discuss the financial results for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. Hosting the call today is Dr. John Coustas, Chief Executive Officer of Danaos Corporation; and Mr. Evangelos Chatzis, Chief Financial Officer of Danaos Corporation. Dr. Coustas and Mr. Chatzis will be making some introductory comments, and then we will open the call to a question-and-answer session. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to Evangelos Chatzis, Chief Financial Officer.

Evangelos Chatzis: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I quickly want to remind everyone that management's remarks this morning may contain certain forward-looking statements and that actual results could differ materially from those projected today. These forward-looking statements are made as of today, and we undertake no obligation to update them. Factors that might affect future results are discussed in our filings with the SEC, and we encourage you to review these detailed safe harbor and risk factor disclosures.

Please also note that where we feel appropriate, we will continue to refer to non-GAAP financial measures such as EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income, time charter equivalent revenues and time charter equivalent dollars per day to evaluate our business. Reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures to GAAP financial measures are included in our earnings release and accompanying materials. With that, let me now turn the call over to Dr. John Coustas, who will provide the broad overview of the quarter. John?

John Coustas: Thank you, Evangelos. Good morning, and thank you all for joining today's call to discuss results for the third quarter of 2026. The geopolitical picture was largely unchanged during the quarter with no visible end to the conflict. The one significant development is that transits through the Bab al-Mandab Strait have become more regular. Liners are gradually moving tonnage back through the Suez Canal, and say for new developments, Red Sea traffic could be restored in the first quarter of 2027. Despite this shift, the container market continued to strengthen, and the liner companies reported strong third quarter results. Open tonnage remains scarce, and the charter market has strengthened with it.

We used those conditions to add approximately $611 million to our contracted revenue backlog, which now stands at $5 billion, with our container fleet 100% contracted for 2026, 94% for 2027, 84% for 2028, 71% for 2029 and 53% for 2030 at healthy rates. The Capesize market also strengthened with charter rates at multiyear highs, and our dry bulk segment contributed $22.4 million of adjusted EBITDA for the quarter against $9.1 million a year ago. We decided to defer the carve-out and sale of a minority stake in the segment in the Norwegian market for now so that any transaction is executed at the time and on terms that optimize value for our shareholders.

The Board declared a special dividend of $5 per share and raised the quarterly dividend to $1 per share, in line with our policy of rewarding shareholders. In October, we marked 20 years since our listing on the New York Stock Exchange, and Moody's upgraded our senior unsecured notes to Ba1 and changed the outlook of our Ba1 corporate family rating to positive, which confirms our solid performance and financial strength. We'll continue to work to create value and strengthen the company for the benefit of all stakeholders. With that, I'll hand the call over back to Evangelos, who will take you through the financials for the quarter.

Evangelos Chatzis: Thank you, John, and good morning again to everyone. I will review the results for the quarter, and we will then open the call to Q&A. Adjusted net income for the third quarter was $152.1 million or $8.32 per share compared with $124.1 million or $6.75 per share in the third quarter of 2025. That is an increase of $28 million or approximately 23% on a per share basis.

This improvement is the combined result of a $23.6 million increase in operating revenues a $4.6 million reduction in net finance expenses and a $5.3 million increase in dividend income by our Star Bulk holding, partially offset by a $5.2 million increase in total operating expenses and $0.3 million increase in loss of equity investments. Let me start with revenues. Container vessel revenue increased by $8.7 million to $247.8 million total. Our newbuilding deliveries contributed an incremental $8.2 million, reflecting one 6,000 TEU vessel delivery in the fourth quarter of 2025 that commenced a 7-year charter and three 8,250 TEU vessels that joined the fleet in the current quarter, each commencing a 5-year charter.

Lower off-hire added a further $4.3 million with container fleet utilization improving to 99.6% this quarter from 98.1% a year ago and higher charter rates contributed $0.3 million. Offsetting these was a $4.1 million reduction in noncash revenue recognition under U.S. GAAP. Dry bulk revenue increased by $14.9 million or 69% to $36.5 million in the current quarter from $21.6 million in the third quarter of 2025. The principal driver, of course, was the strength of the Capesize market, and our dry bulk time charter equivalent rate rose to $32,690 per day from $19,910 per day in the comparable quarter, while we also operated additional Cape vessel that joined our fleet during the second quarter of this year.

As a result, the dry bulk segment adjusted EBITDA increased to $22.4 million compared to $9.1 million in the third quarter of 2025, and the net income rose to $15.8 million from $3.4 million a year ago. Turning now to operating costs. Vessel operating expenses came in at $53.3 million, up only $1 million from the $52.3 million number posted in Q3 of 2025, notwithstanding the increase in the average number of vessels in our fleet. Our daily operating costs declined to $6,790 per day from $6,927 per day a year ago. Our operating costs remain among the most competitive in the industry.

G&A expenses increased by $1.5 million to $14.1 million from $12.6 million in the third quarter of 2025, and the increase relates mainly to higher management fees while corporate G&A was -- came in marginally lower this quarter. On the finance cost side, interest expense, excluding amortization of finance fees and debt discount, increased by $1.4 million to $9.2 million in the current quarter, up from $7.8 million in the third quarter of 2025. And there are 2 components to that. Average indebtedness increased by approximately $0.5 billion to $1.29 billion this quarter as we drew on our committed financing for our newbuilding deliveries. And that added $5 million in interest expense.

This effect was meaningfully mitigated by a reduction in our average cost of debt service of approximately 1.3%, reflecting lower SOFR rates and the lower coupon following the refinancing of our bond. Working in the other direction, capitalized interest on vessels under construction rose to $9.6 million from $6 million as our newbuilding program advanced, reducing interest expense by $3.6 million. At the same time, interest income increased by $6 million to $9.8 million this quarter from $3.8 million a year ago, obviously driven by higher average cash balances.

We also received $5.6 million in dividends from our Star Bulk shareholding this quarter compared to $3.8 million a year ago -- sorry, compared to $0.3 million in the third quarter of last year. Adjusted EBITDA increased by 14.2% or $25.7 million to $207.3 million compared to $181.6 million in the third quarter of 2025 for the reasons that have already been outlined on this call. We would encourage you to review our updated investor presentation and the subsequent events disclosures, both of which are available on our website. Turning to some of the highlights. Since the date of our last earnings release, we have added approximately $611 million to our contracted revenue backlog.

As a result, our backlog now stands at a record level of $5 billion with a 4.5-year average remaining charter duration, while contract coverage has already been outlined by John earlier. Within our investor presentation, you will find analytical disclosure on our charter contracts. On the fleet side, in September, we added two 9,000 TEU container ships to our order book for delivery in the first quarter of 2029. Our order book now comprises of 28 container ships with an aggregate capacity of approximately 178,000 TEU and 4 Newcastlemax dry bulk vessels.

On a fully delivered basis, our fleet will consist of 106 container ships of approximately 680,000 TEU and 15 dry bulk vessels, combination of Capes and Newcastlemaxes with a capacity of approximately 2.8 million deadweight. On the financing side, in August, we entered into an additional $200 million Japanese Operating Lease financing transactions with a tenor of 8 years for 2 of our newbuildings that were delivered to us in September of this year. Both transactions have now been consummated. In September, given our strong liquidity position and our committed newbuilding financing, we canceled our revolving credit facility, which was undrawn and was scheduled to mature in December of 2027.

Also in October, Moody's upgraded our senior unsecured notes to Ba1 and moved the outlook on our Ba1 corporate family rating to positive. As of September 30, net debt came in at $327.9 million, equivalent to 0.43x over last 12 months EBITDA. And out of our current fleet of 89 vessels, 78 are unencumbered and debt-free. As of the end of the third quarter, cash stood at $1.06 billion. And together with our Star Bulk holding, total liquidity stood at approximately $1.24 billion. In addition, as of today, we hold approximately $1 billion of committed undrawn facilities in support of our newbuilding program.

Finally, just to note that in October, we paid a quarterly dividend of $1 per share, together with an extraordinary special dividend of $5 per share for a total distribution of $109 million. We continue to have approximately $65 million of remaining authority under our $300 million share repurchase program. With that, I would like to thank you for listening to this first part of our call. Operator, we are now ready to open the call to Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Omar Nokta with Clarksons Securities.

Omar Nokta: Obviously, clearly a nice quarter, continue to add backlog at quite a brisk pace and seemingly at a faster rate than the revenue has been coming in the door, at least the past couple of quarters. This gives you plenty of flexibility and the cash is building quite nicely. And Evangelos, maybe just on your last point, you had mentioned the $5 special dividend in addition to the regular payout that was distributed back in October. I wanted to ask about the $65 million left on the share buyback. How do you guys think about the share repurchase program from here? Where does it sit?

You were active in it or with it the past several years, but you've lightened up here since earlier in the year. Yes, I just wanted to ask, how are you guys thinking about the buyback at this point?

John Coustas: Well, Omar, thanks for, let's say, the question. Thanks for really your attendance in our 20-year anniversary. It was a great event. It's still there. It's obviously under any type of calculation, the stock is undervalued. We are keeping, let's say, the dry powder. We are definitely committed to continue the buyback. In terms of timing, we are watching a bit to see what's the optimal, let's say, time to go and do it. For the time being, we have rewarded shareholders with this special dividend. So we believe that we have really rewarded them. I mean, as far as I said, this leftovers from our buyback, it will definitely be used, but we cannot commit to a time line.

Omar Nokta: And yes, definitely, congratulations on the 20-year anniversary. It was a fun event. And then just a follow-up or a second question, and I'll pass it back. How do you think about the dry bulk business from here? You plan to do the carve-out last month. You put those plans on pause for now. And I guess, how do you weigh revisiting that and doing a separate carve-out or separate listing versus maybe monetizing those vessels in the dry bulk sale and purchase market? How do you evaluate both options?

John Coustas: Yes, I mean the issue of the listing was not monetary. It was much more as a kind of a test of carving out a vehicle that could operate because it's a vehicle normally, the dry bulk, which operates in the spot market. So it's quite a different dynamic than the containers. So we wanted really to get an experience of how a full payout vehicle operates in public markets to which extent you can have it trade at or above NAV. And this was the main reason of doing it. Definitely, it was not really the monetary part of it. And at some stage, we believe we will find the right window to test that type of structure.

Operator: The next question comes from Climent Molins with Value Investor's Edge.

Climent Molins: I wanted to start with a macro question. Red Sea traffic has been increasing materially in recent months. And you hinted at a potential full normalization by Q1. What impact do you expect this to have on congestion across key ports?

John Coustas: I think -- well, to a certain extent, the fact that the actual schedules of the vessels are going to change through the Suez transit. It's not really -- it's a disruption as far as schedules are concerned. So I don't think it's going to help in the short-term disruption to the ports. I mean, hopefully, this change is going to bring lower sailing speeds. So part of, let's say, the capacity, the ton-mile decrease will be absorbed because of lower speeds. But overall, in the short term, it's really there are structural issues with the ports that come into play. So I don't think it's really going to make a huge difference.

Climent Molins: Makes sense. You looked at floating the minority stake in your Capesize platform, but ended up pulling the plug on the transaction. Could you talk a bit about the rationale for floating a portion of your Capesize fleet? And secondly, is there an appetite to add tonnage at prevailing prices? Or do you prefer to maintain the wait-and-see approach we've seen in recent quarters?

John Coustas: Yes. I think I spoke to Omar about the rationale on the listing before. We wanted really to test a full payout vehicle on the spot market, whether it trades close to NAV and whether such kind of construct can be used for future growth of the dry bulk segment. The dynamics on the container side are quite different. So we have not really seen over there full payout vehicles. And all our peers trade at kind of similar discounts.

Climent Molins: Yes. Makes sense. And last question from my side. In the last update, you mentioned you expected to have news regarding the Alaska LNG project by September. Any updates you can give us? Yes.

John Coustas: As you've seen, there was a change in governor in Alaska. And we believe that this is going to give a much better dynamic to the project because the previous governor, he had a hostile, let's say, local congress. Whereas now there's a Democratic congress in Alaska together with representatives, together with Democratic governor. So this is going to be easier to go through. I don't have any specific updates. In any case that we will know more in the first quarter of '27.

Operator: The next question comes from [ Aballi Zuminov ] with Freedom Broker.

Unknown Analyst: I have one question with regards to charter rates. Given your expectations for a potential normalization of Red Sea traffic in quarter 1 of 2027, how do you see containership charter rates evolving throughout 2027? Do you expect a gradual normalization or a more significant correction?

John Coustas: 2027, it's a year with not significant deliveries. I mean I would see, let's say, more supply coming to the market in 2028, which is going to show how well this capacity is going to be absorbed. On the other hand, if we look at, let's say, our kind of charter market, as you see, we are charter 94% 2027, 84% for 2028. So to a large extent, we are insulated from all that. And actually, what we expect really is if the market really corrects to get some opportunities and to get some cheaper vessels in our fleet.

Operator: It appears we have no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Dr. Coustas for any further comments or closing remarks.

John Coustas: Thank you all for joining this conference call and for your continued interest in our story. Look forward to hosting you on our next earnings calls. Have a nice day.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's teleconference. We would like to thank everyone for their participation. Have a wonderful afternoon.

#3009. Pixel Weather’s new feature lets you report your local conditions now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Weather apps are notoriously inaccurate. Google's new feature can help.

Default weather apps are notoriously unreliable, but Google is giving users a chance to help improve things.

A recent update to the Pixel Weather app introduced a new “Report current weather” card. If the weather you’re experiencing doesn’t match what the app is saying, you can report the discrepancy.

“Share the current weather condition,” the card says, “to improve local forecasts.” If you tap it, you’re given options to indicate whether the current temperature is accurate, warmer, or colder than the app says, and what your current conditions are, with options like cloudy, clear, rain showers, strong thunderstorms, and rain showers.

The card also shows what the app currently thinks is happening for you to use as the basis for your report. To find the card, scroll all the way to the bottom of your Pixel Weather app.

Also: Your best Google weather app alternatives (and what I recommend instead)

Google said that it will use your feedback, device location, and “some diagnostic information” to help improve forecasts. Nothing you report will be associated with your Google account. The app doesn’t explain exactly how Google uses your reports, but I’ve reached out to see if the company can offer any details.

As someone who doesn’t put a ton of faith into default weather apps, I see this as a step in the right direction toward regaining some trust. Even if it’s not yet clear how Google will use the information you send, the goal of improving forecasts is an important one.

Also: I switched to MyRadar as my main Android Auto weather app and don’t regret it

A large part of what makes weather apps unreliable is that they lack human insight, and a computer usually can’t grasp the nuance of a local forecast the way a meteorologist would. Experts have also warned of reduced weather forecast accuracy due to recent NOAA budget cuts.

The Apple Weather app has a similar feature, so it’s good to see Google catch up. I couldn’t find a feature like this for Samsung or any other native app. One of the most popular third-party apps, Weather Underground, does feature a “Report your local weather” prompt. It also gathers information from hundreds of thousands of connected home weather stations.

This new Pixel Weather feature was present on three Pixel phones in my home, so the rollout appears to be widespread.

Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a big reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.74% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3007. Uber Riders Can Now Request to Have Their Trips Recorded

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

In four cities, Uber riders can request rides with drivers who use the Record My Ride feature.

Starting this week, Uber riders in select markets will be able to specify that they want their trip recorded on video. The feature, which is being introduced in Baltimore, Indianapolis, St. Louis, and Raleigh, North Carolina, adds a new Recorded Rides choice to the app alongside other familiar ride options like UberX and UberXL. Uber says that the new feature gives “greater confidence that a recording will be there if something doesn’t go as planned.”

After a series of rider safety investigations and sexual assault lawsuit settlements, Uber began looking for ways to boost passenger safety and confidence in the service. The ridesharing platform first tested in-app trip audio recording in late 2019, then piloted the Record My Ride feature in 2022, before finally rolling out the video recording function in earnest, first in San Francisco in 2023, then nationally across the US in 2024.

According to Uber, the knowledge that a trip is being recorded gives both riders and drivers peace of mind.

While drivers can opt out of using the feature in their settings, more than half of its active drivers in the US choose to record their trips in the Record My Ride feature.

Starting this week, Uber riders in those four cities will be able to request a recorded ride during the hailing process in the Uber app and, when possible, be automatically matched with a driver using the feature. Choosing a recorded ride doesn’t affect the fare.

Record My Ride has been available to Uber’s drivers, though not passengers, for a few years now. The feature uses the front-facing camera on the driver’s phone to capture trip audio and video.

“Uber can only review recordings uploaded as part of a safety report or insurance claim,” a representative told CNET.

Not selecting a Recorded Ride doesn’t guarantee that your trip won’t be recorded in some way. Many Uber drivers choose to install separate dash cams in their vehicles, often with multiple cameras recording into the cabin. Uber offers drivers the option to register their dash cam with the service, but this is separate from the pilot.

“Drivers can use a separate dash cam, provided they comply with local laws,” an Uber representative told CNET in an email, “but Recorded Rides specifically matches riders with drivers recording through Record My Ride.”

Uber says it’s exploring additional ways to use recordings to keep its riders and drivers safe. It will soon begin proactively activating the Record My Ride feature on drivers’ devices during trips that may benefit from additional oversight, such as late-night or trips involving teenagers. Uber is also looking into automatically turning on video recordings “when trips are not proceeding as expected,” such as when a trip goes significantly off the projected course or if a crash is detected.

Uber says it’s also looking into testing the automatic activation of audio recording on riders’ phones during nighttime trips. Passengers would have to consent to this, which would require the app to use their phone’s microphone.

#3006. You won’t see a Galaxy Watch 10 until 2028 – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

In an effort to cut costs, Samsung is postponing the launch of the Galaxy Watch 10, according to reports. Here's what to know.

You might have to wait over a year to get the Samsung Galaxy Watch 10: Samsung will not release any new Galaxy smartwatch in 2027, South Korea’s ET News reported on Sunday.

In an effort to cut costs after two quarters of consecutive losses and amid global RAM shortages, Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Business division will switch from an annual release schedule to a biannual one for its smartwatches, according to ET News. The switch follows other cost-cutting measures that will reduce production of the tech giant’s midrange smartphone lineup while increasing its premium Galaxy S27 offerings.

I am not mad at this decision by Samsung. Annual smartwatch updates are usually iterative anyway. Take Apple, for example. Its Apple Watch Series 10, released in 2024, had the same chip as the Apple Watch Series 11, released a year later. The most recent Apple Watch, the Apple Watch Series 12, has the same battery life as the Apple Watch Series 11. I’d expect Apple to keep its new sensors, which debuted on the Series 12 and Ultra 4, for its Series 13 or Ultra 5 next year.

Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9, which debuted with a different chip and added a few more hours of battery, had the same bones as the Galaxy Watch 8.

If some of the biggest features on these smartwatches remain the same for a few years, why not change the release schedule to a biannual one?

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Galaxy Watch 8: I’ve compared both models, here’s my advice

Some of the most substantial updates that arrive on new devices like the Galaxy Watch 9 or Apple Watch Series 12 normally arrive through software updates, which end up landing on previous watch generations upon launch as well.

By switching from an annual release cycle to a biannual one, Samsung could drum up more excitement and anticipation between launches, and be able to surprise its customers with more purchase-worthy updates.

Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#3005. The Best Foldable Phones to Give This Holiday Season

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

For the tech enthusiast in your life, a foldable phone could be an interesting alternative to a traditional smartphone. We've rounded up our top picks, from book-style designs to flip phones.

If you’re shopping for someone this holiday season who deserves something a little more special — and you’ve got the budget to spare — a foldable phone can be a unique and practical gift that your loved one will use long after the holidays are over.

After reviewing our fair share of foldable phones, we’ve narrowed down our top three picks for the holidays and the perfect person on your list for each one. Who knows, you might end up caving in and treating yourself to a brand-new device? (You’ve been warned.)

For more mobile gift ideas, from budget-friendly smartphones to wearable devices, be sure to check out the video below.

The iPhone Duo is far from the first foldable phone, but as Apple’s debut into the market, it’s generated plenty of buzz. The Duo’s superpower is its ability to integrate hardware and software, creating a seamless experience across both displays.

The compact, 5.4-inch cover screen is great for sending texts and emails and checking notifications. The more expansive 7.6-inch inner display is ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working. It feels like using a smaller version of an iPad Mini that you can just fold up and toss in your pocket or bag.

The Duo is a great gift for someone who’s said they want a foldable phone, but refused to get one of the long-standing Android options already on the market. At last, Apple has its own offering that lets you stick with iOS. It’s a handy pick for people who often work on their phones and don’t always want to lug around a laptop. It’s also good for anyone who watches a lot of movies and TV shows on their mobile device. Plus, as a phone-tablet hybrid, it’s just fun to use.

The iPhone Duo isn’t perfect. It doesn’t support Face ID, but Apple did recently add an option to unlock the phone using the front camera. This isn’t as secure as Face ID, so you’ll still need to use Touch ID or a passcode for more sensitive functions like using Apple Pay or accessing passwords, and after around 45 minutes of inactivity.

The Duo’s cameras also aren’t as advanced as what you’ll get with the iPhone 18 Pro models, which have larger main-camera sensors and more advanced optical zoom capabilities. There’s also no telephoto camera on the Duo. Still, most people will be happy with the Duo’s 48-megapixel wide and ultrawide rear cameras, as well as the 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen. The FaceTime camera on the inner display is best suited for video calls rather than snapping quality photos.

Multitasking on the Duo is seamless, but it’s not as flexible as it is on other foldable phones. You can only have two apps open side by side, and you can’t readjust them.

Perhaps the biggest downside is the price. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. That’s why it’s a good idea to keep an eye out for any deals that can help lower the price.

For the Android-lover in your life, there’s no better foldable pick than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Like the iPhone Duo, this phone has a passport-size design. (Technically, Samsung beat Apple to the punch, but let’s refrain from the “Who Did It First?” game for now.)

The Z Fold 8 has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch inner display that’s great for watching videos, working and multitasking with up to three apps, which you can resize to your liking.

It’s also very thin, measuring 9.7mm thick when folded and 4.5mm thick when unfolded. That means it feels similar in thickness to a standard nonfolding phone, even when it’s closed. The Z Fold 8 fits squarely in a palm and easily slides into a pocket – tiny women’s pockets included.

Like the iPhone Duo, the Z Fold 8 doesn’t have a telephoto camera. But the 50-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras on the back and the 10-megapixel selfie cameras do a solid job.

The Z Fold 8 is also priced on the higher end, starting at $1,900 for 256GB. But its compact, sleek design and versatility help to make up for that sticker shock. Again, it’s a good idea to look out for any deals, especially around the holidays.

Some people prefer flip phones for their nostalgic designs and compact size. Motorola has plenty to choose from, but the best and most affordable pick for most people is the baseline 2026 Razr.

The phone features a classic clamshell design and a spacious 3.6-inch cover screen, making it easy to check notifications, reply to texts, control music or follow navigation without opening the phone. The 6.9-inch inner display feels like using an average nonfolding phone, even if the screen is a little narrower and taller.

For most people, the Razr’s 50-megapixel wide and ultrawide cameras and 32-megapixel selfie camera on the inner display will do the trick. There’s no room for a telephoto camera, but the Razr pulls its weight for more casual photography.

The Razr’s processor isn’t as powerful as what you’ll get on the pricier Razr Plus and Razr Ultra, but as long as you’re not playing intensive games all day, you probably won’t notice the difference.

The Razr’s $800 starting price is significantly lower than the cost of book-style folding devices like the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8. The Razr could be a more appealing option for someone who doesn’t need a phone-tablet hybrid but just wants a phone that’s fun to use and taps into the nostalgia of the original Motorola Razr.

No matter which phone you choose, your lucky recipient will enjoy the holiday spirit long after the season has passed, all while making quite the statement.

#3002. Uber, Nuro and Lucid Begin Fully Driverless Testing With Their Luxury Robotaxi

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi is one step closer to a commercial launch.

Nearly a year after showcasing their “luxurious” robotaxi at CES, Uber, Nuro and Lucid have started fully driverless testing on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area, the companies said Tuesday.

The partnership, announced in July 2025, combines Uber’s ride-hailing platform, Nuro’s self-driving technology and Lucid’s electric vehicles. Autonomous rides take place aboard the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, which I had the opportunity to see first at a CES showcase in January (in the form of a “production intent design”), and then on the road this summer, with a safety driver behind the wheel.

Now, the partnership is ready to take its next big step, beginning with employee rides “soon,” the companies said. They plan to launch commercial robotaxi operations in the first quarter of 2027 in the San Francisco Bay Area, before expanding to Houston later next year. Lucid will begin manufacturing the first vehicles designed specifically for the commercial launch fleet “in the coming weeks.” Uber plans to deploy around 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with the Nuro Driver in the coming years in “dozens” of cities.

“Removing the safety operator from behind the wheel is an important milestone in our partnership with Nuro and Lucid, and a testament to all three partners’ focus on executing against our shared roadmap,” Samarth Kejriwal, Uber’s global head of autonomous mobility, said in a statement. “As we prepare for our first driverless passenger rides in the coming months, we’ll be working closely together to refine our operations, infrastructure and the in-cabin experience to ensure a safer, more comfortable ride.”

Nuro says it’s been conducting “round-the-clock autonomous testing of the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area and Houston” since December 2025, with a safety driver in the vehicle who can take over if needed.

In May, Nuro received a California Public Utilities Commission Drivered Pilot Permit, giving the company the green light to conduct pilot testing for an autonomous passenger service with a safety driver. Nuro also received a California Department of Motor Vehicles Driverless Testing Permit in April, allowing it to test self-driving vehicles without a safety driver.

Uber’s partnership with Nuro and Lucid is just one of dozens it has with other AV companies, including Waymo, Zoox, Avride, Wayve and May Mobility. Adding driverless options to an app that’s likely already on someone’s phone could increase their chances of giving the experience a try — despite the trepidation many people have about self-driving vehicles.

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi can seat up to six passengers, unlike rides from Waymo and Zoox that seat up to four. It has plenty of legroom and ample space for luggage in the back. The vehicle’s sensor suite is equipped with cameras, lidar sensors and radars for autonomous navigation.

It’s been a big year for autonomous vehicles, and it appears 2027 will be no different. The rapid expansion of AVs comes amid heightened scrutiny. Last week, the California DMV banned Waymo’s robotaxis from state freeways after a series of high-profile incidents — after which Waymo paused all of its freeway rides. Waymo, the largest player in the AV space, has been involved in a number of other safety incidents as it expands to more cities. Over the years, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has launched investigations into other AV companies, including Zoox and Tesla.

It’s against this landscape — and the full-speed-ahead race toward autonomy — that Nuro, Uber and Lucid will soon publicly debut their own robotaxi.

#3001. College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

#3000. Claude can ship code for you now – how to try it (if you dare)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Would you let a few Claude agents review and ship your code for you?

Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it. A new feature from Anthropic is banking on more adventurous, agent-first coders being comfortable with handing even that last step off to AI.

With Claude Ship, announced in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward individual developers or companies who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

“Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic said. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

The new feature uses two new agents alongside Code Review, which Anthropic released in March for Teams and Enterprise plans. Code Review first collects, organizes, and posts findings to a PR. Then, Anthropic said, the agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, guide a PR “through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually.”

PR Steward can’t approve or merge pull requests, designed instead to participate “on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members.” It also documents what it changed in each push through comments and provides instructions for how to undo it, should developers want to. Throughout the process, developers can give Claude instructions or tell it to stop by commenting @claude.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free – how it went

As a final step, Claude Approvals references whatever policy the user or team abides by (which developers provide as a repo file), and additional signals developers set, like Code Review findings, before approving changes autonomously if allowed. If not, it will seek out “deeper human sign-off,” Anthropic said.

“It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file,” the release added. Anthropic said it recommends that most customers enable those additional checks “first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals’ green light.”

Admins can select which repos the feature runs in and adjust settings as needed.

But Claude Ship isn’t meant for everyone.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs.

ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz said the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective.

Also: Claude Code vs. Codex: Why I use both and how to choose one (if you must)

“But, it does depend on the team’s workflow and the kind of development they’re doing,” he said. “It’s not something for every team and certainly not for every indy developer, but for certain deployment processes, it could shave a ton of time off turnaround, saving money and potentially sending fixes to customers much faster. ‘Tis cool.”

Ultimately, Gewirtz said he has reasons to both trust the tool and be concerned about what it means for younger developers in the workplace.

“Since that workflow is often assigned to less experienced members of the team, it’s likely that Claude would be as accurate, although it’s one more way to shut the junior members out of where they add value to the company and grow their skills to become senior decision makers,” he said.

Developer platforms overall are adapting to the new state of the industry. Entire, a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents.

Individuals with a Pro, Max, or Ultra subscription can use the /ship command now available in Claude Code, meaning “users won’t notice any significant increase in token usage,” an Anthropic representative explained. Team and Enterprise users can use Claude Ship for Github repos, and it is billed on tokens, so your overall bill may change.

Still, that depends on the number of PRs users are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the new PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command.

Anthropic added that certain Enterprise organizations “can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming” by Jan. 15, 2027.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard

#2999. Epsilon Energy (EPSN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Powder River Basin and Permian wells drove a sharp production climb this quarter.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:23PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Epsilon Energy (EPSN +14.92%) reported a strategic shift toward accelerated development in the Powder River Basin and Permian Basin, focusing on high-return Parkman and Barnett targets. Management indicated that production growth was driven by new well completions and the outperformance of initial production rates relative to internal type curves. The company executed land transactions involving acreage trades and joint ventures to pull forward unconventional development through partnerships with larger-scale operators. Management stated that capital expenditures were focused on operated drilling programs and water infrastructure to support future cost efficiencies and recycling capabilities.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Epsilon Energy Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to Andrew Williamson, Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead.

J. Andrew Williamson: Thank you, operator. And on behalf of the management team, I would like to welcome all of you to today's conference call to review Epsilon's third quarter 2026 financial and operational results. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that our comments may include forward-looking statements. It should be noted that a variety of factors could cause Epsilon's actual results to differ materially from the anticipated results or expectations expressed in these forward-looking statements. Today's call may also contain certain non-GAAP financial measures. Please refer to the earnings release that we issued yesterday for disclosures on forward-looking statements and reconciliations of non-GAAP measures.

With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Jason Stabell, our Chief Executive Officer.

Jason Stabell: Thank you, Andrew, and good morning, everyone. Joining me today are Andrew Williamson, our CFO, and Henry Nelson Clanton, our COO. We will be available for questions following our prepared remarks. On our August call, we indicated that the second quarter would be the low point for production this year and that growth would be driven by our oil development in the Powder River Basin and the Permian. Our third quarter results reflect that trajectory. Oil production grew over 20% sequentially in the third quarter and nearly fourfold year-over-year, driven by a full quarter of contribution from our recent Permian well and the 2 Niobrara DUCs we completed in the Powder River Basin.

Total third quarter production was marginally higher quarter-over-quarter and would have been even higher had it not been for temporary shut-ins. In the Powder River Basin, we shut in our newest Niobrara wells for most of September during an offset operator's frac and took several wells offline for rod pump conversions. In the Marcellus, the operator took advantage of low natural gas prices to complete offset frac operations, compression upgrades and workovers, which all required temporary shut-ins. The Niobrara wells returned to production in late September with no apparent impact from the offset frac.

Our most consequential operational milestone of the quarter came in its final 3 days when we turned to sales the 3-well Bridle Bit pad, our first operated Parkman development in the Powder River Basin. The pad came online a month ahead of schedule and on budget and at IP30 rates that were approximately 30% above our type curve. Based on these results and the timely availability of the same drilling rig we contracted earlier in July, we accelerated our next 3-well Parkman pad by 2 months. We began drilling the three wells in early November, and they are expected online in 2027, most likely early in the second quarter after the winter weather abates in Wyoming.

During the third quarter, we also executed several land transactions with large-scale operators in the Powder River Basin. We traded acreage to join 2 EOG-operated units planned for 4-mile Niobrara laterals beginning in late 2027. In a separate transaction with a large private operator, we contributed acreage to a joint venture covering multiple drilling units in exchange for a carried interest and the opportunity to participate alongside the operator. These transactions high-grade our investment program.

They pull forward activity at very attractive rates of return on acreage where we had no development planned over the next 5 years, and they let us develop the Niobrara and Mowry on that acreage with partners who have the scale to do it very cost efficiently. In the Permian, Continental Resources closed its acquisition of our previous operator in the last week of September. Based on our initial discussions, we now expect 2 gross 0.5 net Barnett completions in December, with first production in early 2027. Previously, this development was expected in Q1 of next year. In the Marcellus, we expect incremental production from ongoing development to come online by February. Turning to current production.

With the Bridle Bit pad now online and our Niobrara wells back on production, fourth quarter net production through mid-November was approximately 7,900 BOE per day, including approximately 3,100 net barrels of oil per day. That is up approximately 40% compared to the third quarter daily sales figures. That sets up the fourth quarter for material sequential growth in production, revenue and cash flow. And as a result, we are affirming our full year production guidance. Overall, the story this quarter is execution. Our new wells are performing at or above expectations, at or below our capital estimates, and ahead of schedule.

We have also set up to pull forward high-return unconventional development through partnerships with high-quality operators in the basin. With new wells coming online across the Powder River Basin, Permian and Marcellus, we are positioned for an exciting period of growth in production, cash flow and shareholder value in 2027 and beyond. Andrew and Henry will now provide additional detail on our results, outlook and operations. Andrew, I'll turn it over to you.

J. Andrew Williamson: Thanks, Jason. For the quarter, production was up slightly quarter-over-quarter with declines in Marcellus gas production, offset by oil-weighted growth in the PRB and the Permian. As Jason mentioned, third quarter production came in slightly below expectation due to temporary shut-ins in the PRB and the Marcellus. With the new high working interest Parkman wells online ahead of schedule, we're seeing a step change in volume growth in the fourth quarter. As a result, we are affirming our oil and total production guidance for the year. Also on the quarter-over-quarter, adjusted EBITDA was up 50% on higher revenue in the PRB and lower overhead costs after the transition-related expenses related to last year's acquisition rolled off in the second quarter.

On the capital side, third quarter capital expenditures were $18.3 million, with the biggest contributors being the Bridle Bit Parkman wells and water facilities work in the Powder River Basin. Drilling on the two Barnett wells in the Permian also started during the quarter and is now complete. We expect those completions to start next month. As Jason noted, the increase in our full year capital guidance of approximately $8 million reflects activity pulled forward from 2027 into the fourth quarter in the PRB and the Permian. This is a timing change rather than a cost increase, and we expect a corresponding reduction in 2027 capital. Turning to the land transactions Jason described, neither transaction involved cash consideration.

Through the acreage trade, we now hold an approximately 8% working interest in the EOG-operated unit covering approximately 5,000 gross acres with 8 4-mile Niobrara wells planned for development starting in late 2027. Under the joint venture with a large private operator, we contributed a majority of our interest in 3 units in Campbell County, Wyoming, in exchange for a carried interest in the gross cost of 24 wells. That's 15 Nios and 9 Mowry set for development starting in 2028. We retain the option to participate with an incremental 14% working interest in addition to the carry.

Together, these transactions pull forward development of approximately 6 net locations normalized to 10,000-foot laterals at very attractive rates of return on acreage where we had no activity planned over the next 5 years. We have also been active in managing our commodity price risk. Over the course of this year, we have added to our oil hedge book at opportunistic times in a rising market, locking in attractive prices for 2027 and early 2028. These hedges help protect the cash flow that funds our development program as we move into a period of higher activity.

The 2026 trading activity has materially improved our hedge book, which had been weighed down by the legacy oil hedges we assumed in the Peak acquisition last year. That said, we retain significant oil price exposure, with well less than half of our expected 2027 oil production currently hedged. Our balance sheet remains in great shape. We ended the quarter with $42.5 million drawn on our credit facility with a leverage ratio of roughly 1x, calculated on net debt to trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA. And we expect to end the year well below our stated leverage target of 1.5x. Also, our fall borrowing base redetermination is underway, and we expect to announce the result this quarter.

Looking ahead to 2027, we expect higher activity across all three of our core areas, led by our operated Parkman development in Converse County in the Powder River Basin, continued Barnett development in the Permian and new Marcellus development signaled by our operator partner. We feel comfortable that this growth program can be undertaken while preserving the balance sheet. We plan to provide a formal 2027 capital budget and guidance with our fourth quarter 2026 results in the first quarter of next year. Now to Henry.

Henry Nelson Clanton: Thank you, Andrew, and good morning to everyone. Today, I'd like to begin with our operated assets in Wyoming. We executed two projects in the third quarter and both came in under budget and ahead of plan. Our 3-well Bridle Bit Parkman pad in Campbell County was our first operated drilling program with the post-acquisition integrated team, and it's going very well. The wells were drilled and completed and were placed on production late September, about a month ahead of plan. The wells have been tracking above forecast, and on a combined net basis, IP30 rates averaged just under 1,600 barrels of oil per day.

The wells were outfitted with production tubing prior to flowback, making them available for lift when needed. Currently, all three wells continue to flow under a managed choke protocol. As with our Niobrara wells, the production facilities were built out ahead of first production, which allowed the wells to be brought online without delay. Our two Niobrara wells, the Iberlin State pad, continued to perform above expectations with combined net IP30 rates just under 450 barrels of oil per day. While the wells were shut in for an offset operator's frac, we used the downtime to run production tubing and gas lift valves, making the wells available for lift when needed.

Both wells have returned to production at the same rates as before the shut-in with no apparent frac interference. In our Converse County acreage in the Powder River Basin, we had the opportunity to pull forward the development of a 3-well Parkman program in the Inot unit and have begun drilling 2 months ahead of plan. Currently, drilling operations are progressing per plan, with drilling expected to be completed in December. These are 2-mile laterals in which we hold approximately 75% working interest. Completions are planned for the spring, and first production is expected in the second quarter of 2027. Regarding frac water sourcing, our Inot water impoundment facility is complete with approximately 1.15 million barrels of storage.

We are currently drilling the water supply well, which is expected to provide approximately 10,000 barrels per day. The facility will supply all of the water required for these completions. And as I mentioned last quarter, it has been designed to handle produced water recycling in the future, which would lower our water sourcing and disposal costs. Regarding our operating cost, the compressor rightsizing program is essentially complete, with 22 units being replaced and 1 remaining this month. Gross savings now exceed $110,000 per month. We have also downgraded electric service at 39 locations, with 27 more planned in January, and expect $18,000 gross monthly reduction in operating costs from this program.

In the Permian, our first 3-mile Barnett well, the Patricia Unit 1H, has now been on production since May with normalized rates consistent with the Barnett peers. The Woodford appraisal well mentioned in prior calls was completed and placed on production in September. Early flowback data is being evaluated, and we will continue to monitor its performance as it relates to our future inventory on our acreage. During the quarter, operatorship of the project has transitioned to Continental Resources. Two additional Barnett wells have been drilled, with completions scheduled before year-end. Based upon initial discussions with a new operator, 3 to 4 additional Barnett wells are planned to spud before year-end, including the first 4-mile lateral in the project.

We are encouraged by the operator's early engagement and the expected accelerated development cadence and scaled efficiencies, and we will provide more detail as the program is finalized. In the Marcellus, the 3-well Shevrohesky pad was placed on production in mid-September. The operator plans to complete the 4-well Reilly pad in December, with first production expected by February. A combined net production of 7 million cubic foot a day is expected from these two pads. Now I'll turn it back to Jason.

Jason Stabell: Thanks, guys. Operator, we can now open the lines for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Anthony Perala with Punch & Associates.

Anthony Perala: First off, Henry touched on it a little bit at the end of his remarks, but just if you could give an overview of what you're hearing from the operator in the Marcellus in what's been a weaker shoulder season here? And if there's any changes to planned 2027 activity that we've, kind of -- that you've outlined this year so far as we look into next year?

Jason Stabell: Anthony, this is Jason. Thanks for the question. No indications of change from the operators. Henry mentioned the Reilly pad, which -- of the 2 that he mentioned, so the Shevrohesky pad, which came online in September, we have a very small working interest in that. The Reilly pad is much more meaningful to us. So it makes up the vast majority of that 7 million cubic feet of incremental production net that we expect to see by February. So that all seems to time out with our anticipation that they're going to bring those volumes into a stronger winter market. Obviously, there's been some concern about the weather. We just have to, kind of, wait and see.

But right now, natural gas prices have firmed a little bit. And as we usually see in the Marcellus, we should see our basis differential come in quite a bit. So we historically go from $1 or more differential to Henry Hub to something approaching $0.30 to $0.40. As far as next year's activity, we usually sit down with the operator in December to get a more firm view of their year-ahead plans. So I have no indications that they have any changes with what we've been looking for in 2027. But obviously, if we get updated information, we're going to communicate it in our next sit-down with investors and shareholders.

Anthony Perala: That's great. Yes, kind of, as expected to bring in the stronger winter season, like, you had highlighted. Switching over to the oil development, a lot of moving pieces, nice to see things moved forward rather than to the right. But it seems, like, more to come on the Barnett development as Continental firms up their view. Could you just remind us with some of that activity in the PRB being moved forward, what initial thoughts are for your operated activity in the PRB for 2027?

Jason Stabell: Sure. I'll -- this is Jason again. I can take that, and then if Andrew or Henry have any additions, they can add to it. But as we mentioned in my -- in the press release quote, our operated focus is going to be Parkman. We have two 3-well Parkman pads in Converse County, what we call the Inot unit. The first 3-well pad, we had an opportunity to get that same drilling rig that we were really happy with the performance on this summer, and we're able to slot that in before it got real cold up in Wyoming. And so we took advantage of that. So that pulled forward the drilling.

On the completion side, we're right now talking to pressure pumpers and service providers. But our current thinking is that we're going to be fracking that first 3-well Inot pad in the early part of the third quarter. And then we have a second 3-well Parkman pad in that same Inot unit that right now, we're, kind of, thinking of a mid-next-year spud on those three wells. So that would mean completion coming probably sometime in the third quarter on the operated side. Henry or Andrew, anything to add on that?

Henry Nelson Clanton: Yes. This is Henry. So Jason, I think you mentioned the completions were scheduled for the Inot wells that we're drilling currently. For Q3, we actually are going to be planning those Q1, sorry. So we're looking at pressure pumping services for the wells that we're drilling now. We've got two of the three drilled on our third one as we speak, with pressure pumping, as I was mentioning, scheduled for late Q1, early Q2. We think that the plan looks achievable for us to get those online in Q2.

Jason Stabell: And then, Anthony, you asked about the Permian. Yes, we're really excited to have Continental as the partner. They obviously know the basin very well. They have -- I think the last I checked, they had six rigs running in addition to the rigs that they picked up in the FireBird transaction, including the FireBird rigs that they picked up. So -- and the early indications we have, we'll have some additional sit-down with them to really firm up their view of 2027 plans. But as Henry mentioned, they've indicated to us that there could be additional activity on top of the two wells that we're currently completing that could spud in mid- to late December.

So excited about that, particularly that 4-miler. That will be the first 4-miler in the project. So I think next year could be just as we've been communicating to shareholders and investors, an uptick there, which we're really excited about because we love that asset. Henry, anything else on that?

Henry Nelson Clanton: Yes. I'd just say we've got the 10 producing wells now. We've got the two Western offsets to the Patricia well, the first three-milers Jason mentioned that are drilled and uncompleted. Actual frac operations have begun this week. So those are ongoing with plans to drill two eastern offsets to the Patricia well as well as the 4-miler. So yes, exciting time.

Anthony Perala: Has there been any more data or takeaway from -- I think it was the Woodford bench test well that was drilled this summer that could expand the resource?

Jason Stabell: Henry, why don't you take that one?

Henry Nelson Clanton: Sure. So yes, the well was drilled and completed. A lot of moving parts on it, where the lateral was landed, the length it was, the type of completion that was applied, the flowback technique, the artificial lift that's on it. We're watching it with a lot of interest. It's too early yet to make any technical or economic conclusions and what its potential impact for our development might be over the top of it. But we'll be -- as we firm up decisions and understand the data better, we'll be providing feedback on that. I can say that it did have similar pressures to its Barnett peers. It's productive. They're going to be drilled starting in '28 through 2031.

Nicholas Pope: Got it. And this is just a carve-out that 5,200 acres of the broader 30 -- I guess, you are 38,000 something in the Powder River. Is that right? 37,000?

J. Andrew Williamson: Yes, that's a gross acreage figure, the 5,200; our net there is less than that. So that's a gross acreage figure. And all of that, kind of, making sense commercially from an implied per acre value on the carried interest and that better cost structure participation.

Nicholas Pope: Got it. Excellent. I appreciate that. Additionally, I was looking -- there was an other income line item that seems to have been fairly meaningful in the quarter. It looks like it's something related to water disposal in Wyoming. And I was curious, is that something that's sustainable, potentially growing? Just trying to get some understanding of what that new line item was for other income. I think it was a little over $1 million for the quarter.

J. Andrew Williamson: Yes, Nick, there's two things in there. Part of that is the water facility revenue that we generate selling water to third parties out of our water infrastructure in the Powder. We sold down some interest as we've messaged to the market previously in that Bridle Bit Parkman pad that just came online and got a spud fee or a promote there upfront from our partner. So that's included there as well. I think that's a mechanism that we think about on the operated side in the Powder as we think about, kind of, rightsizing interest in some of these developments.

That's a good lever that we can pull to sell down some interest and get a spud fee and improves our economics there with that spud fee. And we, kind of, do it on a case-by-case basis, but we'll use that lever if we need to, to rightsize the capital program.

Nicholas Pope: That makes sense. And so nothing related to this new -- the water impoundment stuff, that's purely a cost-saving measure for you guys on the operating cost side?
