TL;DR: Surging tech stocks aren't great news for bonds, or for mortgage rates.

Mortgage rates have had some substantial day-over-day swings lately, and today, unfortunately it's an upward swing.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.38% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points higher than yesterday and four basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Recently news about big tech has often pulled rates down. Investor concerns about AI profitability keep cropping up, and when they do, tech stocks and bonds lose their appeal and Treasuries have been picking up the slack. Mortgage rates are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury, and Treasury prices and yields move inversely. More demand for the 10YT drives prices up, and sends yields (and thus, mortgage rates) down.

Today's the opposite, though. Investors are having a bout of tech exuberance as Jensen Huang got reinstated as Nvidia CEO, and lots of excitement about tech stocks and bonds means less enthusiasm for Treasuries.

Here's the thing, though: Markets are fickle. They also move fast. And they aren't the only influence on mortgage rates.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Lately, we've seen two narratives influencing mortgage rates battling it out; depending on which one's stronger, daily rates move higher or lower. Up top I talked about how shifting perceptions of big tech have been driving mortgage rates (and yes, today, pushing them higher, though usually it's pulled rates down.) When rates are moving higher, more often it's been thanks to inflation — and while it's a lightweight work week, we're about to get heavyweight inflation news.

The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely.

The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation, so you can guess how things are likely to go at the Fed's December meeting. Markets already feel fairly certain about a quarter-percent rate hike.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out Wednesday morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

And speaking of: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

P.S.: I don't have to ask if anyone's playing Grand Theft Auto 'cause c'mon, of course. But did anyone else perk up when Lu asked about home loans? Yeah, that was probably just me. Jason and Lucia would have to change a lot about their lifestyle to qualify (we know they're working on building credit, but having all your income be cash you can't really document is not going to work for a lender). But hey, I'm rooting for them.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.88% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#2986. Did Nvidia Make a Big Mistake by Reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO so Quickly?

It took less than two weeks after resigning for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 24, 2026 at 3:45PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) made a big announcement yesterday: Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. It was a sharp and seemingly sudden turnaround from recent days when it looked as though the company's board was ready to move on with Colette Kress as its Interim CEO while it took a long look at the situation and considered a permanent replacement.

While many investors were likely bracing for a potentially long, drawn-out process, that didn't end up happening. Instead, on Monday morning, news came out that Huang was back. Will that prove to be a big mistake?

Nvidia's board was clearly swayed by the U.S. president, who said he was behind the deal to bring Huang back as CEO. While he provided assurances that there weren't national security risks, the fact that an investigation remains ongoing raises questions about whether that assessment might ultimately change.

It also calls into question how the president convinced the board so quickly to reinstate Huang, especially since it recently said it wasn't considering making the move at all. To do a complete 180 so quickly is definitely surprising. It certainly looked as though the board had moved on from Huang.

Although the tech stock was sinking amid news of Huang's resignation, the move to reinstate Huang seemed rushed, calling into question the board's overall governance. It did, however, state in its decision to reinstate Huang that the investigation "will proceed to conclusion." But given that Huang has already been reinstated, it would be an even worse look for the board to change its mind yet again.

Meanwhile, Huang is still scheduled to meet with Congress relating to his involvement with a possible Chinese spy. The issues related to Huang are by no means resolved, and the board's quick and sudden move to reinstate him could end up backfiring if more serious issues are indeed uncovered.

Nvidia's board effectively caved. Even before the president stepped in, it appeared that with the massive decline in Nvidia's share price, the market had spoken -- it wanted Huang back. I believe even without the president's push, Huang would have returned as CEO; it may have just taken a bit longer.

While it is disappointing to see the board not diligently and thoroughly investigate the matter first before making a decision, I don't believe it'll prove to have any lasting or serious effects on the stock. For the time being, it didn't appear to have much of a choice given the stock's massive sell-off.

Nvidia remains a top tech stock to own, and any issues relating to Huang likely aren't going to be enough to weigh on its future. In fact, now can be a good time to buy the stock, as its valuation has taken a beating in recent weeks.

#2984. I Rate Buy Now, Pay Later Apps; Here’s My Holiday Advice

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

“Buy now, pay later” can help stretch your holiday budget further, but pick your BNPL app carefully and avoid loan stacking.

Head of Content, Personal & Student Loans

As Americans compile their shopping lists ahead of the holiday season, I’ve been compiling my own kind of list — a list of 25 data points, gathered across six “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) apps, fed into a rubric of five categories and 22 subcategories, to produce a star rating for each app.

It’s a big list. I check it twice (or 10 times).

By the end, I know more about these apps than anyone should, and I’m eager to bestow my knowledge on the next unsuspecting person who utters “Klarna” in my vicinity.

I should have plenty of opportunities this year. Nearly 2 in 5 holiday spenders (38%) plan to use BNPL, according to NerdWallet’s holiday spending report. Concerningly, the same report found that a higher share of BNPL users expect they won’t be able to make their payments in full and on time compared to credit card users.

Using BNPL for holiday shopping isn’t inherently bad, but there are risks, including sneaky fees and the ease of loan stacking across many providers.

Here’s how to minimize those risks and set yourself up for success this holiday season.

Brenton Harrison, a certified financial planner in Nashville, says many of his clients are turning to buy now, pay later in the “messy middle of life,” when everyday expenses are high and budgets are tight. This is especially true during the holidays.

“They have kids they're providing for, or they’re trying to go travel and see family,” Harrison says. “When those expenses pile up, it can be very attractive to be able to spread out payments.”

Since BNPL divides your total purchase into smaller installments, typically due every two weeks, it feels easier on your cash flow than having to pay all at once.

While Harrison is open to his clients using BNPL, he emphasizes how important it is to understand the terms before opting in. BNPL apps only require a soft credit pull and a short application. When you can apply for a loan in just a few clicks, it’s easy to miss when payments are due or whether they’ll include interest.

But if clients understand the terms and are certain they can make the payments, Harrison says BNPL's set repayment schedule can be a better option than more open-ended financing.

“With a credit card, [a holiday purchase] might be something that they buy over and over and over again, because that interest just continues to accrue over time, and they never pay it off,” he says.

Not all BNPL apps are created equal. I measure the top apps across multiple categories, but I weigh affordability the highest. My thinking is if you’re already strapped for cash, it’s a bad idea to pay extra just to break up the payments.

There are providers, like Affirm and PayPal, that don’t charge interest with a common pay-in-four term (your total purchase, divided into four installments). They also charge no fees, including no late fees for missed payments.

Compare that to apps, like Sezzle and Zip, that may charge an automatic service or origination fee with your first installment, as well as late fees.

Long-term BNPL financing, which can stretch months or even years, usually includes interest, expressed as an annual percentage rate or APR. This is a more expensive payment option than a zero-interest pay-in-four.

Pay close attention to your checkout screen to see what you’re offered. Are the installment amounts equal or is the first installment higher than the others? That may mean there’s a fee. Do you see an APR listed? That means you’re paying interest.

Harrison points out that just because a store partners with a BNPL company doesn’t mean that’s your only option. Download a different BNPL app, search for the store and see if you get access to better terms, like a 0% offer.

Taking out multiple loans with different BNPL providers is known as “loan stacking,” and it’s risky.

Because you’re juggling different payment amounts due on different days, it’s hard to keep track of what’s coming out of your bank account. This is especially true if you set up automatic payments, which most BNPL apps require. If you overdraw your checking account, your bank will likely charge a fee.

According to research published in August by the Federal Reserve, 11% percent of BNPL users had a BNPL payment trigger an overdraft or nonsufficient funds fee from their bank in the prior year. People with less savings were even more likely to pay fees.

Before applying for multiple BNPL loans, look at a typical month of expenses and ask if there’s extra room in your budget for those payments, Harrison says.

“If you’re just assuming that because you’re spreading it out that you’ll be able to pay it, that's where I think people can get in trouble,” he says. “They set it and forget it, and they don't realize, ‘Oh, I am in no better position to pay that next month than I am this month, or I have three of these going at the same time, and collectively, it's more than I can manage.’”

Most apps send payment reminders, so you can potentially reschedule the payment or change your payment method.

Still, it’s best to avoid the headache to begin with. If you’re feeling pressured to spend more this holiday season, communicate your limits clearly with loved ones, Harrison says, and avoid any loans you can’t comfortably repay.

“Think about the purchase itself, especially around the holidays,” he says. “There's a big difference between something that I can pay off over three months and something that I should have never been buying in the first place.”

#2981. ​How Much Autonomy Is Too Much For An AI Agent?

Alexey Spas is the founder and CEO of Instinctools, a software engineering company focused on AI-powered digital solutions.

​What happens when an AI agent you trust breaks its limits of autonomy and won’t take no for an answer?​​

Neither the Australian nor the Canadian government was prepared for this kind of trespassing, yet it happened to their websites. An OpenAI model gained unauthorized access to Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service while researching public medical spending, while an unidentified AI agent attempted to hack Canada’s Library and Archives website. Neither incident resulted in a confirmed compromise of individual records or government systems, but both involved AI agents taking actions beyond their intended research tasks. The activity occurred in May and June 2026 but wasn’t publicly disclosed until September, when OpenAI and the research lab Transluce independently reported their findings.​​​

What this signals to me is that AI agents are forcing both public and private sectors to raise the drawbridge against a threat they didn’t even know was coming. For companies deploying agents at scale, the governance challenge extends beyond choosing a theoretical level of autonomy to ensuring that abnormal behavior can be detected, contained, reconstructed and assigned to a responsible owner.​

MIT recognizes five levels of AI agent autonomy. Starting from level 3, as the human gradually steps back to give the agent more room to act, a handoff problem arises. The system needs to recognize where its authority ends and when escalation to a human is required. The harder failure mode appears when an agent continues pursuing a legitimate goal after crossing that boundary, despite signals telling it to stop.​

This suggests a useful operating principle: the autonomy granted to AI agents can’t safely outpace the maturity of the company’s incident response and AI governance policies. Policies on paper are not enough; they need to be enacted. That maturity rests on four capabilities:

1. Detection: Identifying unusual actions as they happen

2. Investigation: Tracing back the agent’s actions

3. Response: Stopping agent activity and rolling back or mitigating the consequences

4. Accountability: Establishing clear responsibility when an agent’s actions affect a person or a company

A weakness in any one of those capabilities raises the cost of failure: unusual behavior may go unnoticed, incidents may be harder to reconstruct, containment may come too late or responsibility may remain unclear when an agent’s actions affect people or business operations.

Not every scenario can be rehearsed in advance. So the decision to give an agent any degree of autonomy depends on answering a few questions first:​

Every consequential output should have a way to be checked—a second system, a source link or a human-created reference—before the agent is allowed to act on it.​

The Medicare case above illustrates what can happen when an agent treats a block as something to overcome rather than a boundary to respect. A block should stop an agent in its tracks and trigger escalation to a human. It shouldn’t become an obstacle to work around.​

Impact should be classified by severity and blast radius. An agent accessing a public webpage poses a different level of risk than one accessing an internal server or sensitive business systems. The more sensitive the data and consequential the actions an agent can access, the tighter its permissions, oversight and safeguards should be.​

When several vendors are involved, incident ownership can’t fall through the cracks. From where I stand, someone on the customer side needs to be ultimately accountable, even if detection, investigation or remediation depends on external providers. That means defining from the get-go who detects an incident, who notifies whom and who can switch the agent off.

The autonomy ladder can only be climbed when the evidence is there. Autonomy should be earned, with each traceable and reviewable log supporting more trust in the agent. The ladder also runs downward. When the environment, model, tools or performance indicators change, the autonomy limits narrow again until the evidence rebuilds.​

Anthropic found an interesting pattern: new Claude Code users enable auto-approve about 20% of the time. Past 750 sessions, this rate rises to 40%. Yet experienced users also interrupted their agents more often. Anthropic reinforces that effective oversight is not about approving each action but being able to intervene when necessary.​

Enterprise deployments can follow the same principle: greater trust should lead to more selective oversight, not less accountability. Rather than relying on subjective confidence in an agent, organizations can use operational metrics to determine whether its autonomy is justified and where additional controls may be needed. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework Playbook similarly emphasizes incident tracking, response planning and human oversight. Some useful indicators include:​

• How often humans intervene or override an agent​

• The frequency of rejected or blocked actions​

• How often actions require rollback or remediation​

• Actions that fall outside expected behavioral patterns​

• Incidents categorized by action type and severity​

For a professional services group’s AI operational platform developed at Instinctools, the autonomy was phased in: the low-risk employee assistant agent was deployed before higher-risk quoting and advisory agents. The email triage agent only reached all the business units after its accuracy was raised from 74% to 87%, past the client’s 85% target.

Following MIT’s definition of five autonomy levels mentioned above, I keep returning to this distinction between agents’ autonomy and humans’ authority. Freedom to act within defined boundaries belongs to agents. But authority stays with humans who answer for what agents do and decide if and when their scope is ready to grow.​

The test is simple: deploy only those agents that stop when told no and only when you have a framework in place to watch and contain them, investigate what happened and take responsibility if needed. If an agent can reason its way around a limit, it’s not a limit.​​

Management noted that the mainland Chinese retail client contribution to both revenue and assets continued to decline, in compliance with regulatory adjustments implemented since May 2022. Strategic focus has transitioned toward expanding wealth management services and extending 24/5 trading capabilities to global markets.

#2976. Etihad’s New Credit Cards Are Primarily for Status Chasers

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The new cards offer perks like faster paths to status and elevated earning rates when purchasing tickets with partners.

Etihad Guest, the loyalty program of Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, is expanding its U.S. presence by introducing two new credit cards. Most people won’t get much value from these cards, but they can make sense for Etihad frequent flyers who want elite status.

The two cards are the Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card ($99 annual fee) and the Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card ($499 annual fee). Issued by the First National Bank of Omaha, both offer faster pathways to earning and maintaining elite status and the ability to earn extra miles on Etihad purchases.

They also offer extra miles on international transactions (neither has foreign transaction fees) and purchases with Etihad’s partner airlines, which include U.S. carriers like American Airlines and JetBlue Airways.

Here’s what you need to know about the cards.

The Etihad Guest Visa Signature® Card comes with a $99 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the card is offering the following welcome offer for new applicants: Earn up to 40,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 10,000 miles after the first purchase and an additional 30,000 miles after spending $3,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: You’ll also get Etihad Silver status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account. Unlike most airlines, that entry-level status is enough to get you into the business class lounge when traveling through Etihad’s hub at Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport.

You can retain that status by spending $20,000 a year on the card, or $3,000 a year on Etihad purchases.

The Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature® Card comes with a $499 annual fee, and it earns Etihad Guest miles at the following rates:

5 miles per $1 spent on Etihad purchases.

3 miles per $1 spent on Etihad partner airline purchases.

2 miles per $1 spent on non-U.S. purchases.

1 mile per $1 spent on all other U.S. purchases.

The only differences in rewards between the premium and standard cards are increased earning rates for eligible airline purchases.

Welcome offer: Through Feb. 3, 2027, the premium card offers a higher welcome offer compared to the standard card: Earn up to 60,000 welcome Etihad Guest Miles, including 20,000 miles after the first purchase and 40,000 miles after spending $7,000 within the first three billing cycles after account opening.

Elite status benefits: The premium card offers a faster track to elite status: automatic Silver status upon card approval and Gold status after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days of opening your account.

To maintain Gold status, you’ll need to spend $40,000 a year on the card, or $8,000 on Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you’ll have Silver status.

Wi-Fi benefit: After your first Etihad purchase, you’ll get 3,000 Etihad Guest miles, enough to cover Wi-Fi costs on a long-haul Etihad flight. You’ll then get those miles again after each cardholder anniversary.

Travel benefits: The card offers a statement credit for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck and select travel protections. If you already have a premium travel card, you might already have access to these perks.

The card also includes a Priority Pass lounge access membership. However, an Etihad spokesperson told NerdWallet that it’s the entry-level membership tier, so you’ll need to pay for yourself and guests each time you visit a Priority Pass lounge. Most premium credit cards in the U.S. that offer Priority Pass allow complimentary visits for at least the cardholder.

The Etihad cards make the most sense for Etihad’s frequent flyers who are flying to or connecting through Abu Dhabi several times a year.

That’s because the standard card’s accelerated pathway to Etihad Guest’s Silver status tier can unlock the ability to choose business class lounge access in Abu Dhabi as a status perk.

With the premium card, you get a fast track to Gold. If you select lounge access as a Gold status perk, you can not only bring a guest on the same flight into the lounge, but also access Etihad’s worldwide lounge network. That includes Etihad’s own lounges in New York and Washington, D.C., as well as most partner lounges at other Etihad destinations.

Bear in mind that while Etihad has many partnerships with other airlines, it’s not part of an alliance, so you don’t get lounge benefits when traveling on partners. You’ll need to be flying on an Etihad-operated flight to get into the lounge.

If you primarily fly with other carriers, then Etihad status will have limited upside for you.

However, the Priority Pass lounge membership that comes with the premium card does not have that restriction. You can access Priority Pass lounges while flying on any airline, although you’ll need to pay an additional per-person $35 fee each visit.

The earning rates on the Etihad cards are lackluster for everyday spenders. The bonus categories are for airline purchases with Etihad and its partners, as well as international spending.

That means your day-to-day purchases at home, like groceries, dining out and gas, earn only 1 mile per $1 spent.

Plus, there are more ways to earn Etihad Guest miles than spending on an Etihad credit card. For example, you can transfer points to Etihad Guest from Bilt Rewards, Capital One and Citi ThankYou.

Those programs offer cards that typically have better benefits and bonus categories, and they offer flexibility on how you can use your points and miles. With an Etihad card, you can only earn Etihad Guest miles, which expire after 18 months without qualifying flight activity. (If you’re not traveling on Etihad or its partners at least once every 18 months, then you definitely should not get the cards.)

One of the most interesting perks of the new cards is the bonus category for spending with Etihad partner airlines — 2 miles per $1 for the standard card and 3 miles per $1 for the premium version. Typically, airline credit cards reward customers only for spending on the airline, not partners.

There are better cards available, though. Some offer as many or even more points per $1 on flights purchased directly from airlines.

If you want the card solely to earn more Etihad Guest miles, then the answer for most people is no.

While you can earn more miles for purchases with Etihad and partner airlines, the earning rates aren’t attractive enough to justify the annual fees, especially when compared with existing cards with currencies that transfer to Etihad Guest.

Status chasers could benefit from the fast track to elite status — but you would need to be a fairly frequent Etihad flyer to really take advantage of your elite benefits.

You want a travel credit card that prioritizes what’s important to you. Here are some of the best travel credit cards of 2026:

Flexibility, point transfers and a large bonus: Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card

No annual fee: Wells Fargo Autograph® Card

Flat-rate travel rewards: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

Bonus travel rewards and high-end perks: Chase Sapphire Reserve®

Luxury perks: American Express Platinum Card®

Business travelers: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card

#2974. B2B Companies Should Stop Letting B2C Set Their Digital Commerce Roadmap

Jary Carter is CEO and Co-Founder of Oro Inc., the company behind OroCommerce, a B2B eCommerce platform for manufacturers and distributors.

​For years, B2B companies have taken their cues on digital progress from consumer commerce. Amazon was treated as the model that B2B would eventually have to follow, with every buying experience starting to look more like Amazon.

As the CEO of an e-commerce platform who works closely with B2B partners, I can tell you that never happened. Amazon became another channel, not the blueprint for B2B commerce.​

Now agentic purchasing is getting similar treatment. B2B companies have seen this pattern before: A consumer trend gets treated as the future of commerce before anyone asks how well it fits B2B.

So what happens when that thinking starts setting the digital commerce roadmap?

Consumer commerce tends to treat less human involvement as progress. Search, buy, check out, done.​

B2B buyers want plenty of independence, too. But taking the seller out of the experience can take valuable context out with them. ​

For many B2B companies, the seller’s knowledge of the customer is part of the competitive advantage. Digital commerce should build on that advantage, not erase it.​

One specialty distributor we work with learned this the hard way. Its first e-commerce launch struggled so badly that leadership questioned whether digital selling made sense for the business at all. The team later described the experience as “anonymous e-commerce” because it separated buyers from their account context and the people who knew them.​

On its second attempt, the company brought account management straight into the digital experience. Customers could see their dedicated rep inside the portal, while sales and service staff used impersonation to handle onboarding, guide first orders and troubleshoot on the fly.​

Buyers still get the independence they wanted. The difference is that going digital no longer cuts them off from the people who know their account.​

A retail-style roadmap can make the seller look like friction to remove. In B2B, digital commerce should do the opposite: Give the buyer-seller relationship a place to continue online.

The same problem shows up in how commerce teams define flexibility. The conversation often stays at the experience layer: change the storefront faster, launch a new journey, test a different way to buy.​

Useful. But B2B companies usually discover the limits of their technology somewhere else.​

Can you bring an acquired business onto the same setup when it has a different ERP? Add a region with its own catalog and pricing rules? Change an approval process or introduce a new sales model without rebuilding half the system?​

A company can have a highly flexible front end and still struggle with changes like these. Being able to redesign the buying experience quickly doesn’t mean the commerce setup can adapt quickly to the business behind it.​​

For B2B, flexibility is tested when the business changes, not when the homepage does. The roadmap has to account for that.

AI is the newest version of the same pattern. Retail attention has centered on shopping agents, conversational discovery and AI that can research or complete a purchase.

Those ideas may have a place in B2B, too. They just aren’t automatically the best place to start.​

In B2B, AI can play a different role: help sellers know their buyers better, surface customer and deal information faster and take repetitive work out of the sales process.​

While my company’s platform offers AI features, which certainly shapes my view on this topic, the shift I’m pointing to is about identifying where AI makes the most sense in B2B rather than which tools to adopt. ​

More than 75% of B2B orders still arrive through email, PDFs, spreadsheets, voicemail or handwritten notes, according to Distribution Strategy Group. Their research found that AI-based order processing can deliver productivity gains of 20% to 30%. Gartner also found that AI is already saving sellers an average of 4.8 hours per week.​

Some of the highest-value AI in B2B may sit far from the storefront. That is why copying the retail roadmap can send investment toward the most visible use cases instead of the most valuable ones.

Watch what B2C does with search, usability and convenience. But it should not decide what progress looks like for your B2B business. ​

The next priority should come from the processes your company needs to improve, the relationships it needs to strengthen and the markets it plans to enter. Use retail for inspiration. But don’t adopt its story. B2B has a more interesting one to tell. ​

#2969. Why Connectivity Needs To Become Programmable

Mobile networks were designed with a person at the end of every connection. A contract carries a name, and a plan is sized for one phone. When something breaks, someone calls support or walks into a store.

That design fits a shrinking share of the people and things now using networks. Delivery robots, connected cars, smart meters and medical wearables are among the fastest-growing users, and none of them has a name on a contract. At the same time, AI assistants handle more everyday tasks for people, but connectivity is still largely out of their reach.

After years of building connectivity for travelers and distributed teams, I see these as one problem. Whether the user is a person or a device, the connection should be set up and managed through software. In other words, connectivity has to become programmable.

But machines don’t sign contracts, so someone has to own the relationship on their behalf. They also move: A sensor shipped from a factory in Poland may spend its working life in Brazil. Their usage looks nothing like a person’s. A smart meter sends a few kilobytes a day for 10 years, while a robotaxi can move gigabytes in an afternoon, and a consumer-style plan suits neither.

People run into the same friction, though it’s less visible. In our support conversations, the hardest questions are usually about status rather than speed: Is my plan active? Why did data stop at the border? Which line am I paying for? A well-designed system should answer those without requiring a support ticket.

Ericsson counted around 4.5 billion cellular IoT connections at the end of 2025 and expects that number to approach 8 billion by 2031. Its June 2026 Mobility Report also notes that uplink traffic is growing faster than downlink for most operators, and that additional AI traffic could push uplink to three times its 2025 level by 2031.

Software is also starting to act for people. Gartner predicted that 40% of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. If an assistant can book your hotel, people will reasonably expect it to get them online at the destination as well. Today, that step usually leads to a QR code or a carrier portal designed for manual clicks.

Put these trends together, and more connectivity decisions will be made by software acting on someone’s behalf.

A SIM in every device connects the device, but it doesn’t make the connection manageable. Programmable connectivity means the connection itself can be requested, switched, limited and retired through APIs, much as cloud platforms let teams manage servers. I think that requires four capabilities.

• Delegated Identity: Every connection should be traceable to an accountable owner such as a company or a fleet operator, even when software manages it. Otherwise, fraud and misuse are very hard to attribute.

• Programmatic Provisioning: Devices without screens can’t scan QR codes. The GSMA’s SGP.32 specification already allows eSIM profiles on IoT devices to be downloaded, switched and retired remotely. The next step is exposing that capability through APIs, so a fleet platform, an app or an AI assistant can arrange connectivity on demand.

• Policy And Spend Controls: Software should manage connectivity within set limits: which networks, which regions, how much data and what maximum cost. Finance teams already set budgets for cloud usage, and connectivity should work the same way.

• Life Cycle Portability: A connected car or medical device may outlive three generations of network technology and several carrier contracts. Its connectivity has to move with it, across borders and providers, without anyone opening the casing.

Our enterprise customers rarely struggle with the first activation. Problems tend to come months later, when an employee relocates or a device changes hands. Those are the moments where programmable connectivity saves the most time.

A fair objection is that operators will build this themselves, and some already are. Network slicing reserves guaranteed performance for specific use cases, and Ericsson counted 84 commercial offerings built on it in June 2026, up from 65 seven months earlier.

I see the roles as complementary. An operator runs its own network. A platform layer works across networks: countries, operators, device types and budgets. A car built in Germany, sold in Brazil and driven across borders needs both.

I learned this from travel. Travelers plan around destinations, such as Lisbon on Monday and Madrid on Thursday, rather than around operators. The platform’s job is to match that plan with the right network at the right price, without asking anyone to understand roaming agreements. eSIM is what makes this workable: Because the SIM profile is software, a a network identity can be switched or retired remotely, whether on a phone or on a sensor bolted to a shipping container.

Imagine booking a trip through an assistant that, with your permission, also arranges a local data plan within a budget you’ve set. You land, turn off airplane mode and you’re online.

For the person at the center, programmable connectivity should mean fewer decisions. People don’t want to have to compare roaming rates, scan QR codes or follow up on support tickets. Connectivity works best when people don’t have to think about it, and making it programmable is a practical way to get there.​

#2967. What Is a Reconditioning Fee on a Used Car?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Used-car dealers may charge you a reconditioning fee to cover their costs of getting cars ready for sale.

A reconditioning fee is an added dealer charge you might find when buying a used car. It’s intended to cover any costs the dealer incurs to make sure a used car is showroom-ready, from mechanical inspections to detailing.

The reconditioning process varies between dealerships, but typically includes these steps:

A visual exterior inspection. An auto tech does a quick walk-around the vehicle and notes any corrosion, damage or wear.

An interior inspection. The engine and auto interior are examined and tested, and any issues are documented.

A test drive. The car is taken out for a drive to check that it runs well and that the radio, brakes, A/C and other components are all functioning properly.

Service and repair. Any interior or exterior mechanical, functional or cosmetic issues that were found are repaired, including paint, dents, oil changes and major engine work.

Inspection. Once repairs are completed, the car is inspected again to make sure everything looks and functions as it should.

Detailing. This includes deep interior, engine and exterior cleaning as well as any necessary leather refurbishing, bumper repair or wheel restoration.

Reconditioning fees are legal, but that doesn’t mean you have to pay them. Dealers can charge whatever they want for a reconditioning fee, and it’s not uncommon to find them ranging from around $500 to over $2,000.

The good news: Reconditioning fees, like most dealer extras, can be negotiable. Ask the dealer for a breakdown of the reconditioning fee to see what kind of work was done to prepare the car for sale. If the work was minor but the fee is high — for example, if they’re asking for $1,995 but replaced the floor mats only — that’s a good sign it’s a bogus charge.

However, when it comes time for negotiation, don’t just haggle over the reconditioning fee or other individual fees. The best way to negotiate is to focus on the out-the-door price, or the total amount you’re paying for the car. This simplifies the negotiation process and keeps you focused on the true price of your car.

All dealers invest some amount in reconditioning, but those costs are often built into the dealer’s asking price for a vehicle, rather than as a separate charge.

Some dealers opt to add a reconditioning fee to the bill because it allows them to advertise a lower asking price online, which doesn’t include fees. It’s a tactic to get you into their dealership, since the asking price is lower than that of other dealerships.

However, once you arrive, you may find that the out-the-door price is the same — or more — compared with what other dealers are asking.

Some car-buying experts recommend avoiding dealerships that charge reconditioning fees altogether. But remember that the out-the-door price is what matters at the end of the day, so it’s worth comparing prices at multiple dealerships to find the best deal.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like car buying, so we sifted through Reddit threads to get a sense of how users feel about reconditioning fees. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

Reddit users are generally skeptical toward reconditioning fees. Many users view these fees as a bait-and-switch tactic: dealers advertise an attractive price online and then tack on the fee at the dealership, inflating the actual out-the-door cost well above what was listed. Car buyers frequently share stories of being hit with reconditioning fees ranging from a few hundred dollars up to $2,000 or more, often with little or no evidence of what work was actually done.

Car-buying experts on Reddit point out that most dealerships already build reconditioning costs into the sticker price, so if the fee is listed separately, the dealership may be double-dipping. Several users suggest that car buyers ask their dealer for an itemized breakdown of the work done, but most users recommend negotiating the total out-the-door price rather than individual fees.

#2965. Prediction: A $10,000 Investment in Nvidia Stock Will Be Worth This Much by Year-End 2027

Nvidia faces several risks, but it has solid upside despite potential headwinds.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:02PM EST

A lot has changed for Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) in a very short period of time, and this will ultimately have a big impact on where the semiconductor stock trades by the end of 2027. Given the stock's strong performance over the years, it tends to be widely held by retail investors. With a lot on the line, let's see where the stock could be headed over the next year.

The biggest change for Nvidia comes at the top. In a shocking turn of events, co-founder Jensen Huang, who had been the only CEO in the company's history, resigned earlier this month only to be welcomed back by the board less than two weeks later. Huang stepped down after he admitted marital infidelity as reports of multiple affairs bubbled to the surface. Investors focused on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation), who has been accused of being a Chinese spy.

Singapore-based Megaspeed has been a significant Nvidia customer, buying nearly $5 billion worth of its chips over the past few years. However, there are now allegations that many of these chips were illegally being directed to China.

The return of Jensen Huang as CEO for Nvidia is huge. Huang was a visionary who seemingly knew where the market was headed before anyone else. There are multiple examples of the company taking action based on his foresight, including:

These have all helped the company transform from a simple chipmaker into a complete AI infrastructure company that has been getting an increasingly larger percentage of spending per gigawatt of compute capacity.

However, there is still a question of what happens with China. The U.S. has further cracked down on export controls of AI chips. The risk is that there is a lot more indirect Nvidia revenue coming from China, which could disappear.

The Huang situation is not the only news Nvidia has endured this month, though. The midterm elections saw a sweeping victory for Democrats and candidates that ran on anti-data-center campaigns. These candidates have widely called for a data center build-out moratorium, and it is expected that the regulatory environment for building new data centers will get a lot tougher in the coming years. Neoclouds are expected to face the brunt of this, which could be bad news for Nvidia, which saw about 44% of its data center revenue last quarter coming from neoclouds and businesses.

On top of this, Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) revealed that its Claude Mythos model was able to switch models running on Nvidia's GPUs to run on Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD -8.86%) GPUs with little human intervention in just a few days. This process used to take six to 12 months and a dozen engineers. This could be a serious blow to Nvidia's CUDA moat and eventually lead to lower prices and serious gross margin compression.

That said, Nvidia is still well positioned in the medium term, as it has significant supply chain advantages. It has locked up a substantial amount of the supply-constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) required by AI chips, as well as capacity at foundries. In addition, with its Vera Rubin platform, it is now getting $40 billion per gigawatt of compute capacity compared to the $25 billion per gigawatt it is capturing with Grace Blackwell, which is a significant revenue lift. This will help support the 75% growth the company projected for fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) and beyond.

The issues Nvidia faces are likely to keep a cap on its forward P/E multiple, but it should still see solid growth in the medium term. I think it should be able to maintain a forward multiple of at least 12, which would value the stock at around $261 at the end of 2027 based on the fiscal 2029 analyst consensus of $21.75. As such, a $10,000 investment today — getting you 61 shares as I write this — would be worth over $15,900. That’s my prediction.

There is some decent upside to the AI stock from its current beaten-down levels, despite potential risks.

#2962. ​Building A Data Foundation That Makes Enterprise AI Work

Niraj Nagrani is Chief Data and AI Officer at Altimetrik.

After more than 30 years as an enterprise leader, I’ve been through many transformation journeys, from building hyperscale systems and training data for machine learning to migrating from legacy architectures to modern data platforms. Today, I see many organizations struggle to move from a successful AI pilot to a reliable production system​.

The problem is not with foundation models, which have improved exponentially over the past few years. In my experience, the problem almost always comes back to the underlying data architecture.

Many organizations are still working with data that isn’t ready for AI. Data quality and lineage may be governed inconsistently or not governed at all. And governance is often bolted on at the end rather than built in from the start.

I’ve worked with companies running over 100 siloed systems. When information is scattered that widely, it can be almost impossible to establish a consistent view of the business. Unstructured data like contracts, emails and support tickets can disappear into blind spots because they don’t fit neatly into traditional data structures. Another problem is the lack of a shared definition of business entities like revenue, customers or other important measures across systems. ​

Earlier machine learning learned patterns from a curated, labeled dataset to do one narrow task. Agents reason and act in real time across systems. At the moment of action, an agent has to know what a “customer” means, which policy applies, whether the data is current and what it is allowed to see. Without that context, you get a confident wrong action. Earlier machine learning needed clean training data; agents need living context.

The key first step of data modernization is what I call “business rule archaeology.” Over time, organizations accumulate business logic in stored procedures, SQL queries and their dependencies. Some of that logic is documented, but a lot of it isn’t, which makes it difficult to understand how the existing business processes actually work. Companies often underestimate the effort required to untangle these dependencies.​

Before planning for​ modernization, understand how the business uses its data and how its processes operate. From there, organizations can build an incremental migration plan rather than trying to move everything at once.​

​I think about modernization as four steps, and each one becomes a layer of the platform you end up with. First, unify the isolated systems in an open lakehouse built on object storage and open table formats such as Iceberg or Delta, holding one governed copy of structured and unstructured data. Feed it through streaming and change data capture, because agents need current information, not last night’s batch.

Second, define shared business definitions in a semantic layer, so “revenue” or “customer” means the same thing in every system. Third, capture how those entities relate in an ontology and knowledge graph. This is what gives an agent the context for its decisions. Fourth, put governed retrieval across structured and unstructured data, with governance as code providing access management, lineage and a replayable audit trail. Agents also need their own identities with least-privilege access, and cost controls belong in the design from the start, because the cost of running models decides what is affordable at scale.​

Data trust is crucial, but it’s especially challenging when different teams have different standards for what good data looks like. Trust is an interface problem you engineer: one definition, enforced in the pipeline.

One useful mechanism is a data contract, a machine-readable agreement covering schema, quality requirements and service-level expectations between producer and consumer. It functions like a stable API, making the relationship between those parties more predictable.

Many current operating systems and data warehouses were built to answer yesterday’s question for a human. An agent-ready platform has to serve decisions to a machine in real time, with context, semantics and governance built into its design. That is what matters most as we design the next generation of data platform architecture.​

Repositioning cruises move ships between seasonal destinations, often with longer sailings, fewer port stops and lower fares.

A repositioning cruise is a one-way sailing that moves a ship from one region to another. For example, many ships sail in the Mediterranean Sea during the summer and move to the Caribbean Sea for the winter, and that trip between the two is a repositioning cruise.

Repositioning cruises are most common in spring (roughly March to May) and fall (roughly September to November), though they can occur at other times of year.

Because ships are crossing oceans, these trips often include many days at sea. For some travelers, that’s a chance to relax and enjoy the ship’s onboard amenities. Sometimes, these sailings can also be cheaper than traditional cruises.

One key consideration for a repositioning cruise is that the embarkation and disembarkation ports will be different. This means you generally can’t buy a standard round-trip flight to and from the same city. Instead, you’ll need transportation to where the cruise starts and another way home from where it ends, which usually means two one-way flights (or one open-jaw ticket) unless you live near one of the ports. While these one-way sailings may be more affordable than traditional cruises, airfare costs may be higher.

This could be a great opportunity to redeem miles for your flight.

Another feature that sets these cruises apart is that stops along the way tend to include ports that aren’t traditionally part of regular itineraries. These might include islands like Bermuda, the Azores or the Canary Islands, and on some northern routes, Greenland.

Just keep in mind that the main purpose of these sailings is to get to a new region for the next season’s itineraries rather than make daily port stops. So if you’re someone who wants to visit as many places as possible on a cruise, a repositioning sailing may not be the ideal choice.

Repositioning cruises are often longer than standard cruises, commonly running two to three weeks compared with about a week for a typical sailing, which may appeal to travelers looking for an extended vacation. The experience is often more relaxed, with many days at sea and less of a rush to book shore excursions or visit important sites when off the ship.

If there are particular ships with certain amenities — like tattoo parlors or massive waterparks — that you really want to experience, keep in mind that not all ships reposition between regions. Some stay in certain regions year-round.

For ships that do change locations for the season, there are plenty of onboard activities to fill the time. You can enjoy shows, food and wine tastings, organized activities and time at the spa, pool or casino.

Many repositioning crossings are relatively smooth, and modern ships use stabilizers to reduce movement. But since these itineraries cross open ocean rather than staying closer to land, there can be more motion, especially on North Atlantic crossings in fall and winter.

If you tend to get seasick, this could be a dealbreaker. Even if a repositioning sailing is smooth, temperatures can be chilly on the open ocean, especially on northerly or spring and fall transatlantic routes, with strong winds that may make suntanning by the pool less appealing.

You can book one of these sailings in the same way you would book a traditional cruise. But if you’re searching for dates and itineraries on a cruise line’s website, they may be listed as transatlantic, transpacific or Panama Canal sailings rather than repositioning cruises, though some lines do use the term "repositioning." There’s even a website that specializes in rounding up these cruises: RepoCruises.com.

Keep an eye out for themed sailings that focus on topics like wine, theater or music, where fellow guests on the ship may share similar interests. Cruise lines often schedule them on repositioning cruises to spur demand.

Here are some repositioning cruises for 2027. They often take place during shoulder seasons, between the most popular cruising times in places like the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

This journey repositions the ship from Miami, where it sails on Caribbean itineraries, to Seattle, where it will visit ports in Alaska during the spring and summer months. Departing April 8, 2027, the 18-night cruise includes stops at various ports in Colombia, Panama and Mexico, as well as San Diego and Los Angeles, before arriving in Seattle on April 26.

Regent Seven Seas Cruises' all-suite luxury ship Seven Seas Mariner will sail between New York and Lisbon, making stops in Canada, Morocco and the Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores.

Departing April 29, 2027, the 16-night journey ends in Lisbon, Portugal, as the ship repositions to Europe, where it will sail various itineraries, including Mediterranean sailings later in the summer season.

Departing Seattle on Sept. 28, 2027, Norwegian Jade will sail to Yokohama, Japan, with stops in Alaska and northern Japan. This is a way to travel across the Pacific with less jet lag, since the journey takes place over several days, with ship clocks typically adjusted gradually (often an hour at a time) during the sailing. Note that the voyage also crosses the International Date Line.

If Greenland has been on your bucket list, this 16-night sailing is a way to get up close and personal with its natural scenery. Departing Reykjavik on Aug. 25, 2027, Azamara Quest will sail from Iceland to the U.S. It will make stops in Greenland, Canada and New England before reaching the Big Apple.

Departing Bergen, Norway, on June 11, 2027, this 28-night sailing aboard Viking Vela sails around Iceland's coast, makes two stops in Greenland and crosses the Atlantic before reaching New York.

#2959. A SpaceX-Tesla Deal Could Come in December. Here's Why 1 Group of Investors Should Be Worried.

A merger is likely to make Tesla's robotaxi more competitive in the future, spelling trouble for its rivals.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:07PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

A merger between Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) and Tesla (TSLA -0.20%) would have far-reaching consequences, not least by combining a leader in physical artificial intelligence (AI) -- Tesla's electric vehicles, robotaxi, and Optimus robots -- with a company that has a rapidly growing AI infrastructure services business (SpaceX).

That combination could have profound consequences for the major near-term catalyst for both companies, namely robotaxi, and that should be considered a threat to Uber Technologies (UBER +0.98%). Here's why.

To be clear and consistent, I don't think aggressively pursuing a merger is in the best interest of Tesla shareholders right now. In truth, we don't know if a bid will occur and what the terms will be. However, it strikes me that Tesla shareholders have waited for years and endured plenty of missed robotaxi timelines, the disappointments of Cybertruck, and industrywide downward revisions to electric vehicle sales, only to sell out just as Tesla is set to scale up its robotaxi rollout.

That's an issue for Tesla shareholders, as they could end up with a larger share of the new company than the 47% ownership stake Bank of America analysts estimated in an all-stock deal. Still, I think there's another group of shareholders who should be more worried: Uber shareholders.

A merger would create even better conditions for Tesla to realize its ambition to become a transportation-as-a-service (TaaS) company running a fleet of low-cost-per-mile Cybercabs. That's a direct threat to Uber's marketplace, at least in the areas where Cybercab has regulatory clearance. The threat has not gone unnoticed, and there's a reason Uber already has multi-partner autonomous robotaxi arrangements with companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Wayve.

When Tesla CEO Elon Musk says the "vast majority" of Cybercab will be "Tesla-owned and Transport-as-a-Service," this is highly unlikely to encompass a partnership with Uber.

In addition, merging with SpaceX would bring many benefits for Tesla's robotaxi.

All told, everything points to a merger making it easier for Tesla to ramp robotaxi and drive Cybercab's total cost of ownership (TCO) per mile lower. The latter is the key metric to follow, as it would facilitate a virtuous cycle in which low ride fares encourage further Cybercab fleet expansion. That's a real risk for Uber, because if its robotaxi partners can't achieve a comparable TCO, then Tesla's robotaxi could make significant inroads into some of its most profitable geographies.
