#2926. Dycom (DY) Q3 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Long-haul builds lift the outlook as fiber pacing cools.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:08PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Dycom (DY -18.02%) reported third quarter results that exceeded the high end of its guidance across all primary financial metrics, including revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS. Management raised the company's full-year revenue outlook to a range of $7.66 billion to $7.73 billion, supported by a record total backlog of $12.9 billion. The company stated that significant growth in long-haul and data center interconnect projects is expected to serve as the leading growth driver for the Communications segment in fiscal 2028, helping to offset a projected decline in fiber-to-the-home revenue. Additionally, the company announced a new $200 million share repurchase authorization following the completion of $100.5 million in buybacks during the third quarter.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Dycom Industries, Inc. Third Quarter 2027 Results Conference Call [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to Ms. Callie A. Tomasso, Dycom's Vice President of Investor Relations and Corporate Communications. Please go ahead.

Callie A. Tomasso: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Dycom's fiscal 2027 Third Quarter Results Conference Call. Joining me today are Dan Peyovich, our President and Chief Executive Officer; and Drew DeFerrari, our Chief Financial Officer. Earlier this morning, we released our fiscal 2027, third quarter results along with certain outlook information. The press release and accompanying materials are available in the Investor Relations section of our website, including the outlook expectation summary document, which provides additional outlook metrics beyond what will be discussed on today's call. These materials, which we will discuss during today's call include forward-looking statements made pursuant to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

Our discussion and these statements reflect our expectations, assumptions and beliefs regarding future events and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. A detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties is included in our filings with the SEC. Forward-looking statements are made as of today's date, and we undertake no obligation to update that. Additionally, we will reference certain non-GAAP financial measures during today's call. Explanations of these measures and reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in our press release and accompanying materials. With that, I will turn the call over to Dan Peyovich.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Thank you, Callie, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today. We delivered another strong quarter with record revenue of $2.06 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $311.7 million or 15.2% of revenue. Adjusted EPS was $5.23, every one of these results exceeded the high end of our guidance. Our performance this quarter is a direct result of our market leadership in digital and critical infrastructure paired with strict discipline in project selection to maintain the quality of our revenue and backlog. Quarterly revenue grew 41.6% year-over-year, including 11.2% organic growth in communications. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA grew 42% and adjusted EPS grew 33% year-over-year, demonstrating our commitment and ability to deliver attractive returns for shareholders as our platform scales.

During the quarter, we significantly accelerated our share repurchases, taking advantage of the compelling value in Dycom shares to buy back $100 million of our common stock. As announced this morning, our Board of Directors has replaced the prior program with a new $200 million program for future share repurchases. We finished the quarter with record total backlog of $12.9 billion, a book-to-bill of 1.3x and year-over-year backlog growth of 57%, including 36% growth in communications. This growth gives us visibility and confidence in our long-term growth prospects and we continue to diversify our backlog across demand drivers, positioning ourselves for durable growth in the coming years. Turning now to our segments, beginning with communications.

We had a strong third quarter and expect a solid finish to the year. Communications revenue grew more than 11% in the quarter and is up 17% year-to-date. That performance is backed by robust underlying demand. The country's ever-increasing data consumption requires significant sustained investment in digital infrastructure, specifically in the outside plant and inside plant networks we've built. Our foundational service and maintenance platform directly supports our high-growth program bills, maintaining and repairing our customers' networks day in and day out embeds us deeply into their operations giving us unmatched visibility into their infrastructure, establish local workforce capacity and trusted relationships at the field level.

That presence, combined with our national scale and deep technical expertise gives us a decisive advantage in winning and mobilizing large-scale deployments across numerous types of build programs, including fiber-to-the-home, BEAD, long-haul and data center interconnect, copper reclamation and wireless network modernization and densification. We are pursuing large, long-term opportunities across the diverse programs that is driving durable growth in communications. Following this year of incredible growth, we expect next year to return to a more normalized growth cadence. Based on our current visibility into customer build plans, we anticipate mid-single-digit revenue growth in the Communications segment for fiscal 2028, accelerating to higher growth levels in fiscal 2029.

We also expect adjusted EBITDA margins to expand year-over-year, and we will provide formal fiscal 2028 guidance on our fourth quarter call. As we have continued to diversify our business, our fundamental growth drivers remain strong, with some near-term shifts in customer dynamics as pacing in some programs moderates and others accelerate. Let me walk through each of those drivers. I'll start with fiber-to-the-home, which has been our largest demand driver this year, fueled by increased deployment across key customer programs and our strong competitive position, which has resulted in a significant increase in our leading share of the market. This has been a year of exceptionally strong growth in our fiber-to-the-home business with revenue up 50% through Q3.

We continue to see many years of activity ahead as customers continue to reiterate their long-term build commitments. Having said that, the macro environment, combined with a higher cost of capital, is having an impact on regional fiber overbuilders and some programs have slowed. What's most relevant to Dycom is the effect this is having on several of our large customers who, as the market has seen, have in recent weeks indicated decisions to moderate the pace of their fiber-to-the-home builds next year. Given this near-term shift in dynamics, we expect fiber-to-the-home revenue to be down in fiscal 2028 when compared to fiscal 2027, though still performing at levels above fiscal 2026.

It's important to note that our customers remain committed to their build-out plans. So we expect this to ultimately result in a higher pace in future periods or an extension of the fiber-to-the-home build cycle which increases our confidence in the sustainability of that growth over the longer term. Next is BEAD, many of our customers are preparing for rural fiber passings through the program. We remain well positioned to capitalize on these opportunities and continue to expect construction to start in earnest next year. Continued rapid growth in data consumption, cloud compute and AI are driving the need to connect data centers across the country.

We have spoken in the past about the multiple long-haul and data center interconnect opportunities we have been pursuing as customers broaden their fiber investments, and we continue to make strong progress on this front. Long-haul and data center interconnect builds are tracking ahead of initial expectations and will be the leading growth driver for our Communications segment next year. We got out in front of this demand early, performing several hundred millions of dollars of work in place over the past 2 years.

From there, we are well positioned for future network modernization and densification opportunities. Lastly, customer consolidation is providing another meaningful tailwind. We continue to expect further consolidation across network operators in the coming years. As our customers scale and integrate acquired footprint, they consolidate their vendor base around national partners with the balance sheet, safety record and workforce capacity to execute across multiple states, a trend that favors Dycom. We have been deliberate in diversifying our backlog to balance the timing and velocity of each demand driver and taken together, the program builds provide sustainable growth opportunities well into the next decade.

Our early identification and pursuit across the diverse set of programs is driving the continued growth of the segment as these new programs more than offset the moderating base of fiber-to-the-home work. Our record backlog, deep customer relationships and position at the center of both converged broadband and AI infrastructure give us tremendous conviction from strong growth in the years ahead. Shifting to Building Systems. Our strong execution continued this quarter, driven by robust demand for both electrical and structured cabling systems. We delivered solid growth in the quarter while also securing new awards that extend our visibility beyond calendar 2028.

In addition, the integration of National Technology Integrators is progressing well, and the business is performing in line with our expectations. Our strategy is clear: differentiate through performance and pursue markets with resolute drivers for growth. Evidence of our success can be seen in our revenue growth and margin performance in the DMV region. It's also visible in our growing structured cabling platform, which has expanded in 19 states as key customers bring us into new geographies to support their build-outs. As we engage with our customers to partner on their builds, we have not observed material changes in underlying customer behavior or plan scope as a result of recent policy and permitting uncertainty.

In fact, customer conversations continue to reinforce our confidence in the scale and duration of the data center build cycle. Looking ahead to fiscal 2028, we expect Building Systems to generate total revenue growth in the high teens or better with adjusted EBITDA margins that range from the high teens to low 20s, building on a year of exceptionally strong performance in fiscal 2027 and because this higher-margin segment is growing faster than communications, we expect it to drive continued consolidated margin expansion. Demand continues to grow, our focus remains steadfast, and we are well positioned to capitalize on the long runway ahead.

Reflecting our outperformance in Q3, we are raising our full year revenue outlook to range from $7.66 billion to $7.73 billion. This represents an increase of approximately $125 million at the midpoint compared to our prior guidance range. Moving to our strategic priorities, I'd like to highlight 4 updates. First, we are pleased with our ongoing progress in talent and workforce development, remaining an employer of choice and training a best-in-class field workforce for central to our ability to scale across complex programs. Second, expanding our Building Systems segment and further diversifying the enterprise remain key priorities. The addition of our Building Systems segment has been accretive on every metric, increasing consolidated margins and improving cash flow.

And while we continue to grow our footprint organically, we are looking selectively at M&A in strong markets. Third, margin performance remained solid, with consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin increasing to 15.2% and reinforcing the meaningful earnings uplift we're capturing as we extend our platform and demonstrating our ability to drive compelling shareholder returns as we scale. Fourth, we remain focused on operating cash flow discipline and expect seasonal benefits in Q4. This quarter, operating cash flow was temporarily impacted as we work with customers who are consolidating businesses. Our DSOs were 112 days, and we expect this to normalize and revert to more recent levels in the coming months.

In closing, we are executing our strategy, and our results and record backlog demonstrate both our leadership and digital infrastructure, and our ability to deliver certainty on complex, large-scale program. Significant awards and further diversification in our communications program builds combined with the success of our Building Systems segment, position us well for long-term profitable growth. Our people are the core of who we are and our success is a direct result of their work every day across America. I want to thank our more than 20,000 teammates for delivering safely and at the highest level of quality. With that, I'll turn the call over to Drew for further details on the quarter and our outlook.

H. Andrew (Drew) DeFerrari: Thanks, Dan, and good morning, everyone. We had a strong quarter, driving double-digit growth in revenue, adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS. We also continue to invest in our future growth and repurchased $100 million of our shares during the quarter. Q3 total contract revenues of $2.06 billion grew 41.6% over Q3 of last year. This reflects the strength of our relationships and continued diversification across our customer base. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $311.7 million or 15.2% as a percentage of total revenue increased 42% over Q3 '26.

And consolidated adjusted net income was $158.1 million and adjusted diluted EPS of $5.23 per share increased 33% over Q3 '26 and Communications revenue of $1.615 billion grew 11.2%, driven by robust fiber-to-the-home programs increased long-haul and data center interconnect builds and continued maintenance and operation services. Adjusted EBITDA for communications of $206.4 million was 12.8% of segment revenue, reflecting continued investments to scale our operations and approximately 50 basis points of cost pressure in the segment from higher fuel prices. During Q3, a rural customer filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection and another smaller customer experienced significant financial difficulties.

As a result, the company reserved for uncollectible accounts receivable totaling $22.7 million or $17.1 million net of taxes or $0.57 per diluted share. The majority of the balances was for work performed last year. There was no revenue from these customers in Q3, and we have no backlog of work for either of these customers. Moving on to Building Systems. Revenue was $441.7 million as we continue to experience significant growth in this segment. Adjusted EBITDA was $105.2 million or 23.8% of segment revenue as the business performed exceptionally well. Total backlog at the end of Q3 was $12.9 billion, including $11.2 billion of communications backlog and $1.7 billion of Building Systems backlog.

Backlog expected to be completed in the next 12 months is $6.7 billion, including $5.4 billion from communications and $1.3 billion from Building Systems. Strong cash flows remain a key focus area. The combined DSOs of accounts receivable and contract assets net were 112 days, reflecting the timing of work and collections during the quarter and the temporary effects from customer consolidation. We expect DSOs to revert to normalized level in the coming months. As we look ahead, we expect normal seasonal cash flow trends, and we expect to generate several hundred million dollars of operating cash flow during Q4. During Q3, we prioritized share repurchases and bought back 345,000 shares of our common stock for $100.5 million.

This week, our Board of Directors approved a new $200 million authorization for share repurchases through May 2028. This authorization replaces the remaining amount of our prior authorization and further enables us to continue to opportunistically repurchase shares. We ended the quarter with cash and equivalents of $202.8 million, total liquidity of $949 million and pro forma net leverage of approximately 2.3x adjusted EBITDA, providing us with financial flexibility for continued strategic growth and investment. Based on our outperformance in Q3, we have raised our full year revenue outlook, and we now expect total contract revenues to range from $7.66 billion to $7.73 billion.

This revised outlook is an increase of approximately $125 million at the midpoint compared to our prior range of expectations. For the Communications segment, we now expect full year contract revenues ranging from $6 billion to $6.04 billion for Building Systems. We now expect full year contract revenues ranging from $1.66 billion to $1.69 billion. We are maintaining our fiscal '27 outlook for consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin, that is expected to increase compared to last year, comprised of strong margins in the Building Systems segment, partially offset by a decline in Communications margins from cost pressures to scale the operations and from higher fuel costs.

For the fourth quarter, we expect consolidated revenues of $1.63 billion to $1.70 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $204 million to $218 million and adjusted diluted EPS of $2.48 to $2.78 per share, excluding the impact of intangible amortization. Our outlook for Q4 reflects normal seasonal factors such as fewer available workdays due to the holidays, reduced daylight work hours and winter weather conditions. As a reminder, Q4 of last year included 14 weeks of operations based on our fiscal calendar compared to only 13 weeks in Q4 of this year.

Our performance this quarter highlights Dycom's position as a leader in digital infrastructure and our backlog and line of sight to customer programs with confidence in our continued growth in the years ahead. Operator, this concludes our prepared remarks. You may now open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question will come from Eric Luebchow from Wells Fargo.

Eric Luebchow: Dan, maybe you could dive a little bit more into what you're seeing in the fiber to the home market, especially the outlook you gave for next year. Are you seeing more of a slowdown from some of the smaller customers? You called out a couple that were having some financial difficulty or is some of the larger programs that are going through a little bit of moderation? Just a little bit additional color there would be really helpful.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: So this is happening earlier than we expected. We thought it was going to be about another year out. But what I was trying to note on the call is the overbuilders have slowed down in many cases, the overbuilders have stopped. The pressure that the bigger customers are feeling is just not the same as it was when they were accelerating their plans. So it gave them an opportunity to just take another look at what they're facing is, take a look at their overall programs. the highlight here is that they're maintaining their overall course and expectations. So there's still 40 million, 50 million passings to do across the country.

Our customers have not come in on their total expectation. But what they are doing is looking at that year-over-year. So next year is going to come in from this year for some of our big customers. And overall, we think across the fiber-to-the-home space. And I would just point to this is something we've been planning for, for some time, why we've been diversifying the overall demand drivers. So to see growth like we have year-over-year, really just shows the positioning that we have in the space and the opportunity set in front of us.

Eric Luebchow: Great. And maybe you mentioned the copper reclamation efforts underway. Maybe you could talk a little bit more about the pacing you're seeing there with your customers. You talked about that becoming a bigger growth driver into next year. And as we look at that segment, does that have any impact longer term on the service and maintenance business as more copper is decommissioned or do you think it's just purely upside from the study run rate you have today?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: I'll answer those in reverse order. So on the service and maintenance, you have to think about that more as an installed base. So we have to have men and women around the country that even this Thursday Thanksgiving can respond within 1 hour or 2 hours to an event. And a lot of that can -- it includes driving time, right, to get out to some of these rural spots. So you have to have a certain amount of revenue, a certain amount of manpower or a certain amount of equipment and resources to do that.

So we don't think that we're going to see significant impact as we change from fiber to copper and we haven't seen that to date. On the first part, copper decommissioning is increasing very quickly. You've heard multiple of our customers have talked about it. They've had success and getting the ability now to start decommissioning those, one, through regulatory approvals. But two, there's enough fiber in place that they can actually go and start pulling out a lot of this copper, where Dycom is, again, this is something we've been training into. This is a different skill set. This is a different type of equipment. We have our own proprietary piece of equipment that we're using.

So we've had tremendous success and really see that as a good growth driver in the coming years.

Operator: Our next question will come from Manish Somaiya from Cantor Fitzgerald.

Manish Somaiya: Just going back to fiber-to-the-home. Dan, are you still assuming continued share gains?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: I think that's probably a big highlight for this year, Manish. I would tell you that we have done exceptionally well at expanding our market share this year. These programs are highly complex and where Dycom is differentiated in our ability to respond to our customers when they need expansion of those programs when they need certainty of what kind of passing they're going to hit in a given quarter. And that's gone tremendously well. If you look at the beginning of the year, the overall outlook we gave for Communications, we're up about $375 million in what we gave for the outlook now on the total year. A large part of that is from expanding into additional markets.

So as we look towards next year, Manish, there's still opportunity, and I still think we're well positioned to do it. But with the pace of these, it's prudent for us to really take that overall program in and again, just very pleased that we have the other demand drivers that are going to provide growth.

Manish Somaiya: So just turning to the long-haul conversion then. Obviously, the backlog went up pretty dramatically quarter-over-quarter. How should we think about the conversion of that backlog in '28? And then just pertaining to margins, Dan, you said margins should be up year-over-year in fiscal '28. What's contributing to that? And then just from an overall communications segment, you've talked about organic growth rate being 10% to 12% and margins sort of in that 13% plus/minus range. How should we sort of frame that segment, I guess, going forward?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Sure. So starting with the long-haul, incredibly pleased, more than doubled our backlog for the quarter-over-quarter compared to last quarter and really at a great pace against that $20 billion that we talked about 2 years ago and that we highlighted. So that's been a huge part of our strategy. I talked about fiber-to-the-home being complex and how we have really differentiated ourselves in the industry. The long-haul work the data center interconnect is multiple times more complex than fiber-to-the-home. So we think we're incredibly well positioned there. Manish, part of that backlog increase that we had this quarter is work that other folks were awarded some time ago, and were not able to really meet our customer satisfaction.

So we're pleased with how we're performing in the space. We're very pleased with the overall outlook and that backlog that we have has multiple years of build in front of it, shifting overall to just the communications and margin. I think, again, it's a really important point that this year, we did a lot of building, right? We're training our talent for the future. We're getting ready for the growth and the expansion. We're training into these different demand drivers but also we're responding to our customers' needs. With all of that customer growth on fiber-to-the-home programs, what often happened and you saw it this quarter was a really good example.

We had a customer within the quarter that wanted to highly accelerate their fiber-to-the-home passings and their fiber-to-the-home build in fact more than one customer. And when that happens, we're ready to answer the call, which means we're sending out hundreds of people, sometimes hundreds of crews to go really try and get ahead of that. It's just not the most efficient. So that's the margin pressure that you saw this quarter. That's part of that and that's part of the margin pressure you've seen this year.

And that's what gives us confidence as we look towards next year, Manish, with the mix of work and with where those programs are from a maturity point and continued margin expansion in the Communications segment. We'll get more on that as we get to next quarter.

Manish Somaiya: And then, Dan, just on a higher level, the organic growth rate in communications. How should we think about that beyond, I guess, '28 in the past, you've said 10% to 12% margin sort of in that 13% type range. If you can just help us sort of understand how we should think about that segment going forward?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes, I think about it from a growth perspective. So that we give an outlook to mid-single-digit growth for communications for next year. Remember, too, this year, our Q1 was incredibly weather favorable, incredibly weather favorable. It's more active like a Q2 or Q3. So obviously, we're not going to bake that into our expectations and our outlook for next year. And then the other part is there's other programs, seeing how BEAD comes through, provides upside to where that could be. And then I also noted in my prepared remarks that we look at FY 2029 as additional growth on top of what we're going to expect next year. So a lot of things moving in the right direction.

And we do maintain overall that longer term plus or minus 13%. But specific to next year, we'll give you more insight to that as we get to next quarter.

Operator: Our next question will come from Brent Thielman from Oppenheimer.

Brent Thielman: Dan, just on the long-haul Middle Mile business, obviously, kind of an important growth driver here in this segment into fiscal '28 especially kind of offsetting some of this fiber-to-the-home step you talked about. Are you like actively ramping up on that today on some of these programs to levels that kind of give you comfort in those accelerating contributions? Or just what else are you seeing and hearing from customers that kind of drives the confidence there?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: It's an important note, Brent, on the dynamics of a long-haul or DCI build compared to fiber-to-the-home. So I was just explaining to Manish, the fiber-to-the-home, we can rapidly increase for customers as they need to go hit more homes or as they change how they're thinking about maybe the particular geographies that they want to be in. That's very different in the long-haul work. That's linear route. So it's a much more structured, much more regular tempo, we can map those out and there isn't really a way to go shotgun on those because it's a direct road and direct front.

That gives us a lot of confidence, again, thinking about next year and how those programs are coming together. And yes, to answer your question, that's already -- we're ramping across multiple customers. These awards are across multiple customers. These awards are across large swaths of the United States. And I really think that, again, where Dycom differentiates, I really believe we're one of the only companies out there that could compete across the entire country and have that intimate knowledge of not only the local geographies and geologies and working with the different municipalities, but also have a ton of experience with people that are already working there.

Brent Thielman: Okay. Appreciate that. And then just on Building Systems, maybe just the factors driving the outsized margin performance in the quarter, a couple of really strong quarters here in a row. And I guess, leading to -- given the strong kind of demand backdrop, why something in excess of 20% EBITDA margins isn't sustainable going forward?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Sure. It could be sustainable, Brent. So we centered on this kind of high teens to low 20s to get people around that 20% plus or minus range overall. With showing these last couple of quarters that we can obviously outperform that every quarter is not always going to be exactly the same depending on timing, even though we're working on more than a dozen data centers in the power space and even more than that in the structured cabling. You still have to look at how they might come together in a given quarter. So that's a little bit of a broader range.

We will certainly tighten that up as we get towards next year when you would give you all an outlook. But a ton of confidence, these are fantastic teams. It really comes back to speaking to our strategy buying strong companies in very robust markets that we really have a good idea of what the future is to look like. So all signs point to really strong continued growth and continued profitability.

Operator: Our next question will come from Sangita Jain from KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Sangita Jain: Dan, I don't really want to go back to the mid-single-digit comp growth comment for next year. Because your 12-month backlog in Comms is up low double digits and if we assume that the wireless work shifts to next year, O&M continues to grow low single digits. DCI bookings momentum is strong. So I just want to understand why we should think of low -- mid-single digits as a fair target and if that assumes any BEAD revenue at all?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: So it does include upside. There is no doubt about that, Sangita. I think it depends, one, we are working with our customers right now to finalize exactly what their fiber-to-the-home build plans look like next year. So we wanted to be prudent how we projected that and what we gave you today. And then the second part, to your point, is exactly where BEAD is going to come in. We continue to do well in opportunities there. We're looking forward to getting some of that contracted backlog.

As everybody knows, that program has taken quite a while to come through. we do believe there's upside opportunity for next year, but we're not going to know that until we get a little bit closer, and we really start to see exactly when these time lines are to play out.

Sangita Jain: Got it. And then on the operating cash flow in 3Q, I heard the comments that it's the timing issue. But do we expect it to reverse in 4Q or is it a function of customers being in some type of financial stress and that you need to give them more time for you to recover your cash?

H. Andrew (Drew) DeFerrari: This is Drew. I'll take that one. So -- when I look at the operating cash flow for Q3, we outperformed significantly on the revenue side, and so that's going to have an impact. We're going to consume working capital as we perform that work. So that used some working capital we do expect normal seasonal benefits on the operating cash flow. And so you can see in my prepared remarks, targeting several hundred million dollars in Q4, and then we continue to work with our customers. As we talked about, several have been through mergers in the current year, and that just takes some time to transfer balances and integrate systems.

What I would point out to is even with the build and the share repurchases that we did this year, net leverage is still in that 2.3 range. And that's something that generating significant cash flows going ahead. That number will continue to come down.

Operator: Our next question comes from Frank Louthan from Raymond James & Associates.

Frank Louthan: Great. Can you talk to us a little bit more about the fuel cost impact there? I think in prior calls, you've indicated that, that would mitigate a bit or you mitigated some of that risk. How did that impact the margins? And you mentioned you're still looking at M&A. I'm just curious how you think about that with where your stock is trading versus other uses of cash currently.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: On the margin one. So we're pricing that into contracts as those contracts renew, so right now, as Drew mentioned, we don't see any insight to where the fuel price has been going to be, but we are pricing the contract. So over time, that's going to iron out, and we are having conversations with customers as well. On the M&A front, clearly, you saw us prioritize share repurchases this quarter. You saw the increase in our authorization from our board as well. So with where the market is today, that's obviously been a good opportunity for us and something that we anticipate continuing to lean into and then I would just speak to the discipline we've had around M&A.

Look at the acquisitions and the performance that we've had look at what the multiple has been on the forward and the growth that they've had. So we're going to continue to be highly disciplined. We continue to be focused on very strong geographies, strong markets with strong players.

Frank Louthan: All right. And just to follow up on the pricing for the contracts. Are you moving diesel or other fuel pricing to more of a variable thing within the contract? Are you passing on increases on certain level? How are you pricing that in? Or is it just more of a increasing that as a baseline in the contracts going forward?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Increasing the baseline typically, Frank.

Operator: Our next question will come from Adam Thalhimer from Thompson Davis.

Adam Thalhimer: Can you quantify the long-haul fiber awards in November? And then also, can you give us some color what you're seeing on the bidding side for those projects?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes, roughly, very roughly half and half, half within the quarter and half in between from an award perspective. Yes. From a competitive set, there's -- when you have $20 billion of opportunity out there, it continues to be a very active space, no different to the competition we've seen across the different demand drivers. But as I said earlier, we really think this is where we're well positioned. One, we're really first on the ground, we've been doing a ton of this work. Two, we're getting ahead from a training perspective.

We're getting ahead from an equipment perspective because of the breadth of opportunities that we're engaged in and what we see for that growth and what we see for that backlog. So we believe we're very well positioned, Adam, but it's going to continue to be a competitive space.

Adam Thalhimer: And then, Dan, how should we think about the margin profile for that work versus fiber-to-the-home?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Overall, I would put them in a similar range. The difference that I mentioned earlier is on the fiber-to-the-home if you're rapidly expanding or quite frankly, if a particular market is a particular market, particular geography is slowing down, you're going to have a different kind of margin pressure, but you're going to get a lot more consistency on the long-haul and data center network.

Adam Thalhimer: And then on the Power Solutions side, have you looked at or are you looking at any opportunities outside of the DMV?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: You can see significant growth. They're tracking for something around 40% growth year-over-year. That's a lot when you're starting at over $1 billion of revenue, and it started with almost 3,000 electricians and growing. So significant growth in their space today. That is something that we're always looking at. And I would point to our structured cabling, where now we're in 19 states, so a ton of growth there and ability to really flex and move to where our customers need us. So we're looking at all of that collectively within the Building System, I think we're well positioned to continue.

Operator: Our next question will come from Richard Choe from JPMorgan.

Richard Choe: Just wanted to follow up a little bit on the long-haul and the copper reclamation. I think this gives you some better visibility longer term. How at least for the copper side, how long do you expect that work to last? And how should it ramp up over the next few quarters? And then same with long-haul, maybe just like the pacing of how it should kind of contribute to revenue? And then I have a follow-up.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. long-haul, it's a little earlier for us than we talked about going back 2 years, Richard, just because we've done really well on getting that work. So we're working on multiple projects across multiple customers. We really see next year as being the year where that starts to grow significantly, which is what we had anticipated overall. But obviously, it's going to outpace even some of the fiber-to-the-home changing pace. On the copper -- excuse me, on the duration of that, when we're talking to those customers and we're talking to hyperscalers, we're talking about a decade-plus build to get everything that they need to get done. So a ton of opportunity there.

That's going to go all the way as long as the fiber-to-the-home builds go, that's when you can start pulling out the copper. So you still got 5 or 6 years at least, and it's going to trail beyond that. So lots of opportunity to continue to pull out copper. And as everybody can imagine, with decades and decades and decades of putting copper in the ground, there's quite a bit to take out nationwide.

Richard Choe: And with there being a little bit of a shift here with the, I guess, near-term fiber plans, maybe it seems like you're saying the long-term plans still seem to be in place for a fiber-to-the-home? Does it make sense to adjust maybe your cost structure a little bit to be some kind of pullback here or some shifting? Or do you think that's too kind of shortsighted.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: So we don't look at it. Our crews in the Communications segment are highly fungible. So we've been training folks to move into the long-haul into the data center interconnect work, we've been working on that for a while. That's the investments that you saw this year were part of that. So with growth, we're going to have head count growth. That's part of where we're going next year. So we're really looking at just reallocating those resources.

Operator: Our next question will come from Steven Fisher from UBS.

Steven Fisher: Just wanted to follow up on the fiber-to-the-home. I'm really trying to understand what are the biggest factors that are causing this decline next year? Is it consumer health? Is it cost of capital? Is it competitive dynamics, including things like Starlink and just in terms of the customer process and curious when you get the visibility from your customers on what their plans are to spend I know you told Sangita that there still could be upside, it's kind of early, but just curious for what the biggest drivers of that change are? And kind of how you see the dialogue and process playing out with your customers?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Our customers are reaffirming their overall build programs, Steven. So we really believe that the economics that they continue to see are strong, all the conversations that they're having both publicly and with us point to them continuing those programs. What's really changed is just the competitive pressure. Before what all of our customers learned is it really needed to be first with fiber. That became mantra across the industry.

But with overbuilding slowing down and with overbuilding in a much different place today than it was a few years ago, it just gives our customers an opportunity to take another look at it, balance out their CapEx and again, I think it's really important to note, this is a very recent conversation, right? This is our customers talking about this in the last few weeks, not the last few months. And as they said, their budgets and they set their plans for next year, we're spending time with them to really understand how that's going to play through overall. And with some customers, you're looking at elongated cycle and some you look at flattening.

But all in all, there's still tons of opportunity in the vibrant space.

Steven Fisher: That's very helpful. And then if you could maybe give a little bit more color on BEAD. I think you've talked in the past about having perhaps $500 million of verbal awards. Is that still the case? Has any of that become backlog -- and I think you've talked about it being in the Northeast. Is all of that in the Northeast. I'm curious, I know you're expecting it to go into construction next year. What still has to happen get what you are most confident into moving forward?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. Very, very, very small amounts that would be in our backlog today. So we're still looking to get that converted -- that number has certainly grown over time. And it is highly sourced across the country across customers, so it's not one play. We just started engineering in the Northeast was that comment a quarter -- I think that was a quarter ago. Yes, it really discounted that timing.

I think what the sub grantees, which are our customers, what they're working towards is before they kind of get to get up to the starting line, they want to get all the ducks in a row, make sure that they understand exactly where they're headed and the pace of their bills because there are constraints on the time there's -- they want to make sure that they got the dollars figured out the right way. So it's taking a little longer overall. But we think certainly next quarter or the quarter after, we'll have good updates around that.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael Funk from Bank of America.

Michael Funk: So I want to go back to the fiber-to-the-home build comments and maybe help me better understand some of the pressure points. I thought some of your previous commentary or discussions that we had was that aggregate demand for fiber builds far outstripped your capacity that even if you saw one or more customers slow that'd be made up from others. So first of all, I want to make sure I understand that correctly.

And then second point there, is what gives you confidence that this is a temporary slowdown beyond customers, reaffirming long-term plans and that it is not, in fact, maybe some pullback because of fewer competitive threat from LEO and/or reprioritization of FWA build and spending over fiber. And then I have a follow-up, please.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: I think it's important to listen to what our customers have said publicly, Michael. So as they've talked about, the competitive pressure is easing, that's why they're relooking they have not talked about overall changing what their build program or plan was, just purely the pacing and I think on the LEO comment, I mean, again, I was listening to what our customers are saying, but also you just don't see consumers switching from fiber to satellite. So I think, obviously, that's a positive for our customers as well. From an overall pacing, I'm not sure exactly which comment you're referencing, but we have been able to continue to grow with our customers.

I think one of the things that's differentiated us is that when they have called and wanted to accelerate and we saw a lot of that this year that we were able to bring them the resources that they need to hit the numbers that they wanted to hit. So that doesn't mean that there was a line waiting out the door. We think we did a really good job of balancing that, making sure our customers are successful. So as you see multiple of our customers now rethinking and relooking at their pacing, that's what we're reflecting in the outlook for next year.

Michael Funk: That was very helpful. And then given the backdrop entering fiscal '28 here, how should we think about -- how are you thinking about capital allocation, is an opportunity to do more acquisitions as maybe some of the multiples might be coming down? Is it a better opportunity to return capital to shareholders -- how should we think about capital allocation and priorities?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Sure. Again, this quarter, you saw share repurchases and you saw an increase in the authorization. So that obviously shows our appetite there and that's a good return from where market dynamics are today. But to be clear, Michael, our acquisition, our strategy around building systems has been playing out exceptionally well. And we do believe and we have seen other businesses out there that are very strong, that could be a good complement. But we're going to be very disciplined in how we think about it. So we've shown that in the past, we've shown our ability to integrate, operate and grow those businesses as well.

So that's how our investors should think about how we're going to be looking at the future.

Operator: Our next question will come from Michael Dudas from Vertical Research Partners.

Michael Dudas: Hi, Drew Dan. Yes. Dan, you mentioned about vendor consolidation, and I'm looking at it from a new business front, the strong book-to-bill like -- are you seeing different customers coming into the fold? Certainly, you seem to be gaining share and mixing with some of your larger names. And on the buildings front, what is the limitations on the growth opportunities for that business as you're looking into '28, maybe even beyond? Certainly, I think you mentioned that you've got business into 2029. Is that still the tightness in that market or generally is going to continue to lead to a more balanced or maybe a more accelerated growth in the future, given the demand for compute.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. I'll start with the second one, Mike. So one, if you look at our Building Systems segment and look at the growth that they brought to Dycom this year, and I would point to our consolidated margins. Last year, our margins were up 100 basis points year-over-year. If you look at the midpoint of our guide this year on consolidated, we're again guiding to be up around 100 basis points. So if you look at the way that, that business is operating, how it augments for our overall book of work, it's really been a great contributor. We see that growth continuing and outpacing the overall growth in our communications next year.

So that gives us confidence in overall margin growth for that business. The limitations there, growing as we've grown significantly, especially on the electrical side this year, that's a lot of head count to add. That's got to come through the union hall there. As you grow, you're starting with larger numbers to grow from. So that's how we're thinking about the future. We are partnered very closely with the union. We continue to look at potential market expansion organically as well. So a lot of confidence in continued growth, but it's, again, no surprise to anybody that electricians and the management teams to lead those groups are in short supply overall. On vendor consolidation on the communications side.

That's just a huge positive for Dycom. These are relationships that we've had for a long time. They're leaning into the scale that Dycom brings here, leading into the certainty that we bring, leaning into the local knowledge that Dycom brings. And we believe that, that consolidation is going to continue and that will continue to benefit us overall.

Michael Dudas: What should be helpful to your mid-single-digit growth opportunities next year? I'm assuming.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. Exactly right. Exactly right. There's -- as they consolidate, there's things that as Drew noted this quarter, there's things you have to work through. But overall, it's a huge benefit for us, and we expect that to continue.

Operator: Our next question will come from Michael Stratoti from Guggenheim Securities.

Michael Stratoti: Can you just give us a quick update on the wireless business? I know it's not a huge driver -- but can you share roughly how -- what percentage of revenue came in this quarter with that push out from last quarter? And maybe if we're still looking to see that push out come back next year.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. I don't have in front of me what it contributed this quarter and we haven't been publishing that of late, but it's only a few percentage points of our overall revenue for the year, and then roughly flat year-over-year, and we do expect that program to continue as we originally predicted and finish up next year.

Operator: Our next question will come from Liam Burke from B. Riley Securities.

Liam Burke: Dan, there's a bill winding its way through Congress specifically on permitting reform. If it does pass, how much does that help boost your long-haul business?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: So the challenge with permitting is anything that's happening at a federal level, Liam, is only going to apply to federal properties. So often the biggest challenge is not -- there are challenges there. So every help certainly is wanted and will definitely help to build. But as you get into lot municipalities, you just have a numbers challenge, right? They only have so many folks that are working, and there's only so much throughput. And at the end of the day, they only want so many people in their towns working at a given point in time. So there is not just some kind of open up the throttle.

We do believe permits are always going to be a big consideration in how you plan these out and the rate and the pace that they can go.

Liam Burke: Great. And on the Building Systems and legacy communications business, are you seeing any cross benefit on the craft side of the business?

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: It's a great point. So we are seeing fungibility between what we're doing structured cabling, so inside the data centers. And then what we can do on our communications side of the business. So folks that are trained to splice fiber, whether it's indoors or outdoors. We are seeing opportunities to flex across those groups, which is going to help with our future growth opportunity and just goes to, again, the investments that we've made in training, the investments that we've made in our people to ensure that we can continue to grow across the enterprise.

Operator: Thank you. And I am showing no further questions from our phone lines. I'd now like to turn the conference back to Mr. Dan Peyovich for closing remarks.

Daniel (Dan) S. Peyovich: Yes. First, Happy Thanksgiving to all. And I just want to pass along huge thanks to the men and women of Dycom that are out there every day working to deliver for our customers. Thank you all, and we will see you next quarter.

Operator: Thank you for participating. This concludes today's program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a wonderful day.

#2924. Lakers eye biggest test of season with more questions than answers

LOS ANGELES — It feels like we've already experienced various phases of the Lakers between the start of the season and Monday's 109-94 win over the Utah Jazz.

The team's fast launch out of the gates was highlighted by a nuclear start to the season for Luka Dončić. Despite surviving a regression to what feels far below the mean, the Lakers came out of their worst stretch of the season on Monday with a 4-1 record and 11 wins in their last 12 games to remain atop the conference with a 15-3 overall record.

And yet, with their biggest test of the season against the San Antonio Spurs on the horizon, Los Angeles's last week of games has assuredly raised some questions. The first being: are they ready for it?

"It'll be good to see," Walker Kessler said of the forthcoming clash against the Spurs. "It'll be a challenge for sure, but I think we're ready. I'm excited to go out there and compete."

San Antonio is tied with the Lakers for the league's top record. Los Angeles has three days off before Friday's game while the Spurs play Portland before the marquee showdown. Nonetheless, the matchup will be perhaps the most anticipated of the season as both teams will play for early bragging rights.

The biggest wildcard — and another one of the Lakers' biggest questions — is if Austin Reaves will be available. The star guard has missed the last five games with a left heel bruise and his absence has been felt in all facets of the game.

When Dončić is on the floor, opposing defenders can focus more on him. When he's off, the time typically reserved for Reaves to run the lineup has seen the Lakers struggle to create offense. Head coach JJ Redick said pregame that he's optimistic Reaves will return to the lineup against San Antonio, but actions speak louder than words.

Just as Redick pointed out in the lead-up to Monday's game, the Lakers had the No. 1 offense through the first 12 games with Reaves on the court for a majority of that time. Since then, with Reaves out, their offense has struggled. And yet, again, they're 4-1 without Reaves, which is a major reference point for the team.

"It's encouraging," Kessler said. "Obviously Austin is a very important piece to this team. And so seeing how we compete without him and not at our full strength is good. It builds resiliency because [you're] not going to be always at full strength going in the season. Things happen. It's a long season

"So it's encouraging to see, but, obviously, we miss him and excited for him to be back out there."

Trials and tribulations are part of an 82-game season. But the fact that the Lakers have endured all of this and still stay atop the league early in the season might be the answer to every question.

"Every day we continue to get closer and closer," said Lakers rookie Cameron Carr after his career-high nine-point outing on Monday. "We have a very unique group of guys and I think God put us here for a reason. We just connect. … The puzzle pieces are put together."

#2920. Anthropic IPO: Here's What a $5,000 Investment Could Look Like in 5 Years

Anthropic's $81.3 billion IPO came with eye-popping revenue growth, but roughly $895 billion in compute commitments and a swing back to an operating loss in Q3 are hard to ignore.

By Johnny Rice – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:17PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

One of the most anticipated initial public offerings (IPOs) in market history has finally gone public. Anthropic (ANT -6.54%), the company behind Claude, priced its offering at $83, above the initial target. Those shares began trading on Nov. 19, opening at $111.50 before finishing their debut session at $97.17, still 17% above the IPO price.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

The company raised a whopping $81.3 billion, making it the largest public debut ever, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies' (SPCX -5.65%) mega-IPO earlier this year. And at Thursday's close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis, instantly making it one of the largest public companies on the planet.

If you manage to get ahold of $5,000 in Anthropic stock, what might that investment look like five years from now?

Anthropic brought in $41 million in revenue in 2023 and $4.6 billion in 2025, then did $33.2 billion in just the first nine months of 2026, up roughly 1,200% from the same stretch a year earlier. That is incredible growth that we really haven't seen at this scale.

The bull case centers around this continuing. The bet is that Claude gets embedded in business processes across industries, and the sort of wholesale transformation of work we've seen in coding happens elsewhere.

One of the most encouraging figures for the bull thesis is Anthropic's net revenue retention, which sits at about 900%. That means customers find Claude valuable enough not only to stick around, but to scale their usage -- and spending -- ninefold in a single year.

The bear case is really centered around what all that growth costs. Anthropic's amended filing showed about $895 billion in purchase commitments and leases, mostly for compute and infrastructure -- the chips and data centers its models run on. About half of that is due before the end of 2030. And while Anthropic notched an operating gain in Q2 this year, it swung back to a $567 million operating loss in Q3.

And then, of course, the bear case also assumes the incredible revenue growth we've seen slows down considerably. In the bear case, Claude remains highly valuable in the programming world, but its broader use across most of the rest of the economy is limited.

The truth is that it is remarkably hard to predict where a stock like Anthropic's will be even a year from now. This truly is terra incognita.

That said, I believe it will be closest to the bear case. I'm not sure investors appreciate just how precarious Anthropic's position is. It must commit to spending on compute and infrastructure well before it actually books the corresponding revenue. And with usage-based billing, its customers' spending habits can turn on a dime.

My biggest issue is that I fail to see a durable moat. I think the most likely scenario is that artificial intelligence (AI) will look more like a commodity in a few years, and that Anthropic will find that its customers are happy to look elsewhere if it means they can pay less.

#2917. Why Analog Devices Stock Fell Nearly 20% Today

The chipmaker crushed fourth-quarter estimates, so why did Wall Street hit the panic button? Let's look under the hood at the guidance quirks and spending plans behind today's sell-off.

By Anders Bylund – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:26PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Analog Devices ›

Analog Devices (ADI -17.37%) reported fourth-quarter results early Tuesday morning. The analog and mixed-signal chip designer crushed Wall Street's consensus estimates and followed up with in-line guidance.

And investors hated it. The stock fell as much as 19.7% in the morning session, recovering slightly to a 16.6% drop as of 3:23 p.m. ET.

Analog Devices' headline figures were great in Q4 2026. Earnings rose 80% year-over-year to $4.06 per share. Revenues jumped 42% to $4.37 billion. The analyst consensus had called for earnings near $3.89 per share on roughly $4.32 billion in top-line sales. The guidance ranges for next quarter were broadly in line with current Street projections.

But the drop makes sense when you dig below the usual numbers. Q1 revenue guidance is in line with Street expectations, but it's still a disappointing slowdown after a fantastic Q4 result. Operating margins will fall due to high component costs and holiday-season factory shutdowns.

Moreover, Analog Devices' chip-making facilities are running at full capacity, limiting the company's ability to actually take on more orders. More manufacturing capacity is on the way with a 150% year-over-year increase in capital expenditures, but the new production lines won't make any chips until the second half of 2028.

Analog Devices is a victim of its own roaring success. When your factories are already humming at full tilt and channel inventories are finally back to normal levels, there simply isn't much room left for upside surprises in the near term.

Instead of another beat-and-raise quarter, shareholders are getting a massive $1.6 billion to $1.9 billion capital spending bill next year -- and they won't see a single chip roll off those new lines until fiscal year 2028. The stock entered this report priced for perfection, trading at a beefy 37 times trailing earnings after Tuesday's big drop. From there, in-line guidance and a long wait for the next growth spurt were all the excuse traders needed to hit the eject button.

Tuesday's reversal erased a portion of those gains as renewed selling pressure swept across the semiconductor industry. Trading volume reached 379.2 million shares, approximately 107% above its three-month daily average of 183 million, reflecting continued volatility and heightened investor activity.

Nvidia's sharp reversal following Monday's historic rally highlights the volatility surrounding AI stocks as investors reassess their valuations and long-term growth prospects. However, the recent price swings contrast with the company's underlying financial performance. Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, representing 103% year-over-year growth, and raised its fourth-quarter outlook, suggesting demand for AI infrastructure remains exceptionally strong.

Wall Street also remains relatively optimistic about Nvidia's prospects. Bernstein recently upgraded the stock to Outperform while maintaining a $200 price target, implying approximately 29% upside from Tuesday's closing price of $155.38. Looking ahead, Nvidia's ability to sustain its growth will ultimately matter more than short-term market volatility. Investors should pay particular attention to whether major technology companies maintain their AI infrastructure spending, alongside developments involving U.S.-China semiconductor restrictions and regulatory scrutiny.

#2911. Fantasy Basketball: Landry Shamet, AJ Dybantsa are among players on hot streaks — but what do the stats tell us?

Fantasy basketball managers should keep an eye on these hot streaks. Landry Shamet is shooting 51.5% from 3 over his last five games, Donovan Clingan is racking up double-doubles and blocks, and Jalen Smith is in the middle of a career year for the Bulls. Corey Kispert and Aaron Wiggins are sleepers who are fueling the Hawks' 11-6 start with sharpshooting, while rookie AJ Dybantsa is heating up in Washington. Whether you want a long-term hold or a short-term streamer for roto, category or points leagues, here is what each trending player's recent stats mean for your lineup.

Shamet has been on fire lately, averaging 16.4 points on 55.8% shooting, including 51.5% from deep over the last five games, helping the Knicks go undefeated over that stretch. He reached the 20-point mark twice in the five games and has hit it three times on the season, which is remarkable considering he only topped 20 points twice through all of last season.

He is averaging 26.9 minutes per game through 17 appearances this year, which is up from 23.0 minutes last season and just 15.2 per game in his first campaign with the Knicks. In his extended playing time, he is averaging a career-high 2.5 made 3-pointers per game, while shooting a strong 44.2% from beyond the arc this season. He has also been very good from the foul line, knocking down 81% on 1.2 attempts per game, helping fuel a career-best 66.4% true shooting percentage. With a championship under his belt, the 29-year-old, ninth-year guard may have found a new level of confidence that has him on track as one of the most valuable shooters in the league.

Clingan is emerging as one of the league's most complete young big men, averaging 11.6 points, 11.3 rebounds and a career-high 2.1 blocks in 26.1 minutes per game. His scoring and rebounding are down marginally from last season, but that's a product of reduced minutes rather than any decline in play, as the Trail Blazers added offseason talent that reshaped the rotation.

The third-year center ranks eighth in the league with eight double-doubles and has already clocked in impressive season highs of 24 points, 18 rebounds and five blocks (twice). His 11.3 rebounds per game also ranks fifth in the league. In addition to his counting stats, he provides efficiency, shooting 59.4% from the field, while averaging 1.0 made threes on 2.4 attempts per game, which amounts to elite 41.5% shooting from long range. He is also extremely reliable when fed in close, as he is averaging 73.5% shooting from within five feet of the basket. Clingan can be expected to continue to excel in his role without needing to be the center of attention.

Kispert is off to an anomalous start to the season, managing to provide a notable impact for his squad in only 12.4 minutes per game through 10 appearances. The sixth-year marksman is averaging 9.3 points on 55.9% shooting, including a blistering 48.8% from deep, with 2.0 made 3s per game.

Wiggins is doing similarly impressive work by averaging 13.9 points on 45.5% shooting, including 40.5% from deep, with a career-best 2.8 made 3s in 25.8 minutes per game. On the other hand, he is hitting a career-low 61.5% from the foul line on a total of 13 attempts through 17 games this season.

Both Kispert and Wiggins' ability to provide such a valuable contribution in limited time has been a big help in the Hawks getting out to an 11-6 start to the season. The sharpshooting is also a defining aspect of the team's identity, as they have been heavily reliant on the long ball, ranking sixth in the league with 14.8 made 3s per game.

Smith is working on a career season, averaging highs across the board, with 14.1 points, 7.5 rebounds, 2.2 assists, 0.7 steals and 1.0 blocks in 25.3 minutes per game. He is also shooting an efficient 54.7% from the field, which is all the more impressive considering he is also averaging a career-high 2.1 made 3-pointers on 5.1 attempts per game, for a 40.3% shooting mark from long range. Additionally, it can not be overlooked that he is hitting 74.2% from within five feet of the basket, which is helping make up for the increase in 3-pointers and boosting his impressive overall shooting percentage.

Smith got a boost from the fact that Nic Claxton was sidelined for the first few weeks of the season, and his strong play has allowed him to keep the starting role. The seventh-year big man has been showing flashes that he had more to offer for a while now, and it finally looks like the tide has turned in his favor. He should continue to build on the momentum of his strong start, which has included four double-doubles and season highs of 26 points, 13 rebounds, three steals and four blocks.

Dybantsa has hit a hot streak, averaging 19.2 points, 8.4 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.6 steals over the last five games, reaching the 20-point mark three times and securing two double-doubles in that stretch. He is shooting 44.3% from the field but just 23.8% from deep over the five games, which, although unremarkable, is still better than his season average of 42.3% from the field and 23.5% from deep.

The rookie has a lot of competition for the spotlight within the Wizards' lineup, as Trae Young, Anthony Davis, and Kyshawn George are leading the team in scoring. However, Dybantsa is still averaging the second-most shots per game on the team, with 14.4 attempts per outing. Moreover, he is doing well getting to the line, with 4.9 attempts per game, but he could still work on his efficiency in that area, as he is hitting 72.1%, for an average of 3.5 makes per outing. He is also doing a decent job of taking care of the ball, with an average of 2.3 turnovers in 34.0 minutes of action per outing. He should continue to develop more flow to his game and is already showing a positive trajectory towards being able to lead his team offensively.
