Management reported that strong cash flow enabled continued share repurchases and reinvestment in the store fleet, with the company remaining on track for its fourth consecutive year of net sales growth.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Abercrombie & Fitch Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker, Mo Gupta, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Mohit (Mo) Gupta: Thank you. Good morning, and welcome to our Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me today on the call are Fran Horowitz, Chief Executive Officer; Scott Lipesky, Chief Operating Officer; and Robert J. Ball, Chief Financial Officer. Earlier this morning, we issued our third quarter earnings release, which is available on our website at corporate.abercrombie.com under the Investors section. Also available on our website is an investor presentation. Please keep in mind that we will make certain forward-looking statements on the call.

These statements are subject to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from the expectations and assumptions we mentioned today. These factors and uncertainties are discussed in our reports and filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. In addition, we'll be referring to certain non-GAAP financial measures during the call. Additional details and reconciliations of GAAP to adjusted non-GAAP financial measures are included in the release and the investor presentation issued earlier this morning. With that, I will turn the call over to Fran.

Fran Horowitz: Thanks, Mo, and thanks, everyone, for joining. I'm pleased to report another strong quarter for our business. Net sales grew 11% to a third quarter record of $1.4 billion, ahead of our expectations and our 16th consecutive quarter of growth. We've grown the business each quarter for 4 years running, and that momentum continues. You've heard me emphasize the importance of balance, and we showed it again this quarter. All 3 regions and both brands delivered double-digit net sales growth with each seeing growth rate accelerate from second quarter levels. The strong top line, coupled with disciplined inventory management, enabled us to deliver healthy sales growth with higher AUR and lower promotions.

This performance flowed to the bottom line, where we delivered an operating margin of 15.5%, nicely above our expectations. And we continue to execute against our capital allocation priorities, investing in marketing, stores, digital and technology, all to support long-term growth while increasing net income per diluted share 62% year-over-year to $3.82. We also used our balance sheet to repurchase $100 million of shares in the quarter, bringing our year-to-date total to $382 million or 9% of shares outstanding at the beginning of the year. This marked our 11th straight quarter of share repurchases. Our teams continue to deliver for customers around the world, and we entered the important holiday season with momentum across brands and regions.

With that strong performance, we are raising our full year net sales and earnings expectations. We continue to expect fiscal 2026 to mark our fourth consecutive full year of net sales growth with consistent strong double-digit operating margins and significant cash return to shareholders through share repurchases. Turning back to the quarter. All 3 regions delivered double-digit net sales growth. The Americas grew 11% with stable traffic trends as we moved from back-to-school into fall. EMEA delivered 12% net sales growth with comparable sales up 4%, a significant sequential improvement from the second quarter. Germany performance improved nicely as the team continued to dial in marketing, promotions and inventory to customer traffic and demand.

Several other European markets returned to growth on healthy conversion trends, and the U.K. continues to be a consistent growth market. APAC performed ahead of our expectations again this quarter, growing 24% on strong traffic, particularly in stores. While still evaluating the right go-to-market strategies in the APAC region, the team has continued to invest in marketing and manage inventory, and we've seen stronger top line performance, especially in Hollister. Diving further into the brands, Hollister had a great back-to-school season to start the quarter and carried that momentum throughout, delivering 11% net sales growth on top of 16% growth and record third quarter sales last year.

As we discussed last quarter, the team prioritized receipts heading into back-to-school to support customer demand, and we continue to Read & React as the season progressed. That discipline allowed us to keep inventory tight, reduce promotional levels and deliver higher AUR. Growth was balanced across men's and women's with fleece, knits, graphics and bottoms performing well. Hollister's denim campaign with rising star Freya Skye drove strong social engagement and positive fan response to events in both the U.S. and U.K., demonstrating the power of connecting with our customers with culturally relevant talent and experiences.

Following a strong third quarter, Hollister is bringing an exciting flow of newness throughout the holiday season, including new product drops at Target as our continued partnership gives us another way to reach new and existing customers. In our owned and operated stores, we've invested to ensure our customers have the latest brand experience. Year-to-date, we've opened 23 new stores and remodeled or rightsized 48 Hollister stores, a substantial portion of our fleet. Overall, Hollister has made considerable progress, and we're excited for what the brand can do to cap off 2026. At Abercrombie brands, we had an excellent transition into fall with net sales growing 12% and accelerating nicely from the second quarter.

Inventory remained tightly managed and strong product acceptance allowed us to deliver improved AUR and lower-than-expected promotions. Growth was balanced across men's and women's and across tops and bottoms. Women's knits and sweaters performed particularly well, while men's saw strength across jeans and pants. Our active assortment under Your Personal Best continues to perform well. We recently showcased YPB through a partnership with Barry's, the fast-growing global fitness brand, bringing a collection of studio-ready activewear to its highly engaged community through Barry's studios and our direct channels. Abercrombie's momentum extends to our store fleet, an integral part of how customers experience the brand.

Our A&F SoHo store has continued to exceed expectations since opening in July with YPB, footwear and accessories all part of the experience. We've already brought elements of that modern A&F expression to 15 stores in major markets just in time for holiday. We're midway through another successful season with the NFL, connecting with fans in more ways across product, partnerships and experiences. As an official fashion partner of the NFL, the Dallas Cowboys and Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, we're engaging fans at game time events and offering our NFL assortment at select stadiums and on nflshop.com. And in time for holiday, we recently launched a collection co-designed with Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb.

The NFL assortment also extends to abercrombie kids with styles for boys and girls. As we move into the holiday season, we're offering a new digital gift card on the Abercrombie app and website, featuring ideas for every age from babies and toddlers to big kids and adults. Creating memorable holiday experiences has been part of Abercrombie for more than 130 years, and we're building on that heritage in new and relevant ways as we look to finish the year strong. In addition to our strong quarterly results, we've made meaningful progress against our 4 priorities for the year.

That includes growing our brands and owned and operated business while adding new avenues of growth, stabilizing gross margins against external cost pressures, investing in tools and technologies like AI to improve speed and efficiency and maintaining strong profitability to fuel excess cash return to shareholders through share repurchases. On that first priority, our growth continues to start with the customer, a consistent focus that has resulted in net sales growth every quarter for 4 consecutive years. Our teams have stayed close throughout the year, testing, learning and evolving our assortments alongside engaging marketing across brands and regions.

We've invested meaningfully in stores and digital to improve the customer experience while partnerships and new product categories are helping us reach new customers. While early, it's really encouraging to see how our evolved model is driving brand love, awareness and consideration even in well-established markets like the U.S. It's also exciting to see how we can make this much progress on global brand growth, including new partnerships and categories for our brands while still balancing our other 3 business priorities. We've been able to manage inventory and control promotions by focusing on giving the customer the fashion and fit they value, which has enabled gross margin improvement despite freight cost pressure.

We've continued to invest in our digital systems and infrastructure, including deploying AI-based solutions across the customer journey, which we believe is critical to brand health and relevance. And of course, with our strong culture of financial discipline, we've been able to keep our double-digit operating margins and also repurchased 9% of shares outstanding year-to-date. Three quarters in, 2026 has been a year of consistent profitable growth. That momentum, along with a strong start to November, has led us to increase our full year sales and profitability outlook.

We now expect to deliver our fourth consecutive year of net sales growth, another year of strong double-digit operating margins and growth in net income per diluted share while maintaining our target of returning at least $500 million to shareholders through share repurchases. The consistency of our results reflects the strength of our operating model, the health of our global brands and the financial discipline of this team. To our associates around the world, thank you for everything you do to deliver for our customers every day. I'm incredibly proud of what we continue to accomplish together. We're ready for holiday and a strong finish to 2026, and we look forward to updating you all on both in early March.

And with that, I'll hand it over to Robert.

Robert J. Ball: Thanks, Fran, and good morning, everyone. I'd also like to thank our teams around the world for another strong quarter and the work they've done to position us for the holiday season. We delivered record third quarter net sales of $1.44 billion, up 11% year-over-year and above the 5% to 6% growth range we provided in August. Comparable sales increased 6% and AUR grew high single digits, supported by lower promotional activity, driving better-than-expected results to our outlook. We're particularly encouraged by the quality and balance of that growth. Both brands in all 3 regions delivered double-digit net sales growth with sequential acceleration across the business. Starting with our regions.

Net sales increased 11% in the Americas, 12% in EMEA and 24% in APAC. Comparable sales increased 5% in the Americas, 4% in EMEA and 24% in APAC. By brand, Abercrombie brands net sales increased 12% with comparable sales up 6%. Hollister delivered 11% net sales growth against last year's record with comparable sales up 5%. Both brands grew net sales across all 3 regions. Across regions and brands, the spread between net sales growth and comparable sales was driven by net new stores and third-party channel performance. Importantly, we're seeing contributions from multiple sources of growth. Our existing direct-to-consumer business continues to perform, while the new stores and third-party distribution partnerships are providing incremental opportunities to reach customers.

That combination is encouraging as we think about the durability of our growth. Turning to profitability. Third quarter operating income was $223 million, and operating margin was 15.5% of sales, above the 13% to 14% outlook we provided in August. Our results included approximately $20 million of IEEPA tariff refunds, contributing around 150 basis points to operating margin, consistent with our outlook. But importantly, the underlying business also performed ahead of our expectations. At the midpoint of our outlook, operating margin exceeded expectations by approximately 200 basis points, driven primarily by stronger gross margin performance from higher AUR with additional benefit from expense leverage. Year-over-year, operating margin increased approximately 350 basis points from 12% in the third quarter of 2025.

Of that improvement, approximately 150 basis points came from tariff refunds and approximately 80 basis points came from lower year-over-year tariff expense on products sold in the quarter. Higher Q3 AUR was mostly offset by higher freight, so the remaining approximately 100 basis points of operating margin improvement came from operating expense leverage, particularly from marketing and fulfillment and selling expense. We're encouraged by our operating margin performance. Higher AUR and disciplined promotional activity are supporting gross margins, while continued expense management is allowing us to invest in the business and maintain strong profitability. And importantly, we're delivering that performance while continuing to make investments in stores, digital capabilities and the infrastructure needed to support future growth.

Moving below operating income. Our tax rate for the quarter was 29%, better than expected, primarily due to stronger international performance. Net income per diluted share was $3.82 compared with diluted earnings per share of $2.36 last year and above our outlook of $2.90 to $3.20. Both our third quarter outlook and results include approximately $0.40 per share of benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds. We do not currently anticipate any additional IEEPA tariff refunds, and we updated the table in the press release and investor presentation with additional detail on the timing of tariff refunds and ongoing tariff expense. Turning to inventory and the balance sheet.

Ending inventory at cost increased around 4% year-over-year with units up mid-single digits and aligned with our expectations for unit sales growth. We believe inventory remains appropriately positioned as we enter the holiday season, giving our teams flexibility to respond to consumer demand while maintaining promotional discipline. On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $724 million of cash and cash equivalents and approximately $1.2 billion of liquidity. During the quarter, we repurchased $100 million worth of shares, bringing year-to-date repurchases to $382 million and our 11th consecutive quarter of share repurchases. Year-to-date, that represents approximately 9% of beginning of year shares outstanding. We ended the quarter with $468 million remaining on our current repurchase authorization.

Our approach to capital allocation remains consistent. We're investing in the business to support profitable growth, maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning excess cash to shareholders. Turning to the outlook. Our strong third quarter performance and expectations for higher fourth quarter demand support an increase to our full year sales and EPS outlook. As a reminder, our full year outlook includes the entire $120 million of tariff refunds recognized during the second and third quarters. We estimate that the refund will contribute approximately 220 basis points to full year operating margin and approximately $2.15 to full year diluted earnings per share.

Separate from the refunds, our outlook continues to reflect current Section 301 tariff rates of 10% to 12.5% effective on global imports into the U.S. Based on those assumptions, we continue to expect approximately 10 basis points of year-over-year gross margin favorability from lower year-over-year tariff expense on sold product, which we expect to be more than offset by higher freight costs. For the full year, we now expect net sales growth of around 6% from the $5.27 billion in 2025, with growth across regions and brands. We now expect mid-single-digit AUR improvement for the full year and approximately 20 basis points of benefit to net sales from foreign currency.

We continue to expect full year operating margin in the range of 14.5% to 15%, including approximately 220 basis points of benefit from the IEEPA tariff refunds. We're forecasting a tax rate around 28%, diluted weighted average shares of around 44 million and net income per diluted share in the range of $13.70 to $13.90. The EPS outlook includes an estimated $2.15 from IEEPA tariff refunds. For capital allocation, we expect capital expenditures around $260 million. We remain on track to deliver approximately 130 new store experiences, including 50 new stores and 80 remodels and rightsizes against approximately 20 closures.

These investments remain an important part of our growth strategy, allowing us to expand our reach while improving productivity and customer experience of our existing fleet. We continue to expect at least $500 million of share repurchases for 2026. For the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect net sales growth of around 7% from the Q4 2025 level of $1.67 billion with growth across regions and brands. We expect a fourth quarter operating margin around 15%, a modest expansion from the fourth quarter of 2025. This is largely in line with our prior outlook, but has been updated to reflect some incremental freight expense of around 100 basis points.

Despite the increase in freight, we continue to expect modest gross margin improvement year-over-year, partially offset by modest expense deleverage, mainly from incentive compensation. We expect a fourth quarter tax rate of around 28% and net income per diluted share in the range of $4.40 to $4.60. Diluted weighted average shares are expected to be around 43 million, including the anticipated impact of at least $120 million of fourth quarter share repurchases. To close, we are pleased with our third quarter results and the consistency of execution we've delivered throughout 2026. We've now delivered 16 consecutive quarters of sales growth, and we're doing it while maintaining strong profitability, investing in the business and returning significant capital to shareholders.

What gives us conviction in our model isn't just our performance in any single quarter, but it's also our consistency. We're seeing healthy, sustained growth across our core business, expanding our reach through new stores and partnerships and maintaining the financial discipline needed to support both. As we look ahead, we're focused on adding to this track record while investing in the opportunities that can drive our next chapter of growth. We believe that we're well positioned to finish 2026 strong and carry that momentum into 2027, and we look forward to covering both in early March. With that, operator, we're ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will be coming from the line of Dana Lauren Telsey of Telsey Advisory Group.

Dana Lauren Telsey: Congratulations on the nice results. The sequential improvement in each of the brands and regions is very impressive. As you think about the cadence of the quarter, anything to do with the warm weather? Or did that only help you sell, whether it's more sweaters or jeans or other types of items? Anything you saw there? And any distinction in trends between women's and men's? And lastly, just following up on the freight costs. How much of a headwind do you see that going forward? And do your contracts or long-term agreements help to minimize the impact?

Fran Horowitz: Dana, -- so yes, wow, what a quarter. We're really proud and excited about delivering our 16th consecutive quarter, pleased across the entire quarter. The team knows that my favorite word is balance, and we sure found it this quarter. So we saw growth across brands, regions, genders, channels, really, really terrific with improved AUR and a strong bottom line. So it's just proof that the customers are responding to our value proposition. Women's and men's trends again, strong for all -- for both genders across both brands. And I'll hand it over to Robert to talk about the freight.

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Dana, so to your point, freight is a real cost pressure, and we've navigated it before. Our teams have a pretty strong playbook in place, and our operating model ultimately works. Freight did pressure gross margin in Q3 and does remain a headwind for us in Q4, but we're still expecting to grow our gross margins year-over-year in both quarters here. We're not assuming any rates reverse in 2027. We actively manage through sourcing, transportation timing, receipts through our Read & React model. That served us well over a range of different environments, and that's how we see things going forward.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Corey Tarlowe of Jefferies.

Corey Tarlowe: I guess, Fran, the Abercrombie business has been performing quite nicely. Could you talk a little bit about where you see opportunity within the assortment going forward? Is it more about men's, women's, specific categories? Curious your thoughts there as we head into the holiday.

Fran Horowitz: Corey, yes, wow, congrats to the Abercrombie team. Really excited to see that acceleration, 12% growth, really, really terrific and an acceleration from Q2. The brand is very healthy. We actually saw, as you mentioned, great performance across multiple categories. So we push for balance. We never want to focus too much on any one category. So we're seeing really strong performance in, I mean, best sweater quarter we've ever had. Bottoms are selling, strength across actually tops and bottoms, also strength across stores and digital. So really exciting to see across the world that we saw strength across the regions, double digits, as we said. Lots of exciting things happening. The team is ready to go.

I was in the mall this weekend, lots of excitement out there. We are ready to compete for the fourth quarter.

Corey Tarlowe: Great. And just, Robert, I wanted to follow up on the AUR opportunity. It seems like it nicely outperformed expectations this quarter. Could you unpack the drivers of that and what you might expect on that front as we look into holiday?

Robert J. Ball: Yes, really happy with where AUR shook out for the third quarter. I think it's a nice reflection of really strong product acceptance and really disciplined inventory management and promotions. We grew AUR high singles in Q3. We expect mid-single-digit growth now here for the full year. And I think it's really a testament to the teams and the fashion and the value that we are putting together for that consumer. We're delivering against both of those things, and it's showing up in strong demand and ultimately less discounting. For Q4, we still expect AUR growth, not really expecting any sort of major pullbacks on promos. We're happy with where the promotional cadence is for this holiday season.

But again, it starts with great products, disciplined inventory. We love the assortments that are out there for the holiday and the teams are ready to compete. So we'll see where we can go.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Marni Shapiro of The Retail Tracker.

Marni Shapiro: Congrats on a great quarter. The stores look fantastic. I'm curious if you could just give us an update on 2 things. Some of the newer stores you're opening are a little bit smaller, especially in the cities. And I'm curious what you're learning from that? And if it's possible, is it opening up more opportunities for you, specifically at Abercrombie? And then also at the Abercrombie brand, one of my favorite things out there right now is your holiday T-shirt pack. There's a bigger base of core items at Abercrombie than there was in prior years.

And I'm curious when you look at the assortment now, do you feel like there's a good solid almost replenishment mode or things that people are very reliant upon at Abercrombie, especially on the men's side?

Fran Horowitz: Marni, thank you. Let's see. We'll start with the newer stores. So we have been working on our real estate strategy for quite some time, as you're well aware. And we certainly have reduced the size of our stores over time, walking away specifically from any of the big flagships that we used to do. The opportunity that we have, which is super exciting, is to have different sized stores in different markets depending upon what that digital information is telling us when we open up those stores. We're excited about our street locations. I think you mentioned those.

So we're seeing nice responses in Newbury Street in Boston to Greenwich, Connecticut, and that's an opportunity for the Abercrombie store specifically. So yes, right size, right location, right economics, what you hear me say all the time, stores really do matter. And as far as core product goes, again, I'm going to go back to my balance comment. It's about a balanced assortment for the team. And yes, we have some great core product. We have our essential T-shirts, our essential hoodies. We have our Sloane pant. We have our denim. So we do see the customer coming back and replenishing, which is super exciting.

But again, that's replenished with some nice newness even in some of those core products and exciting to see the customer coming back and really voting for the brand.

Operator: And our next question comes from the line of Alex Straton of Morgan Stanley.

Katherine (Katie) Delahunt: This is Katie on for Alex. I know you guys cited stable traffic through the fall and a strong start to November, and that's different than some of what -- some of your peers are saying citing more of a weather-driven slowdown. What do you attribute your relative strength to? And then maybe just with that momentum, obviously, the guidance assumes a little bit of a growth slowdown. Can you kind of -- in the fourth quarter, can you kind of talk us through that? And then give us any color by banner?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Katie, so traffic has been relatively stable. Customers are reacting really well to the assortments, driving strong sales and margins throughout Q3. Our marketing is connecting with the consumers, healthy AUR shows that they're responding to the assortments and the product that we're delivering. We're growing both the productivity of our existing business, the reach of our brands through new stores and partnerships. So we like that balance, and we definitely see more opportunity ahead. In terms of the Q4 sales guide, expecting another strong quarter of growth here, momentum across the brands and the regions. Outlook calls for about 7% sales growth from that $1.67 billion from last year.

Again, growth across brands and regions, supported by strength in that core business. From an AUR perspective, if you think of the walk back from like that Q3 to Q4 walk again, planning to deliver high single-digit AUR growth in Q3, planning for, call it, mid-singles AUR on the full year, and that kind of works out to kind of mid-single-digit growth here in Q4. So promotions are not expecting any sort of meaningful promotion pullback year-over-year, but like we do every quarter, we'll come in day by day and see if we can pull back on the promo here, depth of a discount there and see if we can get some margin growth.

Mauricio Serna Vega: Just wanted to make sure I understood the comment about the quarter-to-date. Fran Horowitz: Sure. Mauricio, yes, super exciting quarter. As far as the partnerships go, we've been talking about evolving our operating model for some time. And the strength of the brand is really allowing us to do that. So we're showing up where our customer is, and that's proof points both in Target, where we had a really nice selling for back-to-school, and we're looking forward to the drop that's happening -- coming up very, very soon. Second year of our NFL partnership, we've expanded. We're now selling through Fanatics and nflshop.com and many of the stadiums, and the customer is responding. So we're excited about what those partnerships can do as we move ahead.

Robert J. Ball: Yes. And as it relates to the quarter-to-date trends, Mauricio, and we talked about a strong start to November. So obviously, coming off of a nice Q3, continuing to see strong November business. That's all reflected in our outlook. Obviously, well positioned here for the holiday season. But as we all know, the biggest selling weeks are still ahead of us. So we're excited to see how these things unfold here in the next couple of months and excited to talk to you about that in March.

Mauricio Serna Vega: Got it. And just one quick follow-up on the gross margin for Q4. Are you expecting expansion? Or is it fair to assume that given a more moderate AUR growth is going to be offset by the freight cost pressure?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Q4 gross margins and largely margins in total, largely consistent with what we implied back in the August guide. Exception being freight pressures. So freight has -- is a real pressure for us. It's about 100 basis points more pressure year-over-year than what we implied back in August. So -- but even with that, Mauricio, still expecting gross margins to improve year-over-year in the fourth quarter. We'll have some modest AUR growth and lower tariff expense that will more than offset that freight rate.

Mauricio Serna Vega: Congratulations on the results.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Kelly Crago of BMO Capital Markets.

Mason Clark: This is Mason Clark on the line for Kelly Crago. I was going to ask about Europe. And what are you guys seeing in the market given the macro challenges? And what brand is outperforming in Europe? And also, there was a big noncomp benefit this quarter. What is driving that? And does that continue into 4Q and FY '27?

Fran Horowitz: Thanks, Mason. I'll start off with the EMEA question. So just a huge shout out to that team and congratulations. The partnership I'm seeing between the EMEA team and the global team is really working really, really nicely. They're dialed in. They're focused on this local customer and exploring this playbook is clearly working. The U.K. specifically has been positive for a while. It's really exciting to see this improvement for Germany. It's a proof point that exploring this playbook now works in a non-English-speaking country, which is terrific. The team is doing what we do. They're controlling their inventory. They're managing their promotions. They're aligning their marketing.

It's just exciting to see, and we've got significant potential ahead of us.

Robert J. Ball: Yes. And as it relates to the noncomp benefit here, so Q3 comps grew 6%, total sales grew 11%. So nice balanced performance across stores and digital with both channels comping positively here. New stores are the largest contributor of growth beyond those comps. And those new stores are really important for us. They help put our brands out in front of more customers and expand our reach. Third party was a little bit of a benefit, but obviously, not the driver here. Partnerships are a little bit smaller, but they are an incremental contributor for us. And it's great because they're helping to introduce our brand to new audiences outside of those owned and operated channels.

So we like the balance, and we're ready to keep going for Q4.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Jon Keypour of Goldman Sachs.

Jonathan (Jon) Keypour: Congrats on the very, very solid results. I'm just wondering if we can go into denim a little bit. I'm wondering in terms of like cuts and silhouettes, what's performing well? Are you guys seeing any kind of renewal to the denim cycle that might be driving the comp? And I'm just sort of wondering how we should think about from a fashion standpoint, maybe where the denim category is going next year?

Fran Horowitz: Jon, it's Fran. So listen, denim is a very important category for us, and that is true for both brands and both genders. But at the same time, which is what the team really focuses on is balance across all of our categories. So what's happening in denim is lots of exciting things. We're seeing the customer really have an opportunity to pick their denim based on their wearing occasion for the day. So there's no longer just one key silhouette that works for them. It really depends on what they're up to for that day or for that evening. So again, a strong category for us, but more importantly, it's balanced.

And what we've seen this quarter is balanced across tops and bottoms and across genders and across brands. So super excited with the results that we put up.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Rick Patel of Raymond James.

Rakesh (Rick) Patel: Congrats on the strong results. We're looking for more granularity on the AUR improvement. How does that look like by category and by geography? Just curious how broad the scope of AUR improvement is and to what degree it might be concentrated in one area more than others?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Rick, it's Robert. So yes, really pleased with where our AUR landed here. Again, we've talked a little bit about the fact that this was pretty broad-based. And it really does reflect the strength of the assortment that we have out there and how disciplined we've been on the inventory side. So not one specific brand, not one specific category or one specific geo. We kind of saw this improvement and this demand picture kind of develop all the way through across the Americas, EMEA and APAC and across both Abercrombie and Hollister. So great demand picture really speaks to the strength of our brands, and it's a really exciting place to be as we head into holiday.

Rakesh (Rick) Patel: And it's also really nice to see the gross margin improvement even with the freight headwind. As we look ahead, can you give us insight on cost inflation? What does that look like in terms of labor and other product costs as we think about the puts and takes outside of tariffs and freight costs?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. I mean great to be in a place where we can grow gross margins in Q3. Again, expect to grow our gross margins again here in Q4. You hit on all of the big categories here. Freight is the biggest mover from a headwind standpoint. Tariffs become a tailwind for us and are a helper. And then we've got this AUR growth that we're expecting in Q4 to help offset that. Not a lot to report. Raw material costs remain manageable, so nothing significant to call out there.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Janine Hoffman Stichter of U.S. Bancorp BTIG.

Janine Hoffman Stichter: Really nice to see the SG&A leverage and just strong financial discipline. Can you help us think about the mix of SG&A in terms of fixed versus variable and maybe contextualize how that's changed over the last few years? And also curious about the partnerships. I think you put the ERP system in place earlier this year. How is that helping you think about future partnerships and the potential to do more over the next few years?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Janine, we've been on quite the journey as it relates to our expense base. And I think it's been pretty stable over the last handful of years. Obviously, being net store openers for working on the fifth year now in a row. We are adding some fixed costs to the base with these new stores, but they're incredibly productive stores, really twice the productivity of the stores that we're closing. So excited to be there. But really, we're investing behind 2 growing brands across regions. And we've been doing that while delivering double-digit operating margins. So we continue to be really confident in the underlying profitability of this business.

In Q3, marketing and fulfillment helped us to deliver expense leverage on the sales outperformance. And so we're excited about where this is headed. But you'll see us continue to invest in these brands. We're focused on sustainable profitable growth over time, not trying to maximize any one thing in any one particular quarter. As it relates to the ERP, definitely great to have that behind us and kind of all up and running and smooth sailing here for the back half of the year. As you recall, the point of that ERP or one of the reasons for that ERP is the ease of plugging in new partners into this business.

And you've seen us do that as we've moved through second and third quarter here. You'll continue to see us test into things here in the fourth quarter, but excited to see what that unlocks for us and the fact that it went -- it was a nice smooth transition here. Team did a great job.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Adrienne Yih of Barclays.

Angus Kelleher-Ferguson: This is Angus Kelleher on for Adrienne Yih. So Hollister comps inflected from negative 3% to positive 5% despite still tricky comps last year. So congrats on that. Really nice to see both banners positive again. How much of that was just better inventory availability after the actions last quarter versus underlying traffic and conversion improvement? And I guess, if possible, if you could rank order the biggest drivers there for Hollister? And then I have a follow-up.

Fran Horowitz: Angus, yes, excited to see what Hollister did this quarter. The brand is in excellent shape. I mean, to pick up 11% on top of -- pick up 16%, excuse me, on top of 11% last year, setting another record quarter is really, really terrific, a great, great back-to-school. Again, strength was across categories. We saw that in fleece and knits and graphics and bottoms, lots of new experiences happening out there across regions. So very balanced growth across all regions and both genders as well. So super excited to see how this brand strength is also allowing us as asked a few times this morning about entering into some new channels as well, expecting another record year. Your follow-up?

Angus Kelleher-Ferguson: And then one for Robert. So you're clearly getting leverage on the P&L this year even with freight still a headwind. And I think it sounds like you are not assuming rates reverse in 2027. As we think about next year, how do you frame, I guess, the building blocks for margin, marketing, incentive comp and ERP investment? And as a follow-up to that, I guess, what level of sales growth do you need to keep driving that leverage?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. Okay. So let me bite those off here. So as it relates to 2027 and I guess what you're asking around is normalization, we're ultimately confident in the overarching margin structure of this business. Obviously, you're calling this out, recognizing not every one of these Q4 headwinds has the same duration. I think the key distinction here is higher freight rates. Freight is a real headwind for us. We're not assuming that, that automatically reverses next year. Incentive compensation is really the other big one that I would call out here. We've had a fantastic back half of the year. We're seeing some incentive compensation roll through the back half here. That will obviously normalize in 2027.

But I think that Q3 helped to demonstrate the underlying operating leverage that this business can drive, even after you separate out that refund benefit. So we're not going to provide 2027 margin guidance today. We will see you in March, and we'll talk more about that in March. But I think what I would just leave you with is the fact that we've been able to navigate these structures and these disruptions for many years now, and we've been able to maintain strong double-digit operating margins, and that's the plan going forward.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Dylan Carden of William Blair.

Dylan Carden: Appreciate it. Curious, a lot of repetition of the word consistency in some of the prepared remarks. And it seems like 2026 has been a year of stability, both on sort of the level of growth and sort of margin stability. And I'm curious if you kind of update the playbook, how you're thinking about the major drivers there of being able to consistently grow from here. And part of the thought might be that the assortment here is relatively more dynamic than it's been in a while and helping you offset some of the sort of larger trip-ups that other competitors are seeing, namely around weather being the most obvious.

And so just any commentary about the larger handholds as it relates to being able to grow consistently and how the assortment plays into that from here? Relatively open-ended, I appreciate. But I would just love to kind of unpack that word that seems to be making it...

Robert J. Ball: All good, Dylan, and I appreciate that you picked up on the consistency trend because we're sitting here with 4 years of growth behind us, consistent double-digit operating margins. We like where we are, but we're still not standing still. And I think the operating model that we have is proven, and it gives us a lot of conviction in the next chapter of growth that we have, which I think you're kind of poking at here. We laid this model out really starting January of 2025. The ambition hasn't changed since then. We're looking to grow sales.

We're looking to keep gross margin in the 60s, deliver double-digit operating margins with strong cash flows and ultimately growing operating income and EPS faster than sales. I think Q3 is a great example of that EPS growth, where we grew 62% year-over-year on EPS, which is a nice example for you. We've got strong brands. We've got healthy profitability. We've got a great balance sheet that allows us to invest for growth and still return capital through repurchases. And I think what's exciting is that we have multiple ways to grow. Our comps are positive. We've got -- our comps remain strong. We're expanding our reach through new categories, new channels, new partnerships and international markets. That's the framework.

And that's really what gives us the confidence and the conviction behind being able to consistently grow and capture these opportunities ahead.

Dylan Carden: I appreciate that. And any comments around the sort of the assortment, how that's changed in the last 5 years as far as being able to sort of dynamically move around larger market functions such as weather or trend?

Fran Horowitz: Dylan, we've talked a lot about how unique our operating model is. And what the team really does is they stay very close to the customer. They keep their inventory very tight. We can test and learn about our assortments. We chase very aggressively. We produce in 17 countries around the world, which helps us stay very, very agile. So I'm very proud of the operating model that we have instituted, and it's clearly working.

Operator: And our next question will be coming from the line of Tom Nikic of Needham.

Tom Nikic: It seems like the business has a lot of momentum heading into the holidays. Just wanted to follow-up on some of the questions around AUR and promos and discounting for the holiday season. Can you just talk about your level of confidence in your ability to maintain pricing integrity even if some other apparel retailers are out there end up being more aggressive on promotions and discounting? And so I'd imagine that not every mall-based retailer has the type of momentum you have. So there may be some peers out there that get more aggressive on discounting. So would just love to get your perspective there.

Fran Horowitz: Tom, yes, I mean, you'll hear me say this today, and I say it probably in every single call, but we don't base our promotions on what the competition is doing. We work with the teams on a weekly basis. We look at our inventories, what's working, what's not working, and that's really how we drive our promotional business. It's a Read & React to what's happening and not what's happening with the competition. We feel very confident about our assortments heading into the fourth quarter, and we'll continue to drive the business that way.

Tom Nikic: All right. Sounds good. And if I could just add a follow-up about -- obviously, you've been a net store grower for a couple of years now. Can you just talk about the performance that you're seeing in your new stores and how additive they've been to the brand overall?

Robert J. Ball: Yes. You heard Fran mention this, but stores really do matter. They are a really critical piece of our whole overarching brand experience, and they go hand-in-hand with digital, which remains a critical growth channel for us as well. We don't really see it as an either/or there. It's really about this omnichannel environment that we've built over the years. We're going to keep investing where we see customer response and returns support it. We're seeing strong returns from our store investments with new stores delivering roughly twice the productivity of our closures. We've got a pretty rigid financial structure here in terms of what we need to see in order to open these locations.

And we want paybacks less than 2 years. We want 20% plus 4-wall margins. And so that's ultimately why we're continuing to invest in this fleet. So there's no real finish line. We're excited to be net store openers here for the fifth year. We've got a great fleet and our focus continues to be on making sure that we can get the best expression of the brands out there for the consumer.

Operator: And I would now like to turn the conference back to Fran for closing remarks.

Fran Horowitz: Well, thank you, everyone. In March, we look forward to updating you after the fourth quarter and wishing everybody a happy holiday season.

Operator: And this concludes today's program. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#2906. Celtics have bigger issues, but can strengthen grasp on NBA Cup bid in DC

Celtics have bigger issues, but can strengthen grasp on NBA Cup bid in DC originally appeared on NBC Sports Boston

The Boston Celtics wrap up what's been a thus-far winless four-game road trip on Tuesday night in the nation's capital. And while the NBA Cup is not likely front of mind for the team — and simply righting the ship amid a four-game losing streak is priority No. 1 — the team has a chance to strengthen its grasp on East Group C during a visit to the Washington Wizards.

The Celtics own a 2-0 record in Group C play, while both the Wizards and Hawks — their final two group opponents this week — have both stumbled in group play. Boston has two pathways to being one of the four teams to advance in Cup play: Win Group C outright, or earn the East wildcard spot by having the best point differential among the three East runner-ups.

Boston currently owns the best point differential in the East at +53. Both the Hawks and Wizards sit at +13 in the event that a Group C tiebreaker is necessary.

With wins over Washington and Atlanta this week, Boston would win Group C outright and likely host the East wildcard winner in Round 1, if they maintain the best point differential among all group winners.

A win over Washington but a loss to Atlanta would still leave Boston with a strong chance to advance as the East wildcard, but would require a healthy point differential. A loss to Washington but win over Atlanta would leave all three teams tied at 3-1 in Cup play and make point differential the tiebreaker for both winner and runner-up in the group.

Two losses this week and Boston would be eliminated from Cup play and would instead compete against two non-Cup qualifiers over the second week of December.

When the Celtics won their first two Cup games, we wondered if there was any chance that Boston and Philadelphia could meet in later-round play, potentially accelerating Jaylen Brown's first game back at TD Garden.

Philadelphia is still alive in Group B play, but a 1-1 record and negative point differential complicates its path. The Sixers would need wins over Miami and Indiana, plus the Knicks to beat Cleveland, in order to win Group B via head-to-head tiebreaker over Miami. Two wins could help Philadelphia push for the East wildcard spot, but a minus-19 point differential through two games basically requires them to dominate those final games.

Hecla Mining (HL -2.68%), a silver and gold miner, closed at $10.90, down 2.7%. #2901. Dell Just Reported Earnings and Raised Its Forecast by $10 Billion. Is the Stock a Buy After Tuesday's Selloff?

Dell shares fell 12% on Tuesday after a rival warned about AI-server profits. Hours later, Dell reported higher margins.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:54PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Dell Technologies ›

Dell Technologies (DELL -11.83%) shares rose about 3% to $305 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the company reported that quarterly revenue more than doubled and raised its full-year forecast. The stock had closed at $295.28 in the regular session, down 12% from Monday's $334.91, as AI hardware shares sold off.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE -16.31%) led that decline. Its shares fell about 16% after executives said on Monday's earnings call that memory and other components could stay scarce through at least the second half of 2028. HPE also guided for its cloud and AI business to keep about 14% of sales as operating profit in fiscal 2027, down from 18.4% in the quarter it just reported. Dell, which sells many of the same servers, fell with it.

Dell's earnings release for the quarter ended Oct. 30 showed revenue of $54.9 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. And adjusted earnings rose 265% to $9.45 per share, well above the $6.59 analysts expected.

Most of the growth came from the Infrastructure Solutions Group, which sells servers, networking, and storage. Its revenue tripled to $42.0 billion. AI-optimized server sales rose 291% to $22.0 billion, and traditional servers and networking rose 235% to $15.0 billion. "We are now a different company," Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke said in the release.

Dell booked $60.2 billion of AI orders in the quarter and ended it with a record AI backlog of $132.3 billion, about two-thirds of the revenue it expects for the whole year.

Gross margin was 21% of revenue, up from 20.7% a year earlier. Helping to drive that increase, the infrastructure business kept 17% of its sales as operating profit, compared with 12.4% a year ago, and its operating income quadrupled to $7.1 billion.

Lower spending also helped. Operating expenses fell to 7.5% of revenue from 12.9%, and Chief Financial Officer David Kennedy said that is driving "higher profitability, even as AI servers become a larger part of our business." AI servers tend to carry thinner margins than storage, so a rising AI share usually pulls margins down, but this quarter it clearly didn't.

On the other hand, PCs were the weak spot. The Client Solutions Group grew revenue by 3% to $12.9 billion, consumer sales fell by 15%, and the segment's operating income slipped by 6% to $704 million.

Dell raised its full-year revenue forecast by $10 billion to $202 billion, up 78% from last year, and its AI server sales forecast to $78 billion from $74 billion. It now expects adjusted earnings of $29.68 per share, up from $25.50. For the fourth quarter, it guided revenue to $56.3 billion and adjusted earnings to $8.40 per share.

Separately, the company returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends in the quarter, and its board approved an additional $25 billion in repurchases. Free cash flow rose to $3.5 billion from $506 million a year earlier.

Inventories rose to $29.4 billion on Oct. 30 from $10.4 billion at the end of January, and total debt rose to $37.7 billion from $31.5 billion. If component costs keep climbing, as HPE expects, Dell may need to keep raising prices, and one quarter of higher margins doesn't show it can do that indefinitely.

The stock is also volatile. It rose about 20% on Monday after Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) reinstated CEO Jensen Huang, then gave back most of that gain on Tuesday.

Even after Tuesday's after-hours gain, the stock trades at about 10 times the adjusted earnings Dell expects for the fiscal year ending in January. That's a low multiple for a company whose revenue just doubled and whose backlog covers much of next year. And while the stock fell on worries about a rival's margins, Dell's own margins rose.

The case depends on AI spending holding up, the same bet behind most AI stocks. Investors who already own plenty of semiconductor stocks and other AI infrastructure names should know Dell adds to that exposure rather than diversifying it. Those who want to see whether component costs hit margins can wait for next quarter's report.

#2899. Rockets clamber over Clippers 116-104

Tonight the Rockets took on a Los Angeles Clippers team, a team that is staggering its way through a dense fog of official opprobrium, that is almost a mirror image of the Rockets. The Rockets stand at 13-5, the Clippers at 4-12. The Rockets are 8-1 at home, the Clippers 0-8 on the road. Would the Clippers find their way to a first road win tonight? If you read the title of this recap, obviously not.

The game, though, was surprisingly close until the end. We can't say that the Clippers fired up the tank machine late, because they don't have their own picks for the next five seasons. There's no reason for the Clippers not to try to win, and try they did. It's just that the Clippers team is currently an island of misfit toys, a clipper ship of the damned, a rag tag band of hard luck sports millionaires just trying for one last score. Well, not really, but it is a somewhat odd team.

The team features Darius Garland, Brandon Ingram playing for the first time all season, just to annoy me, cross town transfer Rui Hachimura, Derrick Jones Jr, shooting around 50% from 3pt range until this game, and the ageless wonder, Brooke Lopez still very large and able to shoot 3pters at 38.

It's not a terrible lineup, nor is it particularly good, with the exception of Darius Garland, who looks healthy for the first time in several years, and you can see the quickness, and ability to get anywhere, and shoot from anywhere, on the court. He scored 26pts on 10-21 shooting, 4-10 3pt, and had 8ast to 1 TO. That's about the extent of actually dangerous Clipper players.

That said, this game was simply awkward. The Rockets let the Clippers hang around, seemingly unable to string together both baskets and stops for very long. The Rockets would build a lead out to around 10 points, and the Clippers would bring that down to around 6 points, or less. There might have been a bit of mild panic that the Clippers would indeed manage to get their first win on the road, if someone got hot late for them, and the Rockets scoring dried up.

The Rockets scoring did not in fact dry up, mainly due to a Rockets player who has been quiet for much of the season, rarely asserting himself to lead the way. A deferential role player known to some as "The Slim Reaper" or "KD". This low shooting volume veteran, Kevin Durant, lead the way tonight with 32 points, on 11-19 shooting, 4-6 3pt, 9 rbs, 4 ast, 2 TO, 1 blk. He did this in only 33 minutes. In fact none of the Rockets starters played big minutes tonight, Durant's 33 minutes was the highest on the team. Alperen Sengun continued his good form, going 20pts. 7-11 FG, 1-2 3pt, 8 rbs, 7 ast, an uncharacteristic 5 TO, and 2 blk. Amen Thompson had a great return to form, and was able to get in close to score, also notching 20 pt, on 9-12 FG, 1-1 3pt, 4 rbs, 5 ast, 0 TO, 1 blk.

This game might have been easier if the Rockets had followed a first quarter where they only allowed 15 points to the Clippers, to 25 of their own, by not letting the Clippers back in the game, losing the second quarter 28-22.

The Rockets got a better, if not outstanding, performance from the bench than they did in Denver. Tari Eason had one of the most Tari Eason sequences ever tonight as well. He followed a powerful late clock dunk by ripping the ball from a Clipper at mid court. He then strolled down the lane, alone, to try, well, I don't know what sort of stylish shot he had in mind. He absolutely bricked this uncontested attempt, which was rebounded by a trailing Clipper, whom Eason immediately fouled. Tarissimo!

We saw 25 minutes from Marcus Smart, as he seems to be creeping towards starter level minutes, despite not contributing all that much on the scoresheet. What joy he brings to Ime Udoka's heart, I suppose we will never quite know, but I suspect it's less than he brings to mine.

One big takeaway from this game is that the Rockets moved the ball quickly, and decisively for the most part tonight, aside, oddly from Fred VanVleet who only had 4 ast. The team overall had 36 assists on 46 made baskets, against 13 turnovers. That sort of performance is good to see, as most of the shots generated were good ones, and we saw less of the over passing that sometimes characterizes the team when they want to move the ball around. The Rockets had six players with four or more assists tonight – Durant (4), Sengun (7), VanVleet (4), Thompson (5), Eason (4), Sheppard (5). Durant lead the team with 19 attempts, so it truly was a group effort on offense.

There's not much more about a game that felt awkward at times, but not exactly in doubt. The Rockets take on the Suns, looking for vengeance, in their final NBA Cup game on Wednesday.

The Rockets continue rolling through the regular season at a great win rate. Until next time, Happy Thanksgiving to all of you, and yours.

Rick will follow with a detailed review of our financial results, after which we will open up the call for questions. For the quarter ended September 30th, core net investment income was $0.13 per share. This exceeded our base dividend of $0.04 per share per month, or $0.12 per share for the quarter. As of September 30th, our NAV per share was $6.35, which is down 3.2% from the prior quarter.

As we previously disclosed, PNNT has a considerable balance of undistributed taxable income, which we are required to distribute to shareholders. PNNT is utilizing the supplemental dividends to pay out the undistributed taxable income, and the decline in NAV was largely attributable to these supplemental dividend payments. As previously communicated, the December payment will conclude our supplemental dividend program. Excluding the payment of the supplemental dividends in this past quarter, NAV would have decreased only $0.09, or 1.4%. Despite the ongoing macroeconomic and geopolitical environment, our portfolio remains highly diversified and conservatively positioned, with a median debt-to-EBITDA of 4.6 times, interest coverage of 2.1 times, and a loan-to-value of 44%.

As of September 30th, our portfolio totaled $1.2 billion, and during the quarter, we continued to originate attractive investment opportunities and invested a total of $75 million at a weighted average yield of 9.4%, including $25 million invested into five new platform investments with a median debt-to-EBITDA of 4.8 times, interest coverage of 2.2 times, and a loan-to-value ratio of 36%. We added two investments to non-accrual status and removed one investment, and ended the quarter with five non-accrual investments out of a diversified pool of 160 companies, representing 2.1% of the portfolio at cost and 0.6% at market value. Our PSLF joint venture portfolio continues to be a significant contributor to our core net investment income.

On a last 12 months basis, PNNT's average cash yield on invested capital in the JV was 14.7%. As of September 30th, the JV portfolio totaled $1.2 billion. In July, the JV refinanced the AAA tranches of its $300 million debt securitization, reducing the securitization's weighted average spread by 97 basis points to 1.69% from 2.66%. We expect the JV to continue to be a significant contributor to PNNT's NII in future quarters. Turning to portfolio positioning, I'd like to highlight our government services and defense investments. Government services and defense remains one of our highest conviction sectors and has historically been among our best performing investment areas.

We remain highly constructive on the long-term outlook for government services and defense because the sector possesses several characteristics that align well with our investment philosophy. Demand has historically been supported by durable federal funding priorities and long-term contracts that provide meaningful revenue visibility and stability. Many of these businesses exhibit resilient cash flow profiles, variable cost structures, and are generally less sensitive to broader economic cycles than many commercial industries. In addition, the sector continues to benefit from active M&A markets and strong valuation support, thereby providing multiple avenues for value creation. One example of this is Echelon InvestCo.

Through our equity co-investment in Echelon InvestCo, we have an ongoing equity investment in a fast-growing defense tech company, Shield AI. Shield AI recently announced an acquisition and a capital raise at an indicative valuation for investment of $2.6 million above the value on September 30th of $2 million. This increase equates to $0.04 per share. Within the government services and defense portfolio, our investments are focused on businesses that support the Department of War and other mission-critical government agencies. We focus on companies addressing high-priority national security initiatives, including modernization of defense systems and digital infrastructure, cyber and electronic warfare capabilities, modeling and simulation, counter-drone technologies, and next-generation autonomous systems.

We believe these priorities will remain central to U.S. defense spending for years to come, creating a favorable backdrop for continued investment opportunities. On a combined basis, including the joint venture portfolio, government services and defense represents approximately 12.4% of total investments. Given our experience, sourcing capabilities, and the attractive opportunity set, we intend to increase that exposure over time. Another highlight of our portfolio is AKW, a U.K. provider of adapted bathroom and kitchen products that help elderly and disabled individuals live independently at home. Since taking control of AKW in 2018, we have strengthened management, improved operations, and invested in growth.

On October 27, 2026, AKW acquired Mobility Bathing Group, entering the private pay market and creating cross-selling, marketing, and cost-saving opportunities. We are targeting an exit of the investment in AKW in the next 18 to 24 months. As of September 30, we held $48 million of the first lien term loan, marked at par, and common equity valued at $77.7 million against a cost of $5.9 million. Turning to software, our exposure represents approximately 3.1% of the portfolio. These investments follow our core middle market strategy and consist of cash pay loans with financial covenants, moderate leverage, and relatively short durations. These businesses provide mission-critical enterprise software to regulated industries, including defense, healthcare, and financial services.

Let me now turn to the broader market environment. M&A activity has increased recently, although overall conditions remain uneven. Private equity sponsors remain active, and we are seeing a growing pipeline of attractive opportunities across both new originations as well as add-on investments. We are optimistic that activity levels will remain strong throughout the end of the year and into next year. We expect increased transaction activity to drive repayments across the portfolio, including opportunities to monetize equity co-investments and to redeploy that capital into income-generating investments. In the core middle market, the pricing for high-quality first lien term loans remains attractive, typically ranging from SOFR plus 500 to 550 basis points, with leverage of approximately 4.5x EBITDA.

Importantly, these structures continue to include meaningful covenant protections, which is in contrast to the covenant-light structures prevalent in the upper middle market. We believe the current environment favors lenders with established private equity sponsor relationships, consistent access to deal flow, and disciplined underwriting. These are longstanding strengths of the PennantPark platform. We continue to believe that the core middle market offers an attractive risk-adjusted opportunity. Companies in this segment generally have EBITDA of $10 million-$50 million and often operate below the practical threshold of the broadly syndicated loan and high-yield markets.

As a result, lenders can typically conduct extensive diligence, negotiate meaningful financial covenants, structure transactions with appropriate leverage and equity cushions, and maintain regular access to company financial information. Since our inception nearly 19 years ago, PNNT has invested $9.9 billion at an average yield of 11.1%, while maintaining a loss ratio on invested capital of roughly 20 basis points annually, a testament to our consistent and disciplined approach through multiple market cycles. As a provider of strategic capital who fuels the growth of our portfolio companies, in many cases, we participate in the upside of that company by making an equity co-investment. Our returns on these equity co-investments have been excellent over time.

Overall, for our platform from inception through September 30th, we have invested over $635 million in these equity co-investments and have generated an IRR of 25% and a multiple on invested capital of 2x. Looking ahead, our experienced team and broad origination platform position us well to generate attractive deal flow. We remain steadfast in our commitment to capital preservation and maintaining a disciplined, patient investment approach. We continue to focus on investing in high-quality middle market companies with strong free cash flow generation. We capture that value through first lien senior secured loans, and we pay out those cash flows in the form of dividends to our shareholders.

At this time, I will turn the call over to Rick for a more detailed review of our financial results.

#2893. Wall Street's $1.4 Trillion Bubble May Be on the Verge of Bursting -- but It's Not Artificial Intelligence (AI)

While Wall Street obsesses over an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, record levels of borrowing could pose an unexpected threat to the stock market.

By Adam Spatacco – Nov 24, 2026 at 5:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Over the past four years, euphoria for artificial intelligence (AI) stocks has fueled a historic rally in the stock market. Enthusiasm surrounding AI infrastructure and software has helped propel the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.50%), Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -1.48%), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +0.85%) to record highs.

Although much of Wall Street's attention is focused on whether AI stocks are overvalued, another vulnerability is lurking in the background. Investors are borrowing unprecedented sums of money to participate in the stock market's ongoing rally. This introduces another layer of risk into an already frothy market.

Let's explore why margin debt represents one of Wall Street's biggest threats and what smart investors can do about it.

Margin debt is a financial term used to describe money investors borrow from a brokerage firm to buy stocks. This practice is more commonly known as leverage. It allows investors to increase their purchasing power without committing an equivalent amount of their own capital up front.

Although borrowing can be lucrative when stocks are rising, leverage works in both directions. For example, imagine you have $10,000 and borrow another $10,000 from a brokerage firm. With $20,000 invested, a 25% increase in the portfolio's value generates a $5,000 gain. This represents a 50% return on your original capital. However, if the portfolio declines by 25%, you would lose $5,000, or half of your original investment. A 50% decline effectively wipes out your original capital.

According to data compiled by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), margin debt reached a record $1.5 trillion in June. To appreciate the magnitude of that figure, let's take a look at borrowing levels during other periods of unusually high speculation in the stock market.

Although today's borrowing levels dwarf the historical figures in terms of absolute dollars, it's important to consider the fact that the stock market has become considerably larger. Nevertheless, the rapid accumulation of debt over the last year or so suggests investors are developing more of an appetite for risk.

One of the most dangerous aspects of using leverage is that investors do not necessarily control when their positions are sold. Brokerage firms require investors to maintain a minimum level of liquidity in their margin accounts. If declining stock prices cause an account to fall below that threshold, investors could face a margin call. This would require them to deposit additional collateral or reduce their positions.

Brokerages also have the authority to liquidate positions without obtaining an investor's permission. When this happens across several accounts at the same time, the forced selling puts additional downward pressure on stock prices. As a result, more margin calls are triggered, and a destructive cycle is created.

With all of that said, current margin debt levels could suggest investors are moderating their risk exposure. At the end of October, margin debt was recorded at $1.4 trillion, or about 3.6% below its peak from June. While this could indicate investors are becoming more cautious, declining balances can also reflect forced liquidations rather than voluntary reductions in risk.

It's important to understand that elevated margin debt doesn't necessarily mean a stock market crash is imminent. Borrowing often increases alongside rising stock prices. Ultimately, margin debt is better viewed as a potential amplifier of market volatility rather than a reliable predictor of when a crash or drawdown will occur.

Even if excessive leverage contributes to a pullback, smart investors should remember that the stock market always demonstrates resilience. The S&P 500 declined by 49% following the dot-com bubble and nearly 57% during the financial crisis. More recently, the index fell 34% during the COVID-19 crash and 25% during the 2022 bear market. Despite these setbacks -- depicted by the grey columns in the chart below -- the S&P 500 eventually recovered and reached new record highs.

The takeaway here is that investors who buy stocks using their own capital wind up having more financial flexibility to endure prolonged downturns than those whose brokerage firms can force them to sell at unfavorable prices.

Although nobody knows whether today's borrowing levels will culminate in another stock market bubble bursting event, history suggests that staying diversified and remaining invested through volatility is a more prudent approach to building long-term wealth than attempting to predict the next market crash.

#2889. What’s wrong with the Boston Celtics? (Topic Tuesday)

Life comes at you fast, huh? A week ago, the Boston Celtics were 11-2 and looking like one of the best teams in the league. There was a lot of "better without you-know-who" talk and Tatum was in the MVP discussion. After four straight losses, including (at least) 2 really bad ones, the umbrellas are out and the forecast is calling for heavy skyfall.

So what happened? Or more specifically, what's going wrong? This is literally the same team that was 11-2, but now the results are different. They played a lot of bad teams early in the schedule, but at least 2 of the teams in this last stretch are bad and/or shorthanded. We can't even blame injuries for this stretch (aside from load management and illness).

Did the league crack the code on the Celtics offense? Is it just a prolonged shooting slump? Are they falling into old bad habits? Are the rotations bad? Are they playing with the rotations too much? Did Joe Mazzulla forget how to coach? Did they stop listening to him? Is it all the refs fault? (Miss you Tommy)

Yes, I know that we're not at 20 games yet. I'm just starting a discussion that may not have a definitive conclusion. And before we get too carried away, it is worth noting that last year's team was 9-8 at this point. All the games count, but a 4 game losing streak is a lot better in November than it is in the Spring. There's still a lot of season left to burn through.

The next logical question is "what does this team need?" Followed shortly by "what moves can they make?" I'm not prepared (mentally, emotionally, whatever) to address that topic yet, but you are welcome to start it here.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

#2874. Open Thread: Happy birthday to David Jones Garcia

Spurs small forward David Jones Garcia has one of the best Spurs "feel good stories," and that's saying a lot on a team that features Julian Champagnie's path from undrafted player to NBA Finals starter, Keldon Johnson's evolution to NBA Sixth Man, and Victor Wembanyama's emergence as the face of the NBA.

David Jones Garcia was born in Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic. After seeing scouts at FIBA tournaments, his family sent David to high school in the United States to offer him the best exposure for future basketball opportunities. He attended DePaul where he became a starter after his first full season. He transferred to St. John's where he continued to excel, but the year was emotionally fragmented with the loss of his father. David vowed to his father on his deathbed he would play at least one regular-season NBA game.

Jones Garcia returned to college, but this time in Memphis under head coach Penny Hardaway. He declared for the 2024 NBA Draft but was undrafted. He spent the 2024-25 season bouncing around the G-League, signing contracts with the Philadelphia 76ers, Mexico City Capitanes, and Utah Jazz affiliate. He eventually made the 2025 G-League All-Rookie Team.

That summer he signed on with the San Antonio Spurs, initially for Summer League finally landing a two-way contract.

On October 22, in the first game of the season, Jones Garcia fulfilled his promise to his father and clocked 4 minutes against the Dallas Mavericks. He spent first half of the season coming off the bench. With a penchant for hitting threes and no traces of fear in his court demeanor, Jones Garcia revealed a confident and competent competitor.

He played in eleven total games before requiring surgery on his right ankle. On February 4, he was ruled out for the remainder of the season.

Jones Garcia signed on with the Spurs again for a second year with a two-way contract. He's seen minor action in four games thus far and picks up fourth quarter minutes each time the Spurs pull away early.

Today David Jones Garcia turns 25, the median age of the squad. His star still on the rise, he's continued to find opportunity and make the most of any situation he faces.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.
