#2868. Giants get timeline on Greg Newsome II injury with pressure now on Paulson Adebo

Greg Newsome II is going to miss more than just his revenge game.

Newsome is expected to miss at least the next four games and could be pressed to return before the end of the regular season after a high ankle sprain that requires tightrope surgery, The Post confirmed.

The Giants have seven games in seven weeks remaining. The high end of his timeline is six weeks on the sideline.

Newsome has not yet been placed on injured reserve, which would sideline him for at least four games and create a roster spot needed to elevate practice-squad contributor defensive lineman Duane Smoot.

The Giants have now lost four defensive starters for long periods of time, including season-ending injuries to edge Brian Burns, linebacker Tremaine Edmunds and defensive lineman Chauncey Golston.

It makes Newsome's recent decision to sign a three-year, $45.75 million contract extension rather than play out the rest of his walk year look wise. Had Newsome finished the season injured or playing at a lesser level through pain and then entered free agency, he might have been asked to accept another prove-it deal.

Without Newsome, the Giants will turn to benched former starter Paulson Adebo (four passes defended and an interception in place of Newsome against the Jaguars) to start next to Deonte Banks, who is having the best year of his career as he nears free agency. It's a toss-up whether Banks or Newsome would be considered the Giants' No. 1 cornerback as both have had shutdown moments this season.

New York Giants cornerback Greg Newsome II (20) reacts on the field during a game against the Arizona Cardinals in East Rutherford, N.J., Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. Bill Kostroun for NY Post

New York Giants wide receiver Malachi Fields (88) and cornerback Paulson Adebo (21) walk off the field after a game at MetLife Stadium in Brooklyn, N.Y., Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Corey Sipkin for NY Post

Second-round pick Colton Hood, who has had a quiet rookie season, is first off the bench to play on the perimeter.

Newsome's surgery is today, according to The Athletic.

#2867. Rebounding may be Dyson Daniels’ best skill after his defense

Dyson Daniels' defense has become his calling card, but his rebounding is making a strong case as his second-best skill.

Sunday's 107–97 home victory over the Detroit Pistons offered another example. The Hawks earned their fourth consecutive win with contributions throughout the roster, but Daniels helped shape the game despite scoring just five points.

He finished with 14 rebounds, eight assists, five steals and two blocks. His rebounds were split evenly between the offensive and defensive glass, giving Atlanta seven additional opportunities while helping end Detroit possessions at the other end.

That balance explains why his rebounding deserves its own recognition. Daniels does more than collect available defensive boards. He actively extends possessions, giving teammates another chance to score when the initial shot does not fall.

For an offense working through inconsistent stretches, those extra opportunities matter. An offensive rebound can turn an empty possession into a putback, a kickout three or another chance to attack an unsettled defense. Daniels can contribute to that process without needing a play called for him.

Head coach Quin Snyder recognizes how unusual that production is from a guard.

"It's been pretty unusual what [Dyson] has been able to do to rebound the ball," Snyder said.

Daniels' anticipation translates naturally from defending to pursuing rebounds. Reading a possession, recognizing where the ball could go and reacting before an opponent are valuable in both situations. His willingness to compete in traffic adds another element to that awareness.

His defensive rebounds also connect directly to Atlanta's preferred pace. When Daniels secures the ball himself, he can initiate the next possession without waiting for an outlet pass. That gives the Hawks an opportunity to advance quickly and find advantages before the opposing defense gets organized.

His eight assists against Detroit illustrated the broader value of having another player capable of gathering the ball and creating for teammates. Rebounding and playmaking can work together, helping Atlanta move from a defensive stop into its offense.

There is a reasonable argument for placing his passing alongside his rebounding when evaluating his strongest skills. However, the Detroit performance showed how controlling possessions can influence a game even when his scoring remains limited.

Daniels' shooting still matters to Atlanta's long-term offensive ceiling. His rebounding does not erase that area for improvement, but it gives him another dependable way to help when shots are not falling.

The Hawks already rely on Daniels to disrupt opponents. His work on the glass helps ensure those defensive efforts produce completed stops while creating second chances offensively.

That is what makes his rebounding so valuable. It strengthens both ends of the floor and reinforces why his impact reaches well beyond his point total.

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 â 2 vote:

The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
